Möbius sieve, and Mertens' function
vector<int> mobius(int n){
    vector<int> mu(n+1, 1); vector<bool> comp(n+1, false);
    vector<int> primes;
    for (int i = 2; i <= n; i++){
        if (!comp[i]) { primes.push_back(i); mu[i] = -1; }
        for (int p : primes){
            if ((long long)p*i > n) break;
            comp[p*i] = true;
            if (i % p == 0) { mu[p*i] = 0; break; }   // p² divides p*i
            mu[p*i] = -mu[i];
        }
    }
    return mu;
}
// Mertens: M(n) = Σ_{k≤n} μ(k).  Grows like O(√n) empirically;
// the Mertens conjecture |M(n)| < √n is FALSE (disproved 1985).
Interview angle

"Count pairs with gcd 1" and "count subsets whose gcd is 1" are the two standard Möbius questions. The reframing to say aloud: counting things divisible by d is trivial; the Möbius sum converts trivial counts into exact-gcd counts, and it is inclusion–exclusion over the primes.

Problem set — 14 problemstheory & programming
  1. Theory

    Prove ∑_{d|n} μ(d) = [n=1].

    Solution

    For n = 1 the only divisor is 1 and μ(1) = 1. For n > 1 with distinct primes p₁,…,pₖ, divisors with a squared factor contribute 0, so only the 2ᵏ squarefree divisors matter. A squarefree divisor is a subset S of the primes, contributing (-1)^{|S|}. Grouping by size,

    ∑_{j=0}^{k} C(k,j)(-1)₌ = (1 + (-1))ᵏ = 0. ∎

    This is exactly the inclusion–exclusion cancellation identity of Chapter 4 problem 2, and it is the reason both techniques produce the same alternating signs.

  2. Theory

    Prove the Möbius inversion formula.

    Solution

    Assume g(n) = ∑_{d|n} f(d). Then

    ∑_{d|n} μ(d)g(n/d) = ∑_{d|n} μ(d)∑_{e | (n/d)} f(e) = ∑_{e|n} f(e) ∑_{d | (n/e)} μ(d)

    (swapping the order: the pairs (d,e) with de | n are the same set either way). The inner sum is [n/e = 1], which is 1 only when e = n. So the whole thing is f(n). ∎

    Structurally: g = f * 1 and μ * 1 = ε, so g * μ = f * 1 * μ = f * ε = f. The theorem is just associativity plus the fact that μ inverts 1.

  3. Theory

    Derive φ(n) = ∑_{d|n} μ(d)n/d from ∑_{d|n}φ(d) = n.

    Solution

    The hypothesis says id = φ * 1. Inverting, φ = id * μ, i.e.

    φ(n) = ∑_{d|n} μ(d) · (n)/(d) = n∑_{d|n}(μ(d))/(d) = n∏_{p|n}(1 - \frac1p),

    the last step because the sum is multiplicative and at a prime power only d = 1, p contribute. ∎

    So the familiar product formula for the totient is a Möbius inversion in disguise — and this derivation generalises: any multiplicative function defined by a divisor sum has a product formula obtained the same way.

  4. Theory

    Count the number of pairs (i,j) with 1 ≤ i,j ≤ n and gcd(i,j) = k.

    Solution

    gcd(i,j)=k iff i = ki', j = kj' with gcd(i',j')=1 and i',j' ≤ ⌊ n/k⌋. So the answer is the coprime-pair count for m = ⌊ n/k ⌋:

    ∑_{d=1}^{m} μ(d)⌊ m/d⌋².

    Sanity check by summing over all k: ∑_k #{gcd = k} = n², which is the statement that every pair has some gcd. ✓

    Asymptotically the coprime count is (6)/(π²)m² + O(mlog m), so the density of pairs with gcd exactly k is (6)/(π²k²) — and those densities sum to (6)/(π²)·(π²)/(6) = 1 ✓, a satisfying consistency check.

  5. Theory

    Prove that the probability two random integers are coprime is 6/π².

    Solution

    The probability both are divisible by d is 1/d². By Möbius inversion the probability their gcd is exactly 1 is ∑_{d\ge1} μ(d)/d².

    Now ∑_d μ(d)/d^s = 1/ζ(s), because ζ(s)∑_dμ(d)d^{-s} = ∑_n n^{-s}∑_{d|n}μ(d) = ∑_n n^{-s}[n=1] = 1. With s = 2 and ζ(2) = π²/6, the answer is 6/π² ≈ 0.6079. ∎

    An independent heuristic gives the same thing: ∏_p (1 - 1/p²) = 1/ζ(2) by the Euler product, i.e. "for each prime, they are not both divisible by it, and the events are independent". That the two derivations agree is the Euler product formula.

  6. Theory

    Count squarefree numbers up to n.

    Solution

    By inclusion–exclusion over squares of primes: subtract multiples of 4, of 9, of 25, add back multiples of 36, and so on. In Möbius form:

    Q(n) = ∑_{d=1}^{√n} μ(d)⌊ n/d²⌋.

    Only d ≤ √n contributes, so this is O(√n) after a μ sieve to √n. Asymptotically Q(n) ~ n/ζ(2) = 6n/π² ≈ 0.6079n — the same constant, and for the same reason: "squarefree" and "coprime to a random number" are both "avoid every p²".

    At n = 10¹⁸ this is a million terms — instant, where enumerating and testing would be impossible.

  7. Theory

    State the general Möbius function of a poset and specialise it to the subset lattice.

    Solution

    For a locally finite poset P, define μ(x,x) = 1 and, recursively, μ(x,y) = -∑_{x ≤ z < y} μ(x,z) for x < y. Then

    g(y) = ∑_{x ≤ y} f(x) \iff f(y) = ∑_{x≤ y} μ(x,y)g(x).

    • Divisor lattice (x ≤ y iff x|y): μ(x,y) = μ(y/x) — the classical case.
    • Subset lattice (S ⊆ T): μ(S,T) = (-1)^{|T|-|S|} — ordinary inclusion–exclusion.
    • Chain (i ≤ j in ℤ): μ(i,j) = 1, -1, 0 for j-i = 0,1,\ge2 — finite differences.

    So inclusion–exclusion, Möbius inversion and the difference operator are one theorem in three lattices. That unification is the point of the general definition.

  8. Program

    Sieve μ(i) for i ≤ 10⁷ and verify ∑_{d|n}μ(d) = [n=1] for all n ≤ 10⁵.

    Solution
    def mobius_sieve(n):
    mu = [1]*(n+1); primes = []; comp = bytearray(n+1)
    for i in range(2, n+1):
        if not comp[i]: primes.append(i); mu[i] = -1
        for p in primes:
            if p*i > n: break
            comp[p*i] = 1
            if i % p == 0: mu[p*i] = 0; break
            mu[p*i] = -mu[i]
    return mu

mu = mobius_sieve(10**5)
for n in range(1, 10**5+1):
    s = sum(mu[d] for d in range(1, n+1) if n % d == 0)
    assert s == (1 if n == 1 else 0), n

    The if i % p == 0: mu[p*i] = 0; break line is where the squarefree condition enters: if p already divides i, then p² | pi, so μ(pi) = 0, and the break maintains the linear-sieve invariant that each composite is written once by its smallest prime.

    Verifying the defining identity directly is a strong test: it exercises every branch of the sieve and would catch a sign error immediately, which a spot check of a few values might not.

  9. Program

    Count pairs (i,j), 1 ≤ i < j ≤ n, with gcd(i,j)=1, for n ≤ 10⁷, two ways.

    Solution
    # (a) Möbius: O(n)
def coprime_pairs_mu(n):
    mu = mobius_sieve(n)
    return sum(mu[d] * (n//d) * (n//d - 1) // 2 for d in range(1, n+1))

# (b) Totient sum: O(n), often simpler
# pairs with i < j and gcd=1  =  Σ_{j=2..n} φ(j)
def coprime_pairs_phi(n):
    phi = phi_sieve(n)
    return sum(phi[j] for j in range(2, n+1))

    Both are O(n) and must agree. The second is the cleaner derivation: for each j, the valid i are precisely those in [1, j-1] coprime to j, of which there are φ(j).

    Asymptotically both give (3)/(π²)n² + O(n log n) — half the ordered-pair count. Having two independent computations that agree to the last digit is the best correctness check available for this kind of code.

  10. Program

    Compute ∑_{i=1}^{n}∑_{j=1}^{m}gcd(i,j) for n,m ≤ 10⁷.

    Solution
    def gcd_sum_2d(n, m):
    # Σ gcd(i,j) = Σ_d d · #{(i,j): gcd = d}
    #            = Σ_d d · Σ_e μ(e) ⌊n/(de)⌋⌊m/(de)⌋
    #  substitute k = de:  = Σ_k ⌊n/k⌋⌊m/k⌋ · (Σ_{d|k} d·μ(k/d))
    #  and the inner sum is exactly φ(k).
    phi = phi_sieve(min(n, m))
    return sum(phi[k] * (n//k) * (m//k) for k in range(1, min(n,m)+1))

    The derivation collapses a double Möbius sum into a single sum against φ, because id * μ = φ — the identity from problem 3, used in the forward direction. O(n) after the sieve.

    For n, m ≤ 10¹², replace the linear sum with divisor blocks over ⌊ n/k⌋ and a memoised prefix-φ function (Chapter 19 problem 14), giving O(n^{2/3}). This is the standard shape of a hard number-theory contest problem: a Möbius derivation to collapse the sum, then divisor blocks to evaluate it.

  11. Program

    Count squarefree integers in [1, n] for n ≤ 10¹⁸.

    Solution
    import math
def squarefree_count(n):
    r = math.isqrt(n)
    mu = mobius_sieve(r)
    return sum(mu[d] * (n // (d*d)) for d in range(1, r+1))

    O(√n) = 10⁹ at n = 10¹⁸ — a few seconds, and the μ sieve to 10⁹ needs 1 GB as a byte array. Reduce memory by processing in segments, or accept n ≤ 10¹⁴ with a 10⁷ sieve.

    Cross-check against the asymptotic 6n/π²: at n = 10¹⁸ the formula predicts 607{,}927{,}101{,}854{,}026{,}628 and the exact count differs by about O(√n) = 10⁹ — a relative error of 10^{-9}, which is exactly the size of the known error term.

  12. Program

    Given an array of n ≤ 10⁵ values up to 10⁶, count subsets whose gcd is exactly 1.

    Solution
    MOD = 10**9 + 7
MAX = 10**6 + 1
cnt = [0]*MAX
for v in a: cnt[v] += 1
mult = [0]*MAX
for d in range(1, MAX):
    for m in range(d, MAX, d): mult[d] += cnt[m]     # how many are divisible by d
mu = mobius_sieve(MAX-1)
ans = 0
for d in range(1, MAX):
    if mu[d]:
        ans = (ans + mu[d] * (pow(2, mult[d], MOD) - 1)) % MOD
print(ans % MOD)

    F(d) = 2^{mult[d]} - 1 counts the non-empty subsets whose gcd is a multiple of d — easy, because it only depends on how many array elements d divides. Möbius then extracts "gcd exactly 1".

    Cost: O(A log A) for the multiple counts plus O(A log MOD) for the powers — about 3×10⁷ operations. Precomputing all powers of 2 up to n turns the second term into O(A).

  13. Program

    Compute the Mertens function M(n) = ∑_{k≤ n}μ(k) for n ≤ 10¹² and investigate its growth.

    Solution
    from functools import lru_cache
SMALL = 10**7
mu = mobius_sieve(SMALL)
pre = [0]*(SMALL+1)
for i in range(1, SMALL+1): pre[i] = pre[i-1] + mu[i]

@lru_cache(None)
def M(n):
    if n <= SMALL: return pre[n]
    r, i = 1, 2                        # from Σ_{k≤n} M(n//k) = 1
    while i <= n:
        q = n//i; j = n//q
        r -= (j - i + 1) * M(q)
        i = j + 1
    return r

    The recurrence comes from ∑_{d|m}μ(d) = [m=1] summed over m ≤ n: ∑_{k=1}^{n} M(⌊ n/k⌋) = 1. Complexity O(n^{2/3}) with the cutoff tuned.

    Growth: M(n) oscillates around 0 with magnitude roughly n^{1/2}. Mertens conjectured |M(n)| < √n; Odlyzko and te Riele disproved it in 1985, though no explicit counterexample is known (the smallest is believed to exceed 10^{16}). Had it been true it would have implied the Riemann hypothesis — RH is equivalent to M(n) = O(n^{1/2+ε}), which remains open.

  14. Program

    Implement a general "count with exact gcd" helper: given F(d) as a callable, return f(1) = ∑_d μ(d)F(d), and apply it to three different problems.

    Solution
    def exact_gcd_one(F, limit, mu=None):
    """F(d) counts configurations where d divides everything relevant."""
    if mu is None: mu = mobius_sieve(limit)
    return sum(mu[d] * F(d) for d in range(1, limit+1) if mu[d])

# 1. coprime pairs in [1,n]²
exact_gcd_one(lambda d: (n//d)**2, n)
# 2. non-empty subsets of an array with gcd 1
exact_gcd_one(lambda d: pow(2, mult[d], MOD) - 1, MAX-1)
# 3. lattice points visible from the origin in an n×n grid
exact_gcd_one(lambda d: (n//d)**2, n)      # same as (1): visible ⟺ gcd=1

    Factoring out the pattern makes it obvious that these are the same problem with different F — which is the real content of this chapter. Once you can write down "how many configurations have d dividing everything", the Möbius sum is mechanical.

    The third example is a nice one to know: a lattice point (x,y) is visible from the origin (no other lattice point on the segment) exactly when gcd(x,y)=1, so the visible fraction of the grid is 6/π² — the same constant yet again.

IV. Combinatorics
Chapter 26

The counting principles and bijective proof

Almost all of combinatorics is four rules applied carefully. The hard part is never the arithmetic; it is being certain you counted each object exactly once, and the discipline that guarantees it is exhibiting a bijection.

Four principles, each trivial and each the source of a characteristic error.

SUM disjoint choices add |A ∪ B| = |A| + |B| if A ∩ B = ∅ PRODUCT independent choices multiply |A × B| = |A| · |B| BIJECTION a bijection preserves size |A| = |B| if a bijection exists DIVISION k-to-1 map divides |A| = |B| / k

Sum fails silently when the cases overlap — the repair is inclusion–exclusion (Chapter 30). Product fails when the second choice's count depends on the first; it is fine if the count is the same even though the options differ (choosing a second card from 51 works, whichever card was first). Division fails when the map is not uniformly k-to-1, which is the commonest subtle error in counting arrangements with symmetry.

Bijective proof

The strongest form of a counting argument is a bijection: instead of computing both sides, exhibit a reversible correspondence. It is more convincing, it usually generalises, and it often is an algorithm.

Three bijections worth carrying
SUBSETS ↔ BINARY STRINGS
  S ⊆ {1..n}  ↔  the n-bit string with bit i set iff i ∈ S
  ⟹ |P(A)| = 2ⁿ, and enumeration by bitmask is the bijection made code.

COMPOSITIONS ↔ STARS AND BARS
  x₁+...+x_k = n with xᵢ ≥ 0  ↔  arrangements of n stars and k−1 bars
  ⟹ C(n+k−1, k−1) solutions.

LATTICE PATHS ↔ SEQUENCES OF MOVES
  monotone paths (0,0)→(m,n)  ↔  strings with m R's and n U's
  ⟹ C(m+n, m) paths.

Stars and bars deserves emphasis because it converts a huge class of problems into one binomial. To place n indistinguishable items into k distinguishable boxes, write n stars and k-1 bars in a row; the bars cut the stars into k groups. Every arrangement gives a solution and vice versa, so the count is C(n+k-1, k-1). With the constraint x_i ≥ 1, first give each box one item and count the rest: C(n-1, k-1).

Principle

Before counting, answer two questions explicitly: are the objects distinguishable? and does order matter? The four combinations give four different formulas, and nearly every wrong answer in combinatorics comes from answering one of them wrong rather than from an arithmetic slip.

The twelvefold way

Placing n balls into k boxes, under the four distinguishability choices and three constraints, gives twelve counts — and essentially every elementary counting problem is one cell of this table.

Balls / Boxesanyinjective (≤1 each)surjective (≥1 each)
distinct / distinctkⁿk^{\underline{n}}k!S(n,k)
identical / distinctC(n+k-1,n)C(k,n)C(n-1,k-1)
distinct / identical∑_{j≤ k} S(n,j)[n≤ k]S(n,k)
identical / identicalp_k(n)[n≤ k]p(n,k)

Here k^{\underline{n}} = k(k-1)···(k-n+1) is the falling factorial, S(n,k) is a Stirling number of the second kind (Chapter 33), and p(n,k) counts partitions of n into exactly k parts.

Interview angle

"How many ways to…" is answered by locating the cell: distinguishable? ordered? repetition allowed? Saying "the balls are distinct and the boxes are distinct with no constraint, so kⁿ" shows a model rather than a recalled formula, and it survives the follow-up where one constraint changes.

Problem set — 15 problemstheory & programming
  1. Theory

    How many 5-card poker hands are there? How many contain exactly one pair?

    Solution

    Total: C(52,5) = 2{,}598{,}960.

    Exactly one pair: choose the pair's rank (13), choose 2 of its 4 suits (C(4,2)=6), choose 3 distinct other ranks (C(12,3)=220), and a suit for each (4³=64):

    13 × 6 × 220 × 64 = 1{,}098{,}240, a probability of about 42.3%.

    The trap is choosing the three kickers as C(12,1)C(11,1)C(10,1), which counts each set of kickers 3! = 6 times — the division principle applied wrongly by forgetting to divide. Choosing the set with C(12,3) avoids it entirely.

  2. Theory

    Prove stars and bars: the number of non-negative integer solutions to x₁+···+x_k = n is C(n+k-1, k-1).

    Solution

    Map each solution to a string of n stars and k-1 bars: write x₁ stars, a bar, x₂ stars, a bar, …, x_k stars.

    This is injective: different solutions give different star counts between bars. It is surjective: any arrangement of n stars and k-1 bars decodes to a solution by reading off the gaps (possibly empty). So it is a bijection, and the number of arrangements is the number of ways to choose which k-1 of the n+k-1 positions hold bars: C(n+k-1,k-1). ∎

    For x_i ≥ 1, substitute y_i = x_i - 1 ≥ 0 summing to n-k, giving C(n-1,k-1). For x_i ≥ c_i, subtract the lower bounds first — the same substitution handles every lower-bound variant.

  3. Theory

    How many ways to seat n people around a circular table, where rotations are considered the same? What if reflections are also identified?

    Solution

    Linear arrangements: n!. Each circular arrangement corresponds to exactly n linear ones (the n rotations), so by the division principle the count is n!/n = (n-1)!.

    With reflections identified, each circular arrangement is counted twice more, giving (n-1)!/2 for n ≥ 3.

    The n ≥ 3 caveat matters: for n = 1, 2 a reflection fixes the arrangement, so the map is not uniformly 2-to-1 and the division principle does not apply. This is exactly the situation Burnside's lemma (Chapter 34) handles correctly in general — division is the special case where no arrangement is fixed by a non-identity symmetry.

  4. Theory

    Count the anagrams of MISSISSIPPI, and state the general multinomial formula.

    Solution

    11 letters: M×1, I×4, S×4, P×2. Treating them as distinct gives 11! arrangements, but each genuine anagram arises 1!4!4!2! times (permuting identical letters among themselves).

    (11!)/(1!4!4!2!) = \frac{39{,}916{,}800}{1152} = 34{,}650.

    General multinomial coefficient: with n = n₁+···+n_k objects of k types,

    C(n,n₁,…,n_k) = (n!)/(n₁!··· n_k!),

    which also counts the ways to split n distinct objects into labelled groups of the given sizes — the same number, by a bijection between arrangements and assignments of positions to types.

  5. Theory

    Give a bijective proof that C(n,k) = C(n,n-k) and that ∑_k C(n,k) = 2ⁿ.

    Solution

    Symmetry: the map S ↦ {1..n}\setminus S sends k-subsets to (n-k)-subsets, and it is its own inverse — hence a bijection. ∎ No algebra needed, and the identity becomes obvious rather than verified.

    Row sum: both sides count subsets of an n-set. The left counts them by size; the right counts them by the bit-string bijection. ∎

    This is the value of bijective proof: (n!)/(k!(n-k)!) = (n!)/((n-k)!k!) is a true but uninformative verification, whereas "choosing what to include is the same as choosing what to exclude" explains why and immediately suggests generalisations.

  6. Theory

    How many monotone lattice paths from (0,0) to (m,n) avoid the point (a,b)?

    Solution

    Total paths: C(m+n, m). Paths through (a,b): C(a+b,a) · C(m-a+n-b, m-a) — reach it, then continue, by the product principle (the two halves are independent given the intermediate point).

    Answer: C(m+n,m) - C(a+b,a)C(m+n-a-b, m-a).

    Avoiding several points requires inclusion–exclusion, and if the forbidden points form a staircase the alternating sum becomes the Lindström–Gessel–Viennot determinant. Avoiding an entire diagonal is the reflection principle, which produces the Catalan numbers of Chapter 32.

  7. Theory

    Count the binary strings of length n containing no two consecutive 1s, and count those with no three consecutive 1s.

    Solution

    No two consecutive 1s: condition on the last character. Ending in 0 leaves any valid string of length n-1; ending in 1 forces a 0 before it, leaving any valid string of length n-2. So a_n = a_{n-1}+a_{n-2} with a₀=1, a₁=2 — the Fibonacci numbers, a_n = F_{n+2}.

    No three consecutive: condition on the length of the trailing run of 1s (0, 1 or 2), giving a_n = a_{n-1}+a_{n-2}+a_{n-3} — tribonacci, with a₀=1,a₁=2,a₂=4.

    The general pattern: forbidding a run of k gives a k-term linear recurrence. There is also a direct binomial count — choosing j non-adjacent 1s among n positions is C(n-j+1, j), so F_{n+2} = ∑_j C(n-j+1,j), the "shallow diagonal" identity of Pascal's triangle.

  8. Theory

    In how many ways can 8 rooks be placed on a chessboard so that none attacks another? Generalise to n × n with k rooks.

    Solution

    Non-attacking means one rook per row and one per column. Assign to each row a distinct column: that is a permutation of 8 elements, so 8! = 40{,}320.

    With k rooks on n× n: choose k rows (C(n,k)), choose k columns (C(n,k)), and match them (k!):

    C(n,k)² k!.

    Check k=n: 1 · 1 · n! = n! ✓. The rook-polynomial machinery generalises this to boards with forbidden squares, which is exactly the setting where derangements (Chapter 31) arise — a derangement is a non-attacking rook placement avoiding the main diagonal.

  9. Program

    Write generators for permutations, combinations and subsets in lexicographic order, without recursion, and verify the counts.

    Solution
    # next permutation in lex order (the std::next_permutation algorithm)
def next_perm(a):
    i = len(a) - 2
    while i >= 0 and a[i] >= a[i+1]: i -= 1     # find the rightmost ascent
    if i < 0: return False
    j = len(a) - 1
    while a[j] <= a[i]: j -= 1                  # rightmost element > a[i]
    a[i], a[j] = a[j], a[i]
    a[i+1:] = reversed(a[i+1:])                 # the suffix was descending
    return True

# next k-combination of range(n)
def next_comb(c, n, k):
    i = k - 1
    while i >= 0 and c[i] == n - k + i: i -= 1
    if i < 0: return False
    c[i] += 1
    for j in range(i+1, k): c[j] = c[j-1] + 1
    return True

    Both are O(1) amortised per step (the suffix reversal in next_perm averages a constant number of swaps, by the same geometric argument as Chapter 12).

    Verify by counting: n! permutations, C(n,k) combinations, 2ⁿ subsets — and additionally assert the output is strictly increasing lexicographically, which catches the classic bug of using > instead of >= in the ascent search when duplicates are present.

  10. Program

    Count solutions to x₁+···+x_k = n with per-variable upper bounds x_i ≤ u_i, for k ≤ 20 and n ≤ 10⁵.

    Solution
    from math import comb
def bounded_solutions(n, us):
    k = len(us); total = 0
    for mask in range(1 << k):                 # inclusion–exclusion over violations
        s, bits = n, 0
        for i in range(k):
            if mask >> i & 1: s -= us[i] + 1; bits += 1
        if s < 0: continue
        total += (-1)**bits * comb(s + k - 1, k - 1)
    return total

    Why: forcing x_i ≥ u_i+1 is a substitution reducing n by u_i+1, so the count of solutions violating a given set of bounds is another stars-and-bars value. Inclusion–exclusion over which bounds are violated gives the alternating sum.

    Cost O(2ᵏ k) — fine to k = 20. For larger k with small bounds, use a DP over the sum instead: O(k n). Choosing between the two is a matter of which parameter is small, and both are worth having.

  11. Program

    Implement ranking and unranking for k-subsets: given a subset return its index in lexicographic order, and vice versa.

    Solution
    from math import comb
def rank_comb(c, n):                 # c sorted ascending, elements in [0,n)
    k = len(c); r = 0; prev = -1
    for i, v in enumerate(c):
        for x in range(prev+1, v):
            r += comb(n - x - 1, k - i - 1)     # subsets starting with x here
        prev = v
    return r

def unrank_comb(r, n, k):
    c = []; x = 0
    for i in range(k):
        while True:
            cnt = comb(n - x - 1, k - i - 1)
            if r < cnt: break
            r -= cnt; x += 1
        c.append(x); x += 1
    return c

    O(nk) as written, reducible to O(k log n) with binary search over the counts.

    Ranking is what lets you sample a uniformly random k-subset (unrank a random index in [0, C(n,k))), store a subset compactly, or distribute an enumeration across machines by index range. The same technique works for permutations via the factorial number system, which is Chapter 27.

  12. Program

    Count the monotone lattice paths from (0,0) to (n,n) that avoid a given set of blocked cells, for n ≤ 10⁵ and up to 20 blocked cells.

    Solution
    MOD = 10**9+7
def paths(a, b, c, d):               # (a,b) → (c,d)
    if c < a or d < b: return 0
    return C(c-a + d-b, c-a)

def count_avoiding(n, blocked):
    pts = sorted(blocked) + [(n, n)]
    m = len(pts)
    f = [0]*m                        # f[i] = paths to pts[i] hitting no earlier block
    for i, (x, y) in enumerate(pts):
        f[i] = paths(0, 0, x, y)
        for j in range(i):
            px, py = pts[j]
            if px <= x and py <= y:
                f[i] -= f[j] * paths(px, py, x, y) % MOD
        f[i] %= MOD
    return f[-1]

    O(m²) after O(n) factorial precomputation. The recurrence classifies each path by the first blocked cell it hits, which makes the cases disjoint — the sum principle applied correctly, and the reason sorting the blocked cells matters.

    This is the standard technique for "grid paths with few obstacles" and it scales to n = 10⁵ because the grid is never materialised; only the obstacle interactions are.

  13. Program

    Verify the twelvefold way computationally for small n and k by brute-force enumeration.

    Solution
    from itertools import product
from collections import Counter
def brute(n, k, balls_distinct, boxes_distinct, constraint):
    seen = set()
    for assign in product(range(k), repeat=n):        # ball i → box assign[i]
        cnt = Counter(assign)
        if constraint == 'inj' and any(v > 1 for v in cnt.values()): continue
        if constraint == 'sur' and len(cnt) < k: continue
        if balls_distinct and boxes_distinct: key = assign
        elif balls_distinct:  key = frozenset(map(frozenset,
              ([i for i in range(n) if assign[i]==b] for b in range(k)))) 
        elif boxes_distinct:  key = tuple(cnt[b] for b in range(k))
        else:                 key = tuple(sorted(cnt[b] for b in range(k)))
        seen.add(key)
    return len(seen)

    Run for n, k ≤ 5 and compare against the twelve formulas. This is the fastest way to settle which cell a problem belongs to when the wording is ambiguous — and it repeatedly surprises: the "identical balls, identical boxes" cells are partition counts with no closed form, which the brute force makes tangible.

    Note the key construction is the whole content: it encodes exactly what "indistinguishable" means by quotienting the assignment by the relevant symmetry group. Getting that key right is getting the combinatorics right.

  14. Program

    Given a multiset of letters, generate all distinct anagrams in lexicographic order without generating duplicates.

    Solution
    def anagrams(s):
    a = sorted(s)
    out = [''.join(a)]
    while next_perm(a):              # next_perm handles duplicates correctly
        out.append(''.join(a))
    return out

# recursive alternative with explicit dedup at each level:
def rec(counts, cur, n, out):
    if len(cur) == n: out.append(''.join(cur)); return
    for ch in sorted(counts):
        if counts[ch]:
            counts[ch] -= 1; cur.append(ch)
            rec(counts, cur, n, out)
            cur.pop(); counts[ch] += 1

    next_perm already produces each distinct arrangement exactly once for a multiset — the >= in the ascent search is precisely what skips duplicates. That is why it is preferable to generating all n! and deduplicating, which for MISSISSIPPI would generate 39.9 million strings to keep 34,650.

    Both run in O(1) amortised per output, so the total cost is proportional to the answer size — optimal.

  15. Program

    Write a uniform random sampler for each of: a k-subset of n, a permutation, a composition of n into k parts, and verify uniformity statistically.

    Solution
    import random
def rand_perm(n):                     # Fisher–Yates
    a = list(range(n))
    for i in range(n-1, 0, -1):
        j = random.randint(0, i)      # INCLUSIVE of i — the classic bug
        a[i], a[j] = a[j], a[i]
    return a

def rand_subset(n, k):                # Floyd's algorithm, O(k)
    s = set()
    for j in range(n-k, n):
        t = random.randrange(j+1)
        s.add(t if t not in s else j)
    return sorted(s)

def rand_composition(n, k):           # via stars and bars
    bars = sorted(random.sample(range(n+k-1), k-1))
    prev, out = -1, []
    for b in bars + [n+k-1]:
        out.append(b - prev - 1); prev = b
    return out

    Fisher–Yates must pick j ∈ [0,i] inclusive; using [0,i) gives the "Sattolo" algorithm, which produces only cyclic permutations — uniform over a set of size (n-1)!, not n!. The bug is invisible without a statistical test.

    Testing uniformity: for n = 4, sample 10⁶ permutations and chi-square the 24 counts against 10⁶/24. The Sattolo variant fails immediately (6 of the 24 get everything). This is the right way to test any random combinatorial generator — the small case where exhaustive counting is possible.

Chapter 27

Permutations, combinations and multisets

Four formulas cover ordered/unordered selection with and without repetition, and a permutation has structure beyond its count - cycles, inversions and a factorial number system that make it rankable, composable and analysable.

ORDER MATTERS ORDER DOES NOT no repetition n!/(n−k)! = nᵏ falling C(n,k) = n!/(k!(n−k)!) repetition allowed nᵏ C(n+k−1, k)

Those four are the whole of elementary selection. The bottom-right is stars and bars: choosing k items from n types with repetition is the same as distributing k identical items into n boxes.

Cycle structure

Every permutation decomposes uniquely into disjoint cycles. This is the single most useful structural fact about permutations, and it turns many questions into arithmetic on cycle lengths:

order of σ = lcm of cycle lengths parity of σ = (−1)^{n − #cycles} (a k-cycle is k−1 transpositions) σⁿ shift each cycle by n mod its length (Ch. 21) number of permutations of n with exactly k cycles = |s(n,k)| (Stirling 1st kind) expected number of cycles in a random permutation = H_n ≈ ln n expected length of the cycle containing element 1 = (n+1)/2

That last fact is startling and useful: in a random permutation, the cycle through any fixed element is uniformly distributed over lengths 1..n. It is the basis of the famous "100 prisoners and 100 boxes" problem, where following cycles gives a success probability of about 31% instead of 2^{-100}.

Inversions and the factorial number system

An inversion is a pair i < j with σ(i) > σ(j). The number of inversions ranges from 0 to C(n,2), and the generating function is

Σ_σ q^{inv(σ)} = 1 · (1+q) · (1+q+q²) · ... · (1+q+...+q^{n−1}) = [n]_q!

because the Lehmer code c_i = #{j > i : σ(j) < σ(i)} is a bijection between permutations and sequences with 0 ≤ c_i ≤ n-i. That is the factorial number system, and it gives ranking and unranking directly.

Rank and unrank a permutation in O(n log n)
def perm_rank(p):
    n = len(p); bit = Fenwick(n)
    for i in range(n): bit.add(i, 1)
    r, f = 0, factorial(n-1)
    for i, v in enumerate(p):
        r += bit.query(v) * f          # how many unused values are smaller
        bit.add(v, -1)
        if n-i-1: f //= (n-i-1)
    return r

def perm_unrank(r, n):
    avail = list(range(n)); out = []
    for i in range(n):
        f = factorial(n-i-1)
        j, r = divmod(r, f)
        out.append(avail.pop(j))
    return out
Principle

Number of inversions = minimum number of adjacent transpositions to sort (Chapter 7) = the length of the permutation as a word in the simple reflections. So "sortedness" has an exact numerical measure, computable in O(nlog n), and it is what makes insertion sort Θ(n + inv).

Derangement-adjacent counts

Permutations with constraints are usually inclusion–exclusion (Chapter 30) or a determinant. Two to know:

  • Fixed points: the number of permutations of n with exactly k fixed points is C(n,k)D_{n-k} where D_m is the derangement count.
  • Involutions (σ² = id): I(n) = I(n-1) + (n-1)I(n-2) — element n is either fixed or swapped with one of the others.
Interview angle

"Find the next permutation" and "count inversions" are both standard, and the connection between them is worth stating: next-permutation walks the lexicographic order, inversions measure distance from sorted, and both come from the same Lehmer-code structure. Mentioning that std::next_permutation is O(1) amortised, not O(n), is a good detail.

Problem set — 14 problemstheory & programming
  1. Theory

    How many ways to arrange the letters of BOOKKEEPER? How many with all three E's together?

    Solution

    10 letters: B, O×2, K×2, E×3, P, R. Total (10!)/(2!2!3!) = \frac{3{,}628{,}800}{24} = 151{,}200.

    With the E's together, glue them into a single block: now 8 objects (B, O, O, K, K, [EEE], P, R) with O×2 and K×2 repeated:

    (8!)/(2!2!) = \frac{40{,}320}{4} = 10{,}080.

    The block does not get an internal factor because the E's are identical. If they were distinguishable you would multiply by 3! — the standard slip.

  2. Theory

    Prove that a permutation's parity is well defined, i.e. every decomposition into transpositions has the same parity.

    Solution

    Consider the polynomial Δ = ∏_{i<j}(x_i - x_j). A permutation σ acts by permuting the variables, sending Δ to ±Δ (each factor maps to another factor, up to sign). Define sgn(σ) as that sign.

    A single transposition (ab) negates Δ: the factor (x_a-x_b) flips sign, and the other affected factors pair up with matching sign changes. So sgn is a homomorphism sending every transposition to -1, and a product of k transpositions has sign (-1)ᵏ. Since sgn(σ) depends only on σ, all decompositions have the same parity. ∎

    Equivalently: each transposition changes the inversion count by an odd amount, so sgn(σ) = (-1)^{inv(σ)}. This is the invariant behind the 15-puzzle argument of Chapter 7.

  3. Theory

    What is the expected number of fixed points in a random permutation of n? The variance?

    Solution

    Let X_i = [σ(i)=i], so P(X_i=1) = 1/n. By linearity, E[X] = n · \frac1n = 1 — exactly 1, for every n.

    For the variance: E[X²] = ∑_i E[X_i] + ∑_{i≠ j} P(X_i=X_j=1) = 1 + n(n-1)(1)/(n(n-1)) = 2, so Var = 2 - 1 = 1.

    Mean 1, variance 1 — and in fact the number of fixed points converges in distribution to Poisson(1) as n→∞. So the probability of no fixed points tends to e^{-1} ≈ 0.368, which is the derangement result of Chapter 31 arriving from a different direction.

  4. Theory

    Show that the expected number of cycles in a random permutation of n is H_n.

    Solution

    Build the permutation by the "Chinese restaurant" process: place elements 1..n one at a time; element i either starts a new cycle or is inserted into an existing one. When adding element i there are i choices (join after any of the i-1 already placed, or start a new cycle), each equally likely, so a new cycle starts with probability 1/i.

    By linearity, E[#cycles] = ∑_{i=1}^{n} \frac1i = H_n ≈ ln n. ∎

    The process is the Feller coupling, and it also gives the variance H_n - H_n^{(2)} ≈ ln n because the indicators are independent. This is the same 1/i pattern as the record-counting problem of Chapter 11 — and indeed the number of cycles and the number of records are identically distributed, via the "fundamental bijection" that writes each cycle starting from its largest element.

  5. Theory

    Explain the 100-prisoners problem and why the cycle-following strategy succeeds with probability about 31%.

    Solution

    100 prisoners, 100 boxes containing a random permutation of their numbers; each may open 50 boxes and must find their own number; all must succeed.

    Strategy: prisoner i opens box i, then the box numbered by what he found, and so on — following the cycle containing i. He succeeds iff that cycle has length ≤ 50.

    So all succeed iff the permutation has no cycle longer than 50. The probability that a random permutation of 2m has a cycle longer than m is ∑_{k=m+1}^{2m} \frac1k = H_{2m} - H_m → ln 2. Hence success probability 1 - ln 2 ≈ 0.3069, and for n=100 exactly 31.18%.

    The reason a long cycle has probability 1/k: the number of permutations of n with a cycle of length k > n/2 is C(n,k)(k-1)!(n-k)! = n!/k, and such cycles are unique so the events are disjoint. Independent random guessing gives 2^{-100} — the strategy's power comes entirely from making the prisoners' outcomes maximally correlated.

  6. Theory

    Count the permutations of 1..n with exactly k inversions, and give the generating function.

    Solution

    By the Lehmer code bijection, a permutation corresponds to (c₁,…,c_n) with 0 ≤ c_i ≤ n-i and inv = ∑ c_i. So

    ∑_{σ} q^{inv(σ)} = ∏_{i=1}^{n}(1 + q + ··· + q^{i-1}) = ∏_{i=1}^{n}(1-q^i)/(1-q) = [n]_q!,

    the q-factorial. The count with exactly k inversions is the coefficient of qᵏ, the Mahonian number T(n,k), satisfying T(n,k) = ∑_{j=0}^{min(k,n-1)} T(n-1,k-j).

    Computationally: a DP over O(n · C(n,2)) states with prefix sums gives O(n³), or O(n²) per row with a sliding window. Setting q=1 recovers n! ✓.

  7. Theory

    How many permutations of n are involutions? Derive the recurrence and the asymptotic.

    Solution

    An involution has only fixed points and 2-cycles. Condition on element n: either it is fixed (leaving an involution of n-1) or it is paired with one of the n-1 others (leaving an involution of n-2):

    I(n) = I(n-1) + (n-1)I(n-2), with I(0)=I(1)=1.

    Values: 1, 1, 2, 4, 10, 26, 76, 232, … The explicit form is I(n) = ∑_k (n!)/(k!2ᵏ(n-2k)!) — choose k disjoint pairs.

    Asymptotically I(n) ~ (1)/(√2)((n)/(e))^{n/2}e^{√n}, i.e. roughly √{n!}. By the RSK correspondence, I(n) also equals the number of standard Young tableaux with n cells — a striking identity that a purely recursive derivation never suggests.

  8. Program

    Decompose a permutation into cycles, compute its order and parity, and apply it n times efficiently.

    Solution
    def cycles(p):
    n = len(p); seen = [False]*n; out = []
    for i in range(n):
        if seen[i]: continue
        c = []
        j = i
        while not seen[j]:
            seen[j] = True; c.append(j); j = p[j]
        out.append(c)
    return out

def order(p):
    from math import lcm
    o = 1
    for c in cycles(p): o = lcm(o, len(c))
    return o

def parity(p):
    return (len(p) - len(cycles(p))) % 2     # 0 = even, 1 = odd

def power(p, n):
    res = [0]*len(p)
    for c in cycles(p):
        L = len(c); s = n % L
        for i in range(L): res[c[i]] = c[(i+s) % L]
    return res

    All are O(n). The order can be astronomically large — Landau's function g(n), the maximum order of a permutation of n elements, is e^{(1+o(1))√{nln n}}, reaching 232,792,560 at n=100. So compute it with big integers or modulo something, and never by repeated application.

  9. Program

    Count inversions in O(nlog n) and additionally report, for each element, how many smaller elements lie to its right.

    Solution
    def count_smaller_right(a):
    order = {v: i for i, v in enumerate(sorted(set(a)))}
    m = len(order); bit = [0]*(m+1)
    res = [0]*len(a)
    for idx in range(len(a)-1, -1, -1):
        k = order[a[idx]]                    # count already-seen values < a[idx]
        i = k
        while i > 0: res[idx] += bit[i]; i -= i & -i
        i = k + 1
        while i <= m: bit[i] += 1; i += i & -i
    return res, sum(res)

    Sweeping right to left with a Fenwick tree gives both the per-element counts (the Lehmer code) and their total (the inversion count) in one pass, O(nlog n).

    The Lehmer code is exactly what perm_rank needs, so this function does double duty. It is also the answer to LeetCode's "count of smaller numbers after self", and the observation that the answer is the Lehmer code is what connects that exercise to the factorial number system.

  10. Program

    Implement rank and unrank for permutations of n ≤ 20 and verify they are inverse over all permutations of n = 8.

    Solution
    from math import factorial
def unrank(r, n):
    avail = list(range(n)); out = []
    for i in range(n):
        f = factorial(n - i - 1)
        j, r = divmod(r, f)
        out.append(avail.pop(j))
    return out

def rank(p):
    n = len(p); avail = list(range(n)); r = 0
    for i, v in enumerate(p):
        j = avail.index(v)                    # O(n); use a BIT for O(log n)
        r += j * factorial(n - i - 1)
        avail.pop(j)
    return r

from itertools import permutations
for i, p in enumerate(permutations(range(8))):
    assert rank(list(p)) == i and unrank(i, 8) == list(p)

    At n = 20, 20! ≈ 2.4×10^{18} still fits in a 64-bit integer — so a permutation of 20 elements can be stored as a single long long, which is occasionally exactly what a memoisation table needs.

    The exhaustive 8! = 40{,}320 check against itertools.permutations confirms both the bijection and that the ordering agrees with lexicographic — a two-line test that would catch any indexing error.

  11. Program

    Simulate the 100-prisoners problem and compare the cycle strategy to random guessing.

    Solution
    import random
def trial(n=100, limit=50):
    p = list(range(n)); random.shuffle(p)
    for start in range(n):
        cur, steps = start, 0
        while p[cur] != start:
            cur = p[cur]; steps += 1
            if steps >= limit: return False
    return True

wins = sum(trial() for _ in range(100000))
print(wins/100000)              # ≈ 0.3118

# equivalently, and far faster: check the longest cycle
def trial_fast(n=100, limit=50):
    p = list(range(n)); random.shuffle(p)
    return max(len(c) for c in cycles(p)) <= limit

    The simulation converges to 0.3118, matching 1 - (H_{100}-H_{50}) = 1 - ∑_{k=51}^{100}1/k. Random guessing gives 2^{-100} ≈ 10^{-30} — the difference is 30 orders of magnitude from a strategy that adds no information, only correlation.

    A worthwhile extension: vary the limit and plot the success probability. It stays near 1 until the limit drops below n/2, then falls off as 1 - ln(n/limit) — and it is provably optimal, which is the surprising part.

  12. Program

    Count permutations of n with exactly k inversions for n,k ≤ 10⁵ modulo 10⁹+7.

    Solution
    MOD = 10**9+7
def mahonian_row(n, K):
    dp = [0]*(K+1); dp[0] = 1
    for i in range(2, n+1):
        pre = [0]*(K+2)
        for j in range(K+1): pre[j+1] = (pre[j] + dp[j]) % MOD
        for j in range(K+1):
            lo = max(0, j - i + 1)
            dp[j] = (pre[j+1] - pre[lo]) % MOD     # sliding window of width i
    return dp

    The recurrence T(n,k) = ∑_{j=0}^{i-1} T(n-1,k-j) is a sliding-window sum, so prefix sums make each row O(K) and the whole table O(nK) — 10^{10} at the stated limits, too slow.

    For large n and k there is a closed form via the q-factorial and the pentagonal number theorem: T(n,k) = ∑_j (-1)₌ C(n + k - g_j - 1, n-1) summed over generalised pentagonal numbers g_j ≤ k, of which there are only O(√k). That gives O(√k) per query after factorial precomputation — the practical answer at these limits.

  13. Program

    Generate a uniformly random permutation with exactly k fixed points.

    Solution
    import random
def rand_with_k_fixed(n, k):
    pts = random.sample(range(n), k)          # which points are fixed
    rest = [i for i in range(n) if i not in set(pts)]
    d = random_derangement(len(rest))         # derange the remainder
    p = list(range(n))
    for idx, v in enumerate(rest): p[v] = rest[d[idx]]
    return p

def random_derangement(m):                    # rejection sampling
    while True:
        a = list(range(m)); random.shuffle(a)
        if all(a[i] != i for i in range(m)): return a

    Uniformity: every permutation with exactly k fixed points arises from exactly one (fixed-point set, derangement) pair, and both components are sampled uniformly — so the result is uniform over the C(n,k)D_{n-k} such permutations.

    Rejection sampling for the derangement accepts with probability D_m/m! → e^{-1} ≈ 0.368, so it needs about 2.7 attempts on average regardless of m — constant expected overhead, which is why the naive approach is perfectly good here. (A linear-time direct algorithm exists but is rarely worth the complexity.)

  14. Program

    Given a permutation as a product of cycles, compute the minimum number of transpositions to sort it, and produce them.

    Solution
    def sort_by_transpositions(p):
    n = len(p); p = p[:]; swaps = []
    for i in range(n):
        while p[i] != i:
            j = p[i]
            p[i], p[j] = p[j], p[i]           # send p[i] home
            swaps.append((i, j))
    return swaps        # length = n - (number of cycles)

    Minimality: each transposition changes the cycle count by exactly ±1 (it merges two cycles or splits one). The identity has n cycles; a permutation with c cycles therefore needs at least n-c transpositions, and the algorithm achieves exactly that — every swap places an element correctly and splits off a fixed point. ∎

    O(n) total, since each iteration of the inner loop fixes one element permanently. Note this is the minimum over arbitrary transpositions; restricting to adjacent transpositions gives the inversion count instead, which can be Θ(n²) — the two "sorting distances" are genuinely different measures.

Chapter 28

Binomial coefficients and Pascal identities

A dozen identities cover nearly every binomial manipulation you will need, and each has a combinatorial proof that is shorter and more memorable than the algebra. Learn the proofs, not the formulas.

C(n,k) = n! / (k!(n−k)!) = number of k-subsets of an n-set C(n,k) = C(n, n−k) symmetry C(n,k) = C(n−1,k−1) + C(n−1,k) Pascal Σ_k C(n,k) = 2ⁿ row sum Σ_k (−1)^k C(n,k) = 0 for n ≥ 1 alternating row sum Σ_k C(n,k)² = C(2n,n) Vandermonde special case Σ_{i} C(m,i)C(n,k−i) = C(m+n,k) Vandermonde convolution Σ_{i=k}^{n} C(i,k) = C(n+1,k+1) hockey stick k·C(n,k) = n·C(n−1,k−1) absorption Σ_k k·C(n,k) = n·2^{n−1} from absorption + row sum C(n,k) = (n/k)·C(n−1,k−1) the recurrence used to compute it (1+x)ⁿ = Σ_k C(n,k)xᵏ binomial theorem

The proofs worth knowing

Pascal. Classify k-subsets of {1..n} by whether they contain n. Those that do correspond to (k-1)-subsets of the rest; those that do not are k-subsets of the rest. Disjoint and exhaustive. ∎

Vandermonde. To choose k items from m+n objects split into two groups, choose i from the first and k-i from the second, and sum over i. ∎ Setting m=n=k and using symmetry gives ∑_k C(n,k)² = C(2n,n).

Hockey stick. Count (k+1)-subsets of {1..n+1} by their largest element: if the largest is i+1, the remaining k come from {1..i}. ∎

Absorption. Count pairs (a k-subset, a distinguished element of it) two ways: choose the subset then the element (C(n,k)· k), or choose the element then the rest (n · C(n-1,k-1)). ∎

Principle

Almost every binomial identity is double counting: find a set of objects that both sides count, in two different orders. If you cannot find one, try the generating function route — multiply out (1+x)^m(1+x)^n = (1+x)^{m+n} and compare coefficients, which proves Vandermonde in one line.

Divisibility and size

C(n,k) is an integer (not obvious from the formula! — see problems) p | C(p,k) for 0 < k < p the freshman's dream, Ch. 20 Kummer: the exponent of p in C(m+n, m) = number of carries when adding m and n in base p C(2n,n) ≈ 4ⁿ/√(πn) Stirling, Ch. 11 max_k C(n,k) = C(n, ⌊n/2⌋) ≈ 2ⁿ·√(2/(πn)) C(n,k) ≤ (en/k)^k a useful crude bound

The last bound is the workhorse in algorithm analysis: it turns "how many subsets of size at most k" into (en/k)^k, which is polynomial when k is constant and is exactly the bound used in parameterised complexity.

Computing binomials

Four ways, with their ranges
# 1. Pascal's triangle DP: exact, O(n²) time and space, n ≤ few thousand
C = [[0]*(n+1) for _ in range(n+1)]
for i in range(n+1):
    C[i][0] = 1
    for j in range(1, i+1): C[i][j] = C[i-1][j-1] + C[i-1][j]

# 2. Multiplicative, exact integers: O(k), no overflow if the answer fits
def binom(n, k):
    k = min(k, n-k); r = 1
    for i in range(k): r = r * (n-i) // (i+1)   # divisible at every step
    return r

# 3. Factorials mod prime p: O(1) per query after O(n) precompute  (Ch. 17)
# 4. lgamma for floating point: any n, ~13 significant digits    (Ch. 11)

In method 2 the running product r is always C(n, i+1) after step i, so the division is exact — but only in that order. Computing the whole numerator first overflows; dividing at each step does not.

Interview angle

"How many paths in a grid" is C(m+n,m); "with obstacles" is inclusion–exclusion or DP; "staying below the diagonal" is Catalan. Recognising which of the three you are in, and saying why, is the whole question — the formula is the easy part.

Problem set — 15 problemstheory & programming
  1. Theory

    Prove ∑_k C(n,k)² = C(2n,n) combinatorially.

    Solution

    Count n-subsets of a 2n-set split into two halves A and B of size n each. If the subset takes k elements from A, it takes n-k from B, giving C(n,k)C(n,n-k) = C(n,k)² by symmetry. Summing over k counts every n-subset exactly once, so the total is C(2n,n). ∎

    This is Vandermonde with m=n and k=n. The algebraic proof compares coefficients of xⁿ in (1+x)ⁿ(1+x)ⁿ = (1+x)^{2n} — equally short, and it generalises to q-analogues where the combinatorial argument does not.

  2. Theory

    Prove the hockey-stick identity ∑_{i=k}^{n} C(i,k) = C(n+1,k+1) two ways.

    Solution

    Combinatorially: count (k+1)-subsets of {1,…,n+1} by their largest element. If the largest is i+1, the other k elements form a k-subset of {1,…,i}: C(i,k) ways. Summing over i = k..n covers every subset once. ∎

    By telescoping: Pascal gives C(i+1,k+1) - C(i,k+1) = C(i,k). Summing i=k..n, the left telescopes to C(n+1,k+1) - C(k,k+1) = C(n+1,k+1). ∎

    Practical use: it turns a running sum of a column of Pascal's triangle into a single lookup, which is how prefix sums over binomials are answered in O(1).

  3. Theory

    Prove that C(n,k) is always an integer, without invoking its combinatorial meaning.

    Solution

    Induct using Pascal: C(n,k) = C(n-1,k-1) + C(n-1,k). Base cases C(n,0)=C(n,n)=1 are integers, and a sum of integers is an integer. ∎

    Alternatively, by Legendre's formula the exponent of any prime p in n!/(k!(n-k)!) is

    ∑_{i\ge1}(⌊ n/p^i⌋ - ⌊ k/p^i⌋ - ⌊ (n-k)/p^i⌋),

    and each term is 0 or 1 because ⌊ x+y ⌋ ≥ ⌊ x⌋ + ⌊ y ⌋. So every exponent is non-negative. ∎ This second proof is Kummer's theorem in embryo: the number of 1-terms is exactly the number of carries when adding k and n-k in base p.

  4. Theory

    Compute ∑_k kC(n,k) and ∑_k k²C(n,k).

    Solution

    First: by absorption kC(n,k) = nC(n-1,k-1), so the sum is n∑_j C(n-1,j) = n2^{n-1}.

    Second: write k² = k(k-1) + k. Applying absorption twice, k(k-1)C(n,k) = n(n-1)C(n-2,k-2), so ∑ k(k-1)C(n,k) = n(n-1)2^{n-2}. Adding the first result gives

    ∑_k k² C(n,k) = n(n-1)2^{n-2} + n2^{n-1} = n(n+1)2^{n-2}.

    Probabilistic reading: dividing by 2ⁿ, these are E[X] = n/2 and E[X²] = n(n+1)/4 for X ~ Bin(n,1/2), giving Var = n/4 ✓ — which matches npq = n/4.

  5. Theory

    State and prove Kummer's theorem, then use it to find the largest power of 3 dividing C(1000,500).

    Solution

    Kummer: the exponent of p in C(m+n,m) equals the number of carries when adding m and n in base p.

    Proof: by Legendre, the exponent is ∑_i (⌊ (m+n)/p^i⌋ - ⌊ m/p^i ⌋ - ⌊ n/p^i⌋). Each term is 1 exactly when a carry occurs out of position i-1 in the base-p addition, and 0 otherwise. ∎

    For C(1000,500) and p=3: 500_{10} = 200122_3. Adding 200122_3 + 200122_3: digits 2+2=4=11_3 (carry), 2+2+1=5=12_3 (carry), 1+1+1=3=10_3 (carry), 0+0+1=1 (no carry), 0+0=0, 2+2=4 (carry). That is 4 carries, so 3⁴ ‖ C(1000,500).

    Corollary worth knowing: C(n,k) is odd iff k &amp; (n-k) = 0 in binary, i.e. iff k is a submask of n — no carries in base 2. That is the reason Pascal's triangle mod 2 is the Sierpiński triangle.

  6. Theory

    How many binary strings of length n have exactly k ones and no two ones adjacent?

    Solution

    Place the n-k zeros in a row, creating n-k+1 gaps (including the ends). Choose k of these gaps to hold a single one each — no two ones can then be adjacent, and every valid string arises exactly once.

    Answer: C(n-k+1, k).

    Summing over k gives ∑_k C(n-k+1,k) = F_{n+2}, the shallow-diagonal identity of Pascal's triangle and the closed form behind Chapter 26 problem 7. The "gaps" technique — place the unconstrained items first, then slot the constrained ones into the gaps they create — solves a whole family of adjacency problems.

  7. Theory

    Prove C(n,k) ≤ (en/k)^k and use it to bound the number of subsets of size at most k.

    Solution

    C(n,k) = (n(n-1)···(n-k+1))/(k!) ≤ (n^k)/(k!), and k! ≥ (k/e)^k (from e^k = ∑_j k^j/j! ≥ k^k/k!). Hence C(n,k) ≤ (n^k)/((k/e)^k) = (en/k)^k. ∎

    Summing, ∑_{i≤ k} C(n,i) ≤ (en/k)^k as well for k ≤ n/2, since the terms grow by a factor of at least e... more carefully, the standard bound is ∑_{i≤ k}C(n,i) ≤ ((en)/(k))^k.

    This is the bound that makes O(2^k · poly) parameterised algorithms meaningful: enumerating all subsets of size ≤ k from n elements is n^{O(k)}, which is polynomial for fixed k — the difference between FPT and XP.

  8. Theory

    Show that the rows of Pascal's triangle mod 2 form the Sierpiński triangle.

    Solution

    By Kummer with p=2, C(n,k) is odd iff adding k and n-k in binary produces no carries, i.e. iff the binary representations of k and n-k have disjoint 1-bits, i.e. iff k is a submask of n: k &amp; n = k.

    So row n has exactly 2^{s(n)} odd entries, where s(n) is the popcount of n. Plotting the odd entries produces the self-similar Sierpiński pattern, because "submask of n" is a self-similar condition under doubling: row 2n is row n with gaps inserted. ∎

    This gives an O(1) parity test for a binomial and, via Lucas' theorem (Chapter 29), the general statement modulo any prime: C(n,k) ≡ ∏_i C(n_i,k_i) ±od p over base-p digits, which is zero exactly when some k_i > n_i.

  9. Program

    Compute exact C(n,k) for n ≤ 10⁵ as a big integer, and count its digits without materialising it.

    Solution
    def binom_exact(n, k):
    k = min(k, n-k)
    if k < 0: return 0
    num = den = 1
    for i in range(k):
        num *= n - i
        den *= i + 1
        g = math.gcd(num, den)             # keep the numbers small
        num //= g; den //= g
    return num // den

def binom_digits(n, k):                    # via lgamma, no big integers
    import math
    lg = (math.lgamma(n+1) - math.lgamma(k+1) - math.lgamma(n-k+1)) / math.log(10)
    return int(lg) + 1

    Reducing by the gcd at every step keeps the intermediates near the size of the answer rather than near n^k. Even so, C(10⁵, 500{,}000) has about 301,000 digits, so the multiplication cost dominates; the divide-and-conquer product tree plus a single final division is asymptotically better.

    binom_digits gives the size in microseconds for any n, which is often all you need — for instance to check whether the answer fits in a fixed-width type before computing it.

  10. Program

    Build Pascal's triangle mod 2 and render the Sierpiński pattern; verify the odd-entry count is 2^{popcount(n)}.

    Solution
    for n in range(64):
    row = ''.join('#' if (k & n) == k else '.' for k in range(n+1))
    print(row.center(70))
    assert sum(1 for k in range(n+1) if (k & n) == k) == 1 << bin(n).count('1')

    The test (k & n) == k is the submask condition from problem 8, and it replaces any actual binomial computation — an O(1) parity oracle.

    Summing the odd counts over rows 0..2^m-1 gives 3^m (each bit independently contributes a factor of 3: absent, or present in n only, or present in both), which is the Hausdorff-dimension statement log 3/log 2 ≈ 1.585 for the Sierpiński triangle — the same exponent as Karatsuba's, for the same self-similar reason.

  11. Program

    Answer 10⁶ queries for C(n,k) mod 10⁹+7 with n ≤ 2×10⁶, and separately handle n up to 10¹⁸ with k ≤ 10⁵.

    Solution
    # Case A: n bounded — factorials + inverse factorials, O(1) per query (Ch. 17)

# Case B: huge n, small k — multiply k terms directly
def binom_huge(n, k, MOD, invfact):
    if k < 0 or k > n: return 0
    num = 1
    for i in range(k):
        num = num * ((n - i) % MOD) % MOD
    return num * invfact[k] % MOD

    Case B is O(k) per query — fine for k ≤ 10⁵ and a handful of queries, but not for 10⁶ of them. The reduction (n - i) % MOD is essential: n itself exceeds the modulus, and forgetting it gives silent overflow in C++.

    If both n and the query count are huge, the answer is Lucas' theorem (Chapter 29), which reduces to base-p digits and costs O(log_p n) per query.

  12. Program

    Verify Vandermonde's convolution numerically for all m,n,k ≤ 30, and implement a convolution-based binomial product.

    Solution
    from math import comb
for m in range(31):
    for n in range(31):
        for k in range(m+n+1):
            lhs = sum(comb(m,i)*comb(n,k-i) for i in range(k+1))
            assert lhs == comb(m+n,k), (m,n,k)

    The identity says the sequence (C(n,k))_k convolved with (C(m,k))_k is (C(m+n,k))_k — which is exactly the polynomial identity (1+x)^m(1+x)^n = (1+x)^{m+n}.

    Practical consequence: binomial rows can be combined with FFT/NTT in O(nlog n) rather than O(n²). More usefully, it means any DP whose transition is "distribute k items between two independent halves" is a convolution and can be accelerated the same way (Chapter 51).

  13. Program

    Count lattice paths from (0,0) to (m,n) using only right and up moves, that also never go above the line y = x.

    Solution
    def paths_below_diagonal(m, n):        # requires n <= m
    from math import comb
    if n > m: return 0
    # reflection principle: bad paths correspond bijectively to
    # paths to the reflected endpoint (n-1, m+1)
    return comb(m+n, n) - comb(m+n, n-1)

    Reflection principle: a bad path touches the line y = x+1; reflect the portion before its first touch across that line. This is a bijection between bad paths to (m,n) and all paths to (n-1, m+1), so the bad count is C(m+n, n-1). ∎

    With m = n this gives C(2n,n) - C(2n,n-1) = (1)/(n+1)C(2n,n) — the Catalan numbers, which Chapter 32 develops. The reflection argument is the cleanest derivation of them and generalises to the ballot problem and to random-walk hitting probabilities.

  14. Program

    Implement C(n,k) mod m for arbitrary composite m, combining Lucas per prime power with CRT.

    Solution
    def binom_mod_composite(n, k, m):
    res, mods = [], []
    for p, e in factorise(m).items():
        res.append(binom_mod_prime_power(n, k, p, e))
        mods.append(p**e)
    return crt(res, mods)[0]

def binom_mod_prime_power(n, k, p, e):
    pe = p**e
    # Granville/Andrew: track the exponent of p separately via Kummer,
    # and compute the p-stripped factorials, which ARE invertible mod p^e.
    ex = carries_base_p(k, n-k, p)          # exponent of p in C(n,k)
    if ex >= e: return 0
    num = stripped_fact(n, p, e)
    den = stripped_fact(k, p, e) * stripped_fact(n-k, p, e) % pe
    return pow(p, ex, pe) * num % pe * pow(den, -1, pe) % pe

    The two ingredients: Kummer gives the exponent of p (so you know when the answer is ≡ 0), and the p-stripped factorial (n!)_p = ∏_{i ≤ n, p ∤ i} i is coprime to p and therefore invertible mod p^e.

    This handles the notorious "compute C(n,k) mod 10⁶" problems, where the naive factorial-inverse approach fails because 10⁶ = 2⁶5⁶ is composite and factorials are not invertible. Total cost O(p^e + log_p n) per prime power.

  15. Program

    Write a search that finds all binomial coefficients equal to a given value N, for N ≤ 10^{15}.

    Solution
    def find_binomials(N):
    out = [(N, 1), (N, N-1)] if N > 1 else []       # trivial C(N,1)=N
    k = 2
    while True:
        # smallest n with C(n,k) >= N is roughly k + (N k!)^{1/k}
        n = k
        while binom_exact(n, k) < N: n += 1
        if binom_exact(n, k) == N: out += [(n, k), (n, n-k)]
        if binom_exact(2*k, k) > N: break            # k too large from here on
        k += 1
    return sorted(set(out))

    The loop terminates because C(2k,k) ≈ 4^k/√{π k} grows exponentially, so k ≤ log₄ N ≈ 25 at N = 10^{15}. For each k the inner search is a binary search over n.

    Interesting outputs: 3003 = C(3003,1) = C(78,2) = C(15,5) = C(14,6) — the only known number appearing eight times in Pascal's triangle. Singmaster's conjecture says the number of appearances is bounded by an absolute constant; the largest known is 8, and nobody has proved a bound better than O(log N).

Chapter 29

Binomials modulo a prime: Lucas and prime powers

Factorial-inverse binomials break down the moment n exceeds the modulus, because the factorial contains the modulus as a factor. Lucas' theorem repairs it by working digit by digit in base p, and Granville's generalisation extends it to prime powers.

The standard O(1) method — precompute n! and (n!)^{-1} mod p — requires n < p. Beyond that, n! contains p as a factor and is ≡ 0, so the inverse does not exist and the formula is meaningless.

Lucas' theorem

Write n and k in base p: n = Σ nᵢ pⁱ, k = Σ kᵢ pⁱ, 0 ≤ nᵢ, kᵢ < p C(n,k) ≡ ∏ᵢ C(nᵢ, kᵢ) (mod p) In particular C(n,k) ≡ 0 (mod p) iff kᵢ > nᵢ for some digit i.

Proof sketch: in 𝔽_p[x], the Frobenius map gives (1+x)^{p} ≡ 1 + x^{p}, hence (1+x)^{p^i} ≡ 1 + x^{p^i}. So

(1+x)ⁿ = ∏ᵢ ((1+x)^{pⁱ})^{nᵢ} ≡ ∏ᵢ (1 + x^{pⁱ})^{nᵢ} (mod p)

Expanding the right side, the coefficient of xᵏ picks exactly one term from each factor, and base-p representation is unique — so the coefficient is ∏ C(n_i,k_i). ∎

Lucas, in O(log_p n) per query
long long lucas(long long n, long long k, long long p,
                const vector<long long>& fact, const vector<long long>& ifact){
    long long r = 1;
    while (n || k){
        long long ni = n % p, ki = k % p;
        if (ki > ni) return 0;                      // a digit fails
        r = r * fact[ni] % p * ifact[ki] % p * ifact[ni-ki] % p;
        n /= p; k /= p;
    }
    return r;
}
// precompute fact/ifact only up to p — so p must be small enough to sieve

Cost: O(log_p n) per query after O(p) precomputation. With p = 10⁹+7 the precomputation is the bottleneck, so Lucas is used when p is small (a few million) and n is enormous.

Principle

Choose the method by comparing n to p. n < p: factorials and inverse factorials, O(1) per query. n ≥ p, p small and prime: Lucas. modulus is a prime power: Granville/Andrew with p-stripped factorials. modulus composite: do each prime power and CRT. There is no single method that covers all four.

Prime powers

Modulo p^e the obstruction is the same but the repair is more involved. Define the p-stripped factorial

(n!)_p = ∏_{1 ≤ i ≤ n, p ∤ i} i coprime to p, hence invertible n! = p^{⌊n/p⌋} · ⌊n/p⌋! · (n!)_p — recurse on ⌊n/p⌋

Then C(n,k) = p^{E} · ((n!)^*)/((k!)^*((n-k)!)^*) where E is the exponent of p (by Kummer, the number of carries) and the starred quantities are the fully recursed stripped products, which are units mod p^e. If E ≥ e the answer is 0.

The stripped factorial modulo p^e is periodic with period p^e, so it is computed as (a full period)⌊n/p^e⌋ times a partial product — O(p^e + log_p n) after precomputing one period.

Wilson's theorem and the period

The full-period product has a clean value: (p^e!)_p ≡ -1 ±od {p^e} for p odd or p^e = 4, and +1 for p = 2, e ≥ 3. For e = 1 this is Wilson's theorem: (p-1)! ≡ -1 ±od p, because every unit pairs with its distinct inverse except ±1.

Interview angle

"Compute C(n,k) mod m" is a question about which of four regimes you are in, and the strongest answer names the regime before writing code: "m is prime and larger than n, so factorials and inverse factorials, O(n) precompute and O(1) per query." If m is 10⁶ rather than 10⁹+7, noticing that it is composite is the entire question.

Problem set — 14 problemstheory & programming
  1. Theory

    Compute C(1000, 500) mod 7 using Lucas.

    Solution

    Base 7: 1000 = 2·343 + 6·49 + 2·7 + 6 = (2,6,2,6)_7. And 500 = 1·343 + 3·49 + 1·7 + 3 = (1,3,1,3)_7.

    Every digit satisfies k_i ≤ n_i, so the answer is nonzero:

    C(2,1)C(6,3)C(2,1)C(6,3) = 2 · 20 · 2 · 20 = 1600 ≡ 1600 - 228·7 = 4 ±od 7.

    Note how cheap this is compared with computing a 300-digit number and reducing it — four small binomials and a product.

  2. Theory

    Prove (1+x)^p ≡ 1 + x^p ±od p and deduce Lucas.

    Solution

    By the binomial theorem, (1+x)^p = ∑_k C(p,k)x^k. For 0 < k < p, C(p,k) = (p!)/(k!(p-k)!) has a factor p in the numerator and none in the denominator (all factors there are < p), so p | C(p,k). Only k = 0 and k = p survive. ∎

    Iterating, (1+x)^{p^i} ≡ 1 + x^{p^i}. Writing n = ∑ n_i p^i,

    (1+x)^n ≡ ∏_i (1+x^{p^i})^{n_i} ±od p.

    Comparing the coefficient of x^k and using uniqueness of base-p representation gives C(n,k) ≡ ∏_i C(n_i,k_i). ∎

  3. Theory

    For how many k in [0,n] is C(n,k) odd? Prove it.

    Solution

    By Lucas with p=2, C(n,k) is odd iff every binary digit satisfies k_i ≤ n_i, i.e. iff k is a submask of n. The number of submasks of n is 2^{s(n)} where s(n) is the popcount.

    So the count is 2^{popcount(n)}. ∎ For n = 2^m - 1 (all ones) every entry is odd — 2^m = n+1 of them, the full row; for n = 2^m only two are.

    This is the Sierpiński structure of Chapter 28 problem 8, now derived rather than observed, and it generalises: the number of entries in row n not divisible by p is ∏_i (n_i + 1) over the base-p digits.

  4. Theory

    Prove Wilson's theorem and its converse.

    Solution

    Forward: in (ℤ/p)^×, pair each element with its inverse. An element is its own inverse iff x²≡1, i.e. x ≡ ±1 (Chapter 23). So all elements except 1 and p-1 pair off into products of 1, leaving (p-1)! ≡ 1 · (p-1) ≡ -1 ±od p. ∎

    Converse: if n is composite and n > 4, let d be a divisor with 1 < d < n. Then d | (n-1)!, so (n-1)! ≢ -1 ±od n (it is ≡ 0 ±od d while -1 is not). The case n=4 gives 3! = 6 ≡ 2 ≢ -1. ∎

    So (n-1)! ≡ -1 ±od n characterises primes exactly — a beautiful primality test that is useless in practice, since computing (n-1)! mod n takes Θ(n) multiplications.

  5. Theory

    Compute C(20,10) mod 9 by hand, showing why plain Lucas does not apply.

    Solution

    9 is not prime, so Lucas is inapplicable. Use the prime-power method with p=3, e=2.

    Exponent of 3 (Kummer): 10 = 101_3. Adding 101_3 + 101_3: 1+1=2 (no carry), 0+0=0, 1+1=2 — no carries, so 3^0 ‖ C(20,10), i.e. 3 does not divide it.

    Then C(20,10) = 184{,}756, and 184756 = 20528·9 + 4, so the answer is 4. Consistent with the exponent being 0 (the answer is a unit mod 9). ✓

    The general algorithm would compute this without knowing the value: strip the factorials of their factors of 3, invert mod 9, multiply by 3^0.

  6. Theory

    Given m = 10⁶, explain the full strategy for C(n,k) mod m with n up to 10¹⁸.

    Solution

    10⁶ = 2⁶ · 5⁶. Compute C(n,k) modulo 2⁶ = 64 and modulo 5⁶ = 15{,}625 separately, then CRT.

    For each prime power p^e:

    • Compute the exponent E of p in C(n,k) by Legendre/Kummer, in O(log_p n). If E ≥ e, the result mod p^e is 0.
    • Otherwise compute the three p-stripped factorial products modulo p^e, using the period-p^e structure and recursion on ⌊ n/p ⌋. Precompute one period: 64 and 15,625 entries — trivial.
    • Combine: p^E · A · B^{-1} · C^{-1} mod p^e.

    Total O(p^e + log_p n) per prime power, so microseconds. The key realisation is that the small size of p^e — not of n — is what makes it tractable.

  7. Theory

    Count the number of nonzero entries in row n of Pascal's triangle modulo a prime p.

    Solution

    By Lucas, C(n,k) ≢ 0 ±od p iff k_i ≤ n_i for every base-p digit. For each digit position there are n_i + 1 admissible values of k_i, chosen independently, so the count is

    ∏_i (n_i + 1) over the base-p digits of n. ∎

    Check with p=2: ∏ (n_i+1) = 2^{popcount(n)} ✓, matching problem 3. For p=3 and n = 100 = (10201)_3: 2·1·3·1·2 = 12 nonzero entries out of 101 — the row is 88% zeros mod 3.

    Summing over n < p^m gives ((p(p+1))/(2))^m nonzero entries in the whole triangle, so the density of nonzero entries tends to 0 — Pascal's triangle mod p is mostly zeros, and self-similarly so.

  8. Program

    Implement Lucas' theorem and verify against exact big-integer binomials for n ≤ 500 and several small primes.

    Solution
    def lucas(n, k, p, fact, ifact):
    r = 1
    while n or k:
        ni, ki = n % p, k % p
        if ki > ni: return 0
        r = r * fact[ni] % p * ifact[ki] % p * ifact[ni-ki] % p
        n //= p; k //= p
    return r

from math import comb
for p in (2,3,5,7,11,13,101):
    f = [1]*p
    for i in range(1,p): f[i] = f[i-1]*i % p
    inv = [pow(x, p-2, p) for x in f]
    for n in range(500):
        for k in range(n+1):
            assert lucas(n,k,p,f,inv) == comb(n,k) % p, (n,k,p)

    The exhaustive cross-check against math.comb for n ≤ 500 is decisive — it exercises the zero case, the carry-free case, and multi-digit products. Once it passes for several primes there is essentially nothing left that can be wrong.

    Note ifact is computed with Fermat, which requires p prime; asserting that up front prevents the silent-wrong-answer failure mode of Chapter 17.

  9. Program

    Compute C(n,k) mod p^e using the Granville/Andrew method for p^e ≤ 10⁷ and n ≤ 10¹⁸.

    Solution
    def binom_pp(n, k, p, e):
    pe = p**e
    # one period of the p-stripped factorial, mod p^e
    f = [1]*(pe+1)
    for i in range(1, pe+1):
        f[i] = f[i-1] if i % p == 0 else f[i-1]*i % pe

    def stripped(m):                    # (m!)* fully recursed, and the p-exponent
        r, e_cnt = 1, 0
        while m:
            r = r * pow(f[pe], m // pe, pe) % pe * f[m % pe] % pe
            m //= p
            e_cnt += m
        return r, e_cnt

    a, ea = stripped(n)
    b, eb = stripped(k)
    c, ec = stripped(n-k)
    E = ea - eb - ec                     # exponent of p in C(n,k)
    if E >= e: return 0
    return pow(p, E, pe) * a % pe * pow(b*c % pe, -1, pe) % pe

    O(p^e) for the period table plus O(log_p n) per query. The exponent E comes out of the same recursion as Legendre's formula, so no separate Kummer computation is needed.

    Test it against comb(n,k) % p**e for n ≤ 300 and small p^e — including cases where the answer is 0, which is where the E ≥ e branch is exercised.

  10. Program

    Answer 10⁵ queries of C(n,k) mod m with arbitrary composite m ≤ 10⁶ and n ≤ 10¹⁸.

    Solution
    def make_solver(m):
    parts = [(p, e, p**e) for p, e in factorise(m).items()]
    tables = {(p,e): build_period(p,e) for p,e,_ in parts}
    def solve(n, k):
        rems = [binom_pp(n, k, p, e, tables[(p,e)]) for p,e,_ in parts]
        mods = [pe for _,_,pe in parts]
        return crt(rems, mods)[0]
    return solve

    Precompute the period tables once (total size ∑ p^e ≤ m ≤ 10⁶), then each query is O(ω(m)log_p n) — a few hundred operations. 10⁵ queries is well under a second.

    The design point: separating setup from query is what makes this practical. Factoring m and building tables per query would be 10⁵ factorisations; doing it once amortises to nothing.

  11. Program

    Count the number of k ∈ [0,n] with C(n,k) ≡ 0 ±od p, for n ≤ 10^{18}.

    Solution
    def zero_entries(n, p):
    total = n + 1
    nonzero = 1
    m = n
    while m:
        nonzero *= (m % p) + 1
        m //= p
    return total - nonzero

    O(log_p n) using problem 7's formula. At n = 10^{18} and p = 2, the nonzero count is 2^{popcount(n)} — typically around 2^{30}, so more than 99.9999% of the row is even.

    A nice sanity check: for n = p^m - 1 every digit is p-1, so nonzero = p^m = n+1 and there are zero zeros — the full row is nonzero, which matches the fact that C(p^m-1, k) ≡ (-1)^k ±od p.

  12. Program

    Verify Kummer's theorem computationally: for random n, k and p, compare the carry count to the actual p-adic valuation.

    Solution
    def carries(a, b, p):
    c = cnt = 0
    while a or b:
        s = a % p + b % p + c
        c = 1 if s >= p else 0
        cnt += c
        a //= p; b //= p
    return cnt

def valuation(x, p):
    v = 0
    while x % p == 0: x //= p; v += 1
    return v

from math import comb
import random
for _ in range(20000):
    n = random.randrange(1, 400); k = random.randrange(0, n+1)
    p = random.choice([2,3,5,7,11])
    assert carries(k, n-k, p) == valuation(comb(n,k), p)

    The identity v_p(C(n,k)) = carries(k, n-k) in base p is exactly Kummer, and 20,000 random checks make it concrete. The carries function must run until both operands and the carry are exhausted — a final carry out of the top position counts, and forgetting it is the one bug here.

    Practical use: the valuation tells you immediately whether C(n,k) ≡ 0 ±od {p^e} without computing anything, which is the early exit in the prime-power algorithm.

  13. Program

    Given n ≤ 10^{18}, count the number of odd entries in the first n rows of Pascal's triangle.

    Solution
    def odd_entries_upto(n):     # rows 0..n-1
    # Σ_{m < n} 2^{popcount(m)} — digit DP over the binary representation
    total = 0
    ones = 0
    for i in range(n.bit_length()-1, -1, -1):
        if n >> i & 1:
            total += (3**i) * (1 << ones)      # this bit 0, rest free
            ones += 1
    return total

    Why 3^i: fixing a prefix and letting the remaining i bits vary freely, ∑_{free bits} 2^{popcount} = (1+2)^i = 3^i — each free bit contributes a factor of 1 + 2.

    So the total over the first 2^m rows is 3^m, giving the Sierpiński dimension log₂3 ≈ 1.585: the odd entries occupy n^{1.585} of the n²/2 positions, a vanishing fraction. This digit-DP pattern — walk the bits, count what the free suffix contributes — is the general technique for any "count over all m < n" problem with a digit-based condition.

  14. Program

    Implement a fallback-chain binom_mod(n, k, m) that automatically selects the right algorithm.

    Solution
    def binom_mod(n, k, m, cache={}):
    if k < 0 or k > n: return 0
    if m == 1: return 0
    key = m
    if key not in cache:
        f = factorise(m)
        if len(f) == 1:
            (p, e), = f.items()
            if e == 1 and n < p:  cache[key] = ('direct', p)
            elif e == 1:          cache[key] = ('lucas', p)
            else:                 cache[key] = ('pp', p, e)
        else:                     cache[key] = ('crt', f)
    kind = cache[key][0]
    if kind == 'direct': return direct_binom(n, k, m)
    if kind == 'lucas':  return lucas(n, k, cache[key][1])
    if kind == 'pp':     return binom_pp(n, k, *cache[key][1:])
    return crt_binom(n, k, cache[key][1])

    The dispatch encodes the Principle box as executable logic, and caching on m means the factorisation and table building happen once per distinct modulus.

    Worth adding: an assertion in the 'direct' branch that n < p still holds, since a later call with a larger n through the same cached path would silently produce garbage. Caching the decision rather than re-deriving it is a small optimisation with a real correctness hazard, and the assertion is what makes it safe.

Chapter 30

Inclusion-exclusion

Counting things that avoid every one of k bad properties is done by counting things that violate each subset of them, with alternating signs. It converts an intractable "avoid everything" problem into 2^k easy "at least these" problems.

|A₁ ∪ ... ∪ A_n| = Σ|Aᵢ| − Σ|Aᵢ∩Aⱼ| + Σ|Aᵢ∩Aⱼ∩A_k| − ... = Σ_{∅ ≠ S ⊆ [n]} (−1)^{|S|+1} |⋂_{i∈S} Aᵢ| Complementary form — the one you actually use: |none of the properties| = Σ_{S ⊆ [n]} (−1)^{|S|} N(S) where N(S) = #objects having AT LEAST the properties in S

Proof: fix an object x belonging to exactly m ≥ 1 of the sets. On the right it is counted once for each subset S of those m sets, with sign (-1)^{|S|}, so its total contribution is ∑_{j=0}^{m}C(m,j)(-1)^j = (1-1)^m = 0. An object in none of the sets contributes exactly 1 (from S = ∅). So the right side counts exactly the objects with no property. ∎

That binomial cancellation is the same one behind Möbius inversion (Chapter 25) — inclusion–exclusion is Möbius inversion over the subset lattice.

Principle

Inclusion–exclusion is worth using when N(S) — the count with at least the properties in S — is easy, which is usually the case when the properties are "divisible by d_i", "misses colour i", or "position i is fixed". If N(S) depends only on |S|, the 2^n sum collapses to n terms with a binomial factor — which is what makes derangements and surjections closed-form.

The standard applications

Derangements D_n = n! Σ_{k} (−1)^k/k! ≈ n!/e Surjections onto k boxes: Σ_j (−1)^j C(k,j)(k−j)^n = k! S(n,k) Euler's totient φ(n) = n Σ_{d|n} μ(d)/d (properties: p | x) Coprime counting #{x ≤ n : gcd(x,m)=1} = Σ_{d|m} μ(d)⌊n/d⌋ Squarefree count Σ_{d ≤ √n} μ(d)⌊n/d²⌋ Chromatic polynom. P(G,k) = Σ_{S ⊆ E} (−1)^{|S|} k^{c(S)} Permanent Ryser's formula, O(2ⁿ n) instead of n!

Bonferroni inequalities

Truncating the alternating sum after an even number of terms gives an upper bound; after an odd number, a lower bound:

Σ|Aᵢ| − Σ|Aᵢ∩Aⱼ| ≤ |∪Aᵢ| ≤ Σ|Aᵢ|

This matters when the full sum is intractable: the union bound P(∪ A_i) ≤ ∑ P(A_i) is the first Bonferroni inequality and is used constantly in probabilistic analysis (Chapter 38).

Computing it

Subset-sum inclusion–exclusion, and the SOS speed-up
# plain: 2^n subsets, each evaluated in O(n)  →  O(2^n · n)
ans = 0
for mask in range(1 << n):
    sign = -1 if bin(mask).count('1') % 2 else 1
    ans += sign * N(mask)

# sum over subsets (SOS / zeta transform): O(2^n · n) for ALL masks at once
f = base[:]                     # f[mask] = value at exactly this mask
for i in range(n):
    for mask in range(1 << n):
        if mask >> i & 1:
            f[mask] += f[mask ^ (1 << i)]      # now f[mask] = Σ_{S ⊆ mask}

# Möbius (inverse) transform: same loop with -= recovers `base`

The zeta/Möbius transform pair is the subset-lattice analogue of prefix sums and differences. It computes all 2^n subset sums in O(2^n n) rather than O(3^n), and it is the engine behind subset convolution and many bitmask DPs.

Interview angle

"How many numbers up to n are divisible by 2, 3, or 5?" is a three-set inclusion–exclusion done in your head: ⌊ n/2⌋ + ⌊ n/3⌋ + ⌊ n/5⌋ - ⌊ n/6⌋ - ⌊ n/10⌋ - ⌊ n/15⌋ + ⌊ n/30⌋. The follow-up "now with 20 divisors" wants 2^{20} subsets — a million terms, still instant — and the observation that lcm overflow is the real hazard.

Problem set — 15 problemstheory & programming
  1. Theory

    How many integers in [1, 1000] are divisible by none of 2, 3, 5?

    Solution

    1000 - (500 + 333 + 200) + (166 + 100 + 66) - 33 = 1000 - 1033 + 332 - 33 = 266.

    Check against the density argument: 1000 · \frac12·\frac23·\frac45 = 1000·(4)/(15) = 266.67 ✓ — the multiplicative form of the same computation, and exactly φ(30)/30 · 1000 since φ(30) = 8 and 8/30 = 4/15.

    The floors are why the two differ slightly: inclusion–exclusion with floors is exact, the density product is asymptotic.

  2. Theory

    Derive the derangement formula D_n = n!∑_{k=0}^{n}((-1)^k)/(k!).

    Solution

    Property A_i: "σ(i) = i". Then D_n counts permutations with no property. For a set S of size k, permutations fixing at least those k points number (n-k)!, and there are C(n,k) such sets. Since N(S) depends only on |S|, the 2^n sum collapses:

    D_n = ∑_{k=0}^{n}(-1)^k C(n,k)(n-k)! = ∑_{k=0}^{n}(-1)^k(n!)/(k!). ∎

    Since ∑_k(-1)^k/k! → e^{-1}, we get D_n = [(n!)/(e)] (nearest integer) for n ≥ 1, and the probability a random permutation is a derangement tends to 1/e ≈ 0.368 — remarkably fast, correct to 6 decimals by n = 10.

  3. Theory

    Count surjections from an n-set onto a k-set.

    Solution
