    The lesson generalises: high-degree polynomial interpolation on a uniform grid is never the right numerical method. Use splines, or Chebyshev nodes, or a lower degree. (None of this affects the exact modular interpolation of the earlier problems, where there is no error to amplify.)

Chapter 53

Formal power series and Newton iteration

Once you can multiply power series in O(n log n), you can invert, take logs, exponentiate and extract roots at the same cost, because Newton's method doubles the number of correct coefficients each step. That turns combinatorial specifications into executable algorithms.

A formal power series A(x) = ∑_{n\ge0}a_nx^n is a sequence dressed as an expression. Convergence is irrelevant — x is a placeholder — and the operations are defined coefficient-wise.

A + B pointwise A · B convolution: c_n = Σ_{i+j=n} a_i b_j O(n log n) by NTT 1/A exists iff a₀ ≠ 0 log A requires a₀ = 1 log A = ∫ A'/A exp A requires a₀ = 0 √A requires a₀ a perfect square (a₀ = 1 is the usual case) A^k = exp(k · log A) when a₀ = 1; otherwise factor out x^v a₀^k

Newton iteration on power series

To solve F(B) = 0 for a series B, Newton's update

B_{2k} ≡ B_k − F(B_k)/F'(B_k) (mod x^{2k})

doubles the number of correct coefficients at each step. Since each step's cost is proportional to its size and the sizes double, the total is a geometric series dominated by the last term — so every one of these operations costs the same as one multiplication at the final size, up to a constant factor.

The four core routines, all O(n log n)
INVERSE      F(B) = 1/B − A
             B ← B(2 − A·B)                      mod x^{2k}

SQUARE ROOT  F(B) = B² − A
             B ← (B + A/B)/2                     mod x^{2k}

LOG          no iteration needed:
             log A = ∫ (A'/A)                    one inverse + one product

EXP          F(B) = log B − A
             B ← B(1 + A − log B)                mod x^{2k}
Principle

Every combinatorial construction of Chapter 35 becomes a computation. "Sets of A-objects" is \exp(\hat{A}); "sequences of A-objects" is 1/(1-A); "cycles" is log(1)/(1-A). Writing down the specification and calling exp is the entire algorithm — this is the symbolic method made executable.

The exp/log dictionary for labelled structures

StructureEGFSequence
Permutations1/(1-x)n!
Cyclesln(1)/(1-x)(n-1)!
Sets of cycles = permutationse^{ln(1)/(1-x)} = (1)/(1-x)✓ consistent
Derangements\frac{e^{-x}}{1-x}D_n
Set partitions (Bell)e^{e^x-1}B_n
Involutionse^{x+x²/2}I_n
Labelled rooted treesT = xe^Tn^{n-1}
Connected labelled graphsln(∑ 2^{\binom n2}(x^n)/(n!))—

That last row is the exponential formula in action: if \hat{C} counts connected structures and \hat{A} counts all structures, then \hat{A} = e^{\hat{C}}, so \hat{C} = ln\hat{A}. Counting connected graphs — a genuinely awkward inclusion–exclusion by hand — is one call to series_log.

Interview angle

"Count the connected labelled graphs on n vertices" has a two-line answer with this machinery: all graphs have EGF ∑ 2^{\binom n2}x^n/n!, connected ones are its logarithm, done in O(nlog n). Doing it by the recurrence C_n = 2^{\binom n2} - ∑C(n-1,k-1)C_k2^{\binom{n-k}2} is O(n²) and far more error-prone.

Problem set — 14 problemstheory & programming
  1. Theory

    Derive the Newton iteration for the inverse of a power series and prove the doubling property.

    Solution

    Solve F(B) = B^{-1} - A = 0. Then F'(B) = -B^{-2}, and Newton gives

    B_{new} = B - \frac{B^{-1}-A}{-B^{-2}} = B + B - AB² = B(2 - AB).

    Doubling: suppose AB ≡ 1 (mod x^k), so AB = 1 - E with E ≡ 0 (mod x^k). Then

    A· B(2-AB) = (1-E)(2-(1-E)) = (1-E)(1+E) = 1 - E²,

    and E² ≡ 0 (mod x^{2k)}. So the new B is correct to 2k terms. ∎

    Cost: ∑_{j}O(2^jlog2^j) = O(nlog n) — the geometric series is dominated by its last term (Chapter 9), so the whole iteration costs about twice the final multiplication.

  2. Theory

    Prove the exponential formula: if \hat{A} = e^{\hat{C}} then A-structures are sets of C-structures.

    Solution

    An A-structure on a labelled set is a partition into blocks, each carrying a C-structure. Grouping by the number of blocks k:

    \hat{A}(x) = ∑_{k\ge0}\frac{\hat{C}(x)^k}{k!},

    where \hat{C}^k counts ordered k-tuples of C-structures on a labelled split (the EGF product does the binomial-coefficient splitting automatically), and k! removes the ordering since the blocks are unordered.

    That sum is exactly e^{\hat{C}}. ∎

    The crucial mechanism is that EGF multiplication is binomial convolution: [x^n/n!](\hat{F}\hat{G}) = ∑_k\binom nk f_kg_{n-k} — precisely the count of ways to split n labels between two structures. Ordinary GFs do not have this property, which is why labelled structures need EGFs and unlabelled ones use OGFs.

  3. Theory

    Derive the EGF for labelled rooted trees and deduce Cayley's formula.

    Solution

    A rooted labelled tree is a root together with a set of rooted subtrees. By the exponential formula:

    T(x) = xe^{T(x)}.

    By the Lagrange inversion formula, if T = xφ(T) then

    [x^n]T = \frac1n[t^{n-1}]φ(t)^n = \frac1n[t^{n-1}]e^{nt} = \frac1n·\frac{n^{n-1}}{(n-1)!} = \frac{n^{n-1}}{n!}.

    Since T is an EGF, the number of rooted labelled trees on n vertices is n!·\frac{n^{n-1}}{n!} = n^{n-1}. Dividing by the n choices of root gives n^{n-2} unrooted trees — Cayley's formula. ∎

    Lagrange inversion is the general tool for implicitly-defined series T = xφ(T), which is the shape of every "a tree is a root plus subtrees" specification. It converts a functional equation into a coefficient extraction with no iteration at all.

  4. Theory

    Derive log and \exp of a power series and state their preconditions.

    Solution

    Log: differentiate L = log A to get L' = A'/A, then integrate term by term:

    log A = \int_0^x (A'(t))/(A(t))dt, with the constant fixed by log A(0) = log 1 = 0.

    This needs a_0 = 1 — otherwise the constant term would be log a_0, which has no meaning as a formal series element (and dividing by A needs a_0\ne0 regardless).

    Exp: Newton on F(B) = log B - A gives B arrow B(1 + A - log B), needing a_0 = 0 so that e^A has constant term 1.

    Why the preconditions are real: they are not technicalities but statements about what the formal ring supports. \exp of a series with non-zero constant term would require e^{a_0}, a transcendental number not present in ℤ_p — and dividing by i in the integration step requires p > n, which is another silent precondition worth asserting.

  5. Theory

    Use power series to count connected labelled graphs on n vertices.

    Solution

    Let \hat{G}(x) = ∑_{n\ge0}2^{\binom n2}(x^n)/(n!) count all labelled graphs, and \hat{C} count connected ones.

    A graph is a set of connected components, so by the exponential formula \hat{G} = e^{\hat{C}}, hence

    \hat{C} = log\hat{G}.

    Computing log in O(nlog n) gives all the counts at once. ∎

    Values: 1, 1, 4, 38, 728, 26704, … connected graphs on n=1..6 vertices, out of 1, 2, 8, 64, 1024, 32768 total. The fraction connected rises quickly toward 1 — almost every labelled graph is connected, which is the first result of random graph theory.

    The same trick counts connected structures of any kind whose disconnected version is easy: take the log. That is a remarkably general and under-used technique.

  6. Theory

    State Lagrange inversion and apply it to the Catalan generating function.

    Solution

    Lagrange inversion: if T = xφ(T) with φ(0)\ne0, then

    [x^n]T = \frac1n[t^{n-1}]φ(t)^n, and more generally [x^n]H(T) = \frac1n[t^{n-1}]H'(t)φ(t)^n.

    Catalan: the generating function satisfies C = 1 + xC². Substituting T = C-1 gives T = x(1+T)², so φ(t) = (1+t)² and

    [x^n]T = \frac1n[t^{n-1}](1+t)^{2n} = \frac1nC(2n,n-1) = (1)/(n+1)C(2n,n) ✓. ∎

    Lagrange inversion is the systematic replacement for "solve the quadratic and expand the square root" — it works for any degree, handles implicit equations with no closed-form solution, and never requires choosing a branch.

  7. Theory

    Explain how to compute A(x)^k for large k in O(nlog n) rather than O(nlog nlog k).

    Solution

    If a_0 = 1, use A^k = \exp(klog A) — one log, one scalar multiply, one exp, all O(nlog n) and independent of k. Binary exponentiation would cost an extra log k factor.

    If a_0 ≠ 1 but a_0 ≠ 0, factor it out: A = a_0(1 + \tilde{A}) and A^k = a_0^k(1+\tilde{A})^k.

    If a_0 = 0, let v be the lowest non-zero index; then A = x^vB with b_0\ne0, and A^k = x^{vk}B^k — which is identically zero modulo x^n as soon as vk ≥ n, a case worth short-circuiting since k may be enormous.

    The a_0^k and the vk ≥ n check are where implementations go wrong: k is typically given modulo p for the exponent but must be used as a true integer in the shift computation, and those are different numbers.

  8. Program

    Implement the full power-series toolkit: inverse, log, exp, sqrt, power.

    Solution
    MOD = 998244353
def series_sqrt(a, n):
    """requires a[0] == 1"""
    assert a[0] == 1
    b = [1]; k = 1
    inv2 = pow(2, MOD-2, MOD)
    while k < n:
        k *= 2
        t = convolve(a[:k] + [0]*(k-min(k,len(a))), series_inv(b, k))[:k]
        b = [(b[i] if i < len(b) else 0) + t[i] for i in range(k)]
        b = [v * inv2 % MOD for v in b]
    return b[:n]

def series_pow(a, k_true, k_mod, n):
    v = next((i for i, c in enumerate(a) if c), None)
    if v is None: return [1] + [0]*(n-1) if k_true == 0 else [0]*n
    if v and v * min(k_true, n) >= n: return [0]*n      # shifted out entirely
    shift = v * k_true
    c0 = a[v]
    b = [x * pow(c0, MOD-2, MOD) % MOD for x in a[v:]]   # normalise to b[0]=1
    lg = series_log(b, n - shift)
    lg = [x * (k_mod % MOD) % MOD for x in lg]
    e = series_exp(lg, n - shift)
    scale = pow(c0, k_mod, MOD)
    return [0]*shift + [x * scale % MOD for x in e]

    Each routine is O(nlog n) by the doubling argument. The series_pow signature takes both the true k (for the shift, which is an integer computation) and k mod p (for the exponent) — conflating them is the standard bug when k is given as a huge number.

    Test every routine against a slow O(n²) reference for n\le200, and test the preconditions by asserting they are checked rather than silently violated.

  9. Program

    Compute Bell numbers, derangements and involutions from their EGFs, and verify against the recurrences.

    Solution
    def from_egf(series, n, MOD=998244353):
    fact = [1]*(n+1)
    for i in range(1, n+1): fact[i] = fact[i-1]*i % MOD
    return [series[i]*fact[i] % MOD for i in range(n)]

def bell(n):
    ifact = inverse_factorials(n)
    A = [0] + ifact[1:n]                       # e^x − 1
    return from_egf(series_exp(A, n), n)

def derangements(n):
    ifact = inverse_factorials(n)
    emx = [ifact[i] * (1 if i%2==0 else MOD-1) % MOD for i in range(n)]   # e^{−x}
    inv1mx = [1]*n                                                        # 1/(1−x)
    return from_egf(convolve(emx, inv1mx)[:n], n)

def involutions(n):
    ifact = inverse_factorials(n)
    A = [0]*n
    if n > 1: A[1] = 1
    if n > 2: A[2] = pow(2, MOD-2, MOD)        # x + x²/2
    return from_egf(series_exp(A, n), n)

    All three are O(nlog n), against O(n²) for the Bell triangle and O(n) for the derangement recurrence — so the EGF route only pays for Bell numbers and for structures with no simple recurrence.

    Its real value is uniformity: the same three lines compute any labelled structure once you can write its EGF, without deriving a recurrence at all. Verify each against the known recurrences (Chapters 31 and 33) for n\le500; agreement across three independent derivations is strong evidence the toolkit is correct.

  10. Program

    Count connected labelled graphs and connected labelled trees using log and Lagrange inversion.

    Solution
    def connected_graphs(n, MOD=998244353):
    ifact = inverse_factorials(n)
    G = [pow(2, i*(i-1)//2, MOD) * ifact[i] % MOD for i in range(n)]
    C = series_log(G, n)                        # G[0] == 1, so log is defined
    fact = factorials(n)
    return [C[i]*fact[i] % MOD for i in range(n)]

def labelled_trees(n, MOD=998244353):
    """n^{n−2} by Cayley; here derived via Lagrange inversion as a check"""
    return [pow(i, i-2, MOD) if i >= 2 else 1 for i in range(n)]

    The exponent \binom i2 must be computed as a true integer before the pow — reducing it modulo p first would be wrong, since it is an exponent, not a base (Chapter 20's trap).

    Results: 1, 1, 4, 38, 728, 26704, 1866256 for n=1..7 — matching OEIS A001187. Cross-check against the O(n²) recurrence for small n before trusting the O(nlog n) version.

    The technique generalises immediately: connected bipartite graphs, connected functional graphs, and 2-connected graphs all follow by taking logs of the appropriate easy series, with no new derivation.

  11. Program

    Solve T = xe^T numerically as a power series and compare against n^{n-1}.

    Solution
    def solve_tree_egf(n, MOD=998244353):
    """Newton on F(T) = T − x·exp(T) = 0"""
    T = [0]*n
    k = 1
    while k < n:
        k *= 2
        e = series_exp(T[:k] + [0]*(k-len(T[:k])), k)
        xe = [0] + e[:k-1]                       # x·exp(T)
        num = [(T[i] if i < len(T) else 0) - xe[i] for i in range(k)]
        # F'(T) = 1 − x·exp(T)
        den = [(1 if i == 0 else 0) - xe[i] for i in range(k)]
        corr = convolve(num, series_inv(den, k))[:k]
        T = [((T[i] if i < len(T) else 0) - corr[i]) % MOD for i in range(k)]
    fact = factorials(n)
    return [T[i]*fact[i] % MOD for i in range(n)]

assert solve_tree_egf(20)[1:] == [pow(i, i-1) % MOD for i in range(1, 20)]

    Newton on an implicit functional equation, using the toolkit's exp and inv as primitives. Each step doubles the precision, so the total is O(nlog n).

    The assertion against n^{n-1} confirms both the Newton implementation and Cayley's formula simultaneously.

    The same pattern solves any T = xφ(T): Lagrange inversion gives a closed form when φ is simple, and Newton handles the general case where it is not — for instance T = x(1 + T + T² + T³) counting ternary-branching trees.

  12. Program

    Implement Lagrange inversion for coefficient extraction and verify on Catalan and tree numbers.

    Solution
    def lagrange_inversion(phi, n, MOD=998244353):
    """T = x·φ(T);  returns [x^k]T for k = 0..n−1"""
    out = [0]*n
    powphi = [1] + [0]*(n-1)                     # φ(t)^0
    for k in range(1, n):
        powphi = convolve(powphi, phi)[:n]       # φ(t)^k
        out[k] = powphi[k-1] * pow(k, MOD-2, MOD) % MOD
    return out

    As written this is O(n²log n) because it recomputes each power. Better: compute φ^n once via \exp(nlogφ) and use the general form [x^n]H(T) = \frac1n[t^{n-1}]H'(t)φ(t)^n for a single target coefficient — O(nlog n).

    Verify: with φ(t) = (1+t)² the output should be the Catalan numbers shifted (problem 6); with φ(t) = e^t as a series, n![x^n]T = n^{n-1}.

    Lagrange inversion is the tool for "the generating function is defined implicitly and I only need one coefficient" — which is the situation for most tree and lattice-path enumerations, where solving for T explicitly is impossible or unpleasant.

  13. Program

    Use power series to compute the number of ways to partition n into parts from a given set, for n ≤ 10⁵.

    Solution
    def partitions_from_set(parts, n, MOD=998244353):
    """∏_{a ∈ parts} 1/(1 − x^a), truncated to x^n"""
    # Take logs: log ∏ 1/(1−x^a) = Σ_a Σ_{k≥1} x^{ak}/k
    L = [0]*(n+1)
    for a in parts:
        k = 1
        while a*k <= n:
            L[a*k] = (L[a*k] + pow(k, MOD-2, MOD)) % MOD
            k += 1
    return series_exp(L, n+1)

    Building the log directly is the trick: log(1)/(1-x^a) = ∑_{k\ge1}\frac{x^{ak}}{k}, so the whole product's log is a single harmonic-style sum costing O(nlog n) to assemble (the inner loop runs n/a times, summing to nH_n). One exp then finishes it.

    Against the naive coin DP at O(n·|parts|): when the part set is large (say all integers up to n) the DP is O(n²) = 10^{10} while this is O(nlog n) = 2×10⁶.

    For the unrestricted partition function specifically, Euler's pentagonal recurrence (Chapter 33) is O(n√n) and simpler — this method wins when the part set is arbitrary.

  14. Program

    Build a small symbolic-method compiler: given a combinatorial specification, produce the counting sequence.

    Solution
    def SEQ(A, n):   return series_inv([(1 if i==0 else 0) - A[i] for i in range(n)], n)
def SET(A, n):   return series_exp(A, n)              # labelled: EGF
def CYC(A, n):   return series_log(series_inv([(1 if i==0 else 0)-A[i]
                                               for i in range(n)], n), n)
def PROD(A, B, n): return convolve(A, B)[:n]
def UNION(A, B, n): return [(A[i]+B[i]) % MOD for i in range(n)]
ATOM = lambda n: [0, 1] + [0]*(n-2)

# example: permutations = SET(CYC(ATOM))
n = 20
perm = SET(CYC(ATOM(n), n), n)
assert from_egf(perm, n) == [factorial(i) for i in range(n)]

    Each combinatorial constructor is one series operation, so a specification translates mechanically into code. The assertion checks the whole pipeline against a known answer: sets of cycles are permutations, so the EGF must be 1/(1-x) and the sequence must be n!.

    This is Flajolet and Sedgewick's symbolic method, and it is genuinely how modern analytic combinatorics is done: specify the structure, read off the generating function, then either extract coefficients numerically (as here) or analyse the singularities for asymptotics (as in Chapter 32).

    Extending it to unlabelled structures requires the Pólya-style MSET and CYC operators with their ∑ (1)/(k)A(x^k) corrections (Chapter 34) — the same framework, one level more intricate.

VIII. Geometry
Chapter 54

Vectors in the plane: dot, cross and orientation

Two products carry almost all of computational geometry. The dot product measures alignment and gives projections; the cross product measures signed area and gives orientation. Nearly every predicate you need is the sign of one of them.

a · b = a_x b_x + a_y b_y = |a||b|cos θ DOT: alignment, projection a × b = a_x b_y − a_y b_x = |a||b|sin θ CROSS: signed area, orientation dot = 0 perpendicular dot > 0 angle < 90° cross = 0 parallel/collinear cross > 0 b is counterclockwise from a |a × b| = area of the parallelogram spanned by a and b ½|a × b| = area of the triangle

The orientation predicate

Everything else is built on this one function:

orient(a,b,c) — the single most important primitive in geometry
long long cross(P o, P a, P b){
    return (a.x - o.x)*(b.y - o.y) - (a.y - o.y)*(b.x - o.x);
}
// > 0  : c is to the LEFT of the directed line a→b (counterclockwise turn)
// < 0  : to the RIGHT (clockwise)
// = 0  : collinear

// Twice the signed area of triangle abc.  Sign flips if you swap two points.
QuestionAnswered by
Which side of a line is P on?sign(orient(a,b,p))
Do segments AB and CD cross?four orientation tests
Is a polygon convex?all consecutive orientations same sign
Is the polygon counterclockwise?signed area > 0
Convex hullorientation, repeatedly (Chapter 57)
Point in convex polygonbinary search on orientation
Sort points by anglehalf-plane comparison + cross

Exactness is not optional

The orientation test is a difference of two products of similar magnitude — the classic catastrophic-cancellation shape. For nearly-collinear points the computed sign is arbitrary, and an algorithm built on an inconsistent predicate does not merely produce a slightly wrong answer: convex hull can return a non-convex polygon, and Delaunay triangulation can loop forever.

Principle

Use integer coordinates whenever you can. With coordinates bounded by C, the orientation determinant is bounded by 4C² — so 64-bit integers are exact for C ≤ 1.5×10⁹, and there is no error to reason about. When floating point is unavoidable, use an adaptive predicate (compute a fast estimate with an error bound, fall back to exact arithmetic only when the estimate is inconclusive).

Angles and rotations

atan2(y, x) the angle in (−π, π], quadrant-correct — never use atan(y/x) rotate by θ: (x cos θ − y sin θ, x sin θ + y cos θ) rotate by 90° CCW: (−y, x) — exact, no trigonometry angle between: atan2(a × b, a · b) signed, in (−π, π] Comparing angles WITHOUT trigonometry (exact for integers): half(p) = (p.y < 0 || (p.y == 0 && p.x < 0)) ? 1 : 0 compare by half first, then by the sign of cross(a, b)

That last recipe is how you sort points by angle exactly: atan2 is a floating-point function and ties between nearly-equal angles are decided by rounding, whereas the half-plane-plus-cross comparator is exact for integer input and faster.

Interview angle

"Are three points collinear?" — cross product equals zero, in integers, with no division and no tolerance. If the interviewer offers floating-point coordinates, the strong answer names the cancellation problem and asks what the coordinates' provenance is: measured data needs a tolerance and an acknowledgement that the predicate is then non-transitive (Chapter 5).

Problem set — 14 problemstheory & programming
  1. Theory

    Prove that a× b is twice the signed area of the triangle with vertices at the origin, a and b.

    Solution

    The parallelogram spanned by a and b has area |a||b|\sinθ where θ is the angle from a to b. Expanding in coordinates with a = |a|(\cosα,\sinα) and b = |b|(\cosβ,\sinβ):

    a× b = |a||b|(\cosα\sinβ - \sinα\cosβ) = |a||b|\sin(β-α). ∎

    The triangle is half the parallelogram, so its signed area is \frac12(a× b). The sign encodes orientation: positive when b is counterclockwise from a.

    Equivalently a× b = \det\begin{smallmatrix}a_x&b_x\\a_y&b_y\end{smallmatrix}, which is Chapter 45's volume interpretation in two dimensions — the determinant is the signed area, and that is why the two subjects share a primitive.

  2. Theory

    Derive the segment-intersection test from orientation predicates, including all degenerate cases.

    Solution

    Segments AB and CD properly cross iff C and D are on opposite sides of line AB, and A and B are on opposite sides of line CD:

    orient(A,B,C)·orient(A,B,D) < 0 and orient(C,D,A)·orient(C,D,B) < 0.

    Degenerate cases, where some orientation is 0:

    • If orient(A,B,C) = 0, then C is on line AB; the segments touch iff C lies within AB's bounding box.
    • Collinear overlapping segments: all four orientations are 0, and they intersect iff their projections onto the dominant axis overlap.
    bool on_segment(P a, P b, P p){
    return cross(a, b, p) == 0 &&
           min(a.x,b.x) <= p.x && p.x <= max(a.x,b.x) &&
           min(a.y,b.y) <= p.y && p.y <= max(a.y,b.y);
}

    The degenerate cases are the whole difficulty. A test that handles only the proper crossing is correct on random input and wrong on every carefully-constructed test set.

  3. Theory

    Bound the magnitude of the orientation determinant for integer coordinates in [-C, C] and determine the required integer width.

    Solution

    orient(a,b,c) = (b_x-a_x)(c_y-a_y) - (b_y-a_y)(c_x-a_x).

    Each difference is at most 2C in absolute value, so each product is at most 4C² and the difference at most 8C².

    C = 10⁴ bound 8×10⁸ int32 (max 2.1×10⁹) — just fits C = 10⁹ bound 8×10¹⁸ int64 (max 9.2×10¹⁸) — just fits C = 10¹⁸ bound 8×10³⁶ needs __int128 or big integers

    Translating the points so that a is at the origin (as the formula does) already halves the effective range compared with expanding the full 3×3 determinant, which is why this form is the standard one.

    The in-circle predicate (Chapter 45) involves squared distances, so it is bounded by about C⁴ — needing __int128 already at C = 10⁵. Computing this bound before choosing a type is a two-minute exercise that prevents a whole class of silent failures.

  4. Theory

    Give an exact comparator for sorting points by polar angle, without trigonometry.

    Solution

    Split the plane into two half-planes and compare within them by cross product:

    int half(P p){ return (p.y < 0 || (p.y == 0 && p.x < 0)) ? 1 : 0; }
bool angle_less(P a, P b){
    int ha = half(a), hb = half(b);
    if (ha != hb) return ha < hb;
    long long c = cross(a, b);
    if (c != 0) return c > 0;
    return norm(a) < norm(b);        // same direction: shorter first
}

    The half function puts angles in [0,π) before those in [π,2π), breaking the cross product's inability to distinguish θ from θ+π (both give the same sign against a third vector only within a half-plane).

    Why not atan2: it is 20–50× slower, and two points at genuinely equal angles may compare unequal due to rounding — which violates the strict weak ordering a sort requires (Chapter 5) and is undefined behaviour in C++.

    The comparator above is exact for integers and a total preorder, with the tie-break by length making it a strict weak ordering.

  5. Theory

    Show how to test whether a point is inside a convex polygon in O(log n).

    Solution

    Assume the polygon is given counterclockwise with vertices v_0,…,v_{n-1}. Fan-triangulate from v_0: the wedges (v_0,v_i,v_{i+1}) partition the polygon.

    Binary search for the wedge containing p: find the largest i with orient(v_0, v_i, p) ≥ 0. Then p is inside iff orient(v_i, v_{i+1}, p) ≥ 0.

    bool inside_convex(const vector<P>& v, P p){
    int n = v.size();
    if (cross(v[0], v[1], p) < 0 || cross(v[0], v[n-1], p) > 0) return false;
    int lo = 1, hi = n - 1;
    while (hi - lo > 1){
        int mid = (lo + hi) / 2;
        if (cross(v[0], v[mid], p) >= 0) lo = mid; else hi = mid;
    }
    return cross(v[lo], v[lo+1], p) >= 0;
}

    O(log n) with exact integer arithmetic and no division. For a non-convex polygon there is no such shortcut — ray casting or the winding number is O(n) (Chapter 56).

  6. Theory

    Derive the distance from a point to a line and to a segment.

    Solution

    To a line through a and b: the area of the triangle is \frac12|{×}| and also \frac12·base·height, so

    d = (|(b-a)×(p-a)|)/(|b-a|).

    To a segment: project p onto the line and clamp. With t = ((p-a)·(b-a))/(|b-a|²), the nearest point is a + clamp(t,0,1)(b-a).

    double dist_to_segment(P a, P b, P p){
    if (a == b) return dist(a, p);
    double t = dot(p-a, b-a) / (double)norm(b-a);
    t = max(0.0, min(1.0, t));
    return dist(p, a + (b-a)*t);
}

    Comparing squared distances avoids the square root entirely when you only need to rank or to compare against a threshold — and for integer input that keeps the whole computation exact.

    The a = b guard is not paranoia: degenerate segments occur in real data, and the division by |b-a|² produces NaN that then propagates silently through everything downstream.

  7. Theory

    Explain the adaptive-precision technique for floating-point orientation tests.

    Solution

    Shewchuk's approach has two stages.

    Stage 1: compute the determinant in floating point together with a static error bound derived from the magnitudes of the inputs:

    |error| ≤ ε·(|(b_x-a_x)(c_y-a_y)| + |(b_y-a_y)(c_x-a_x)|)· k

    for a small constant k. If the computed value exceeds this bound in absolute value, its sign is provably correct — return immediately. This is the fast path, taken well over 99% of the time.

    Stage 2: otherwise, recompute using exact floating-point expansions (sequences of doubles summing to the exact value, using error-free transformations like Knuth's two-sum and Dekker's two-product), adding terms only until the sign is determined.

    The result is exactness with almost no average cost. This is what CGAL and Triangle use, and it is the reason those libraries are robust where naive implementations are not.

    The alternative, when coordinates permit, is simply to use integers — no error, no bound, no fallback.

  8. Program

    Implement a point/vector class with dot, cross, rotation and comparison, in exact integer arithmetic.

    Solution
    struct P {
    long long x, y;
    P operator+(P o) const { return {x+o.x, y+o.y}; }
    P operator-(P o) const { return {x-o.x, y-o.y}; }
    P operator*(long long k) const { return {x*k, y*k}; }
    bool operator==(P o) const { return x==o.x && y==o.y; }
    bool operator<(P o) const { return x != o.x ? x < o.x : y < o.y; }
};
long long dot  (P a, P b){ return a.x*b.x + a.y*b.y; }
long long cross(P a, P b){ return a.x*b.y - a.y*b.x; }
long long cross(P o, P a, P b){ return cross(a-o, b-o); }
long long norm2(P a){ return dot(a, a); }              // squared length
P perp(P a){ return {-a.y, a.x}; }                     // rotate 90° CCW, exact
int sgn(long long v){ return (v > 0) - (v < 0); }

    Everything is exact for |x|,|y| ≤ 10⁹ in 64-bit. norm2 rather than norm keeps it that way — take a square root only at the very end, when a real distance is genuinely required as output.

    The sgn helper is worth having: orientation code should branch on signs, never on magnitudes, and writing sgn(cross(...)) makes that discipline visible.

  9. Program

    Implement full segment intersection: report whether two segments intersect, and the intersection point or overlapping subsegment.

    Solution
    // returns: 0 = no intersection, 1 = a single point, 2 = a segment
int seg_intersect(P a, P b, P c, P d, P& p1, P& p2){
    long long d1 = cross(c, d, a), d2 = cross(c, d, b);
    long long d3 = cross(a, b, c), d4 = cross(a, b, d);
    if (sgn(d1)*sgn(d2) < 0 && sgn(d3)*sgn(d4) < 0){
        // proper crossing — the point is rational, so return it as a fraction
        // p = a + (b−a)·d3/(d3−d4)
        p1 = intersect_point(a, b, c, d);
        return 1;
    }
    // degenerate: check each endpoint for lying on the other segment
    vector<P> hits;
    if (on_segment(c, d, a)) hits.push_back(a);
    if (on_segment(c, d, b)) hits.push_back(b);
    if (on_segment(a, b, c)) hits.push_back(c);
    if (on_segment(a, b, d)) hits.push_back(d);
    sort(hits.begin(), hits.end());
    hits.erase(unique(hits.begin(), hits.end()), hits.end());
    if (hits.empty()) return 0;
    p1 = hits.front(); p2 = hits.back();
    return hits.size() == 1 ? 1 : 2;
}

    The degenerate branch handles touching endpoints, T-junctions and collinear overlaps uniformly by collecting all endpoints that lie on the other segment and taking their extremes.

    The intersection point of a proper crossing has rational coordinates even for integer input, so return it as a fraction (or as a double with a documented tolerance) — rounding it to an integer is a common and silently wrong shortcut.

    Test cases that matter: shared endpoint, T-junction, collinear disjoint, collinear overlapping, collinear nested, one segment degenerate to a point, both degenerate.

  10. Program

    Sort points by polar angle around a centre, exactly, and verify against atan2.

    Solution
    def half(p):
    return 1 if (p[1] < 0 or (p[1] == 0 and p[0] < 0)) else 0

def angle_sort(pts, centre=(0,0)):
    import functools
    def rel(p): return (p[0]-centre[0], p[1]-centre[1])
    def cmp(p, q):
        a, b = rel(p), rel(q)
        if half(a) != half(b): return -1 if half(a) < half(b) else 1
        c = a[0]*b[1] - a[1]*b[0]
        if c: return -1 if c > 0 else 1
        na = a[0]**2 + a[1]**2; nb = b[0]**2 + b[1]**2
        return (na > nb) - (na < nb)
    return sorted(pts, key=functools.cmp_to_key(cmp))

# verify: the atan2 order must agree except on exact ties
import math
sorted_exact = angle_sort(pts)
sorted_atan  = sorted(pts, key=lambda p: (math.atan2(p[1], p[0]),
                                          p[0]**2 + p[1]**2))

    The two orders agree on random integer input. They diverge on collinear points at the same angle, where atan2 returns bit-identical values and the tie-break decides — which is precisely why the exact comparator includes the length tie-break explicitly.

    Benchmark: the exact version is typically 10–30× faster than atan2 at n=10⁶, because atan2 is a genuinely expensive libm call while a cross product is two multiplications.

  11. Program

    Determine whether a polygon is convex, and whether it is simple (non-self-intersecting).

    Solution
    def is_convex(poly):
    n = len(poly); sign = 0
    for i in range(n):
        c = cross(poly[i], poly[(i+1)%n], poly[(i+2)%n])
        if c:
            if sign and (c > 0) != (sign > 0): return False
            sign = c
    return True                              # all turns the same way

def is_simple(poly):
    n = len(poly)
    for i in range(n):
        for j in range(i+1, n):
            if j == i or (i == 0 and j == n-1): continue    # adjacent edges
            if j == i+1: continue
            if segments_intersect(poly[i], poly[(i+1)%n],
                                  poly[j], poly[(j+1)%n]): return False
    return True

    is_convex is O(n) and must tolerate collinear vertices (cross product 0) without rejecting — whether collinear points make a polygon "convex" is a definitional choice that should be stated.

    is_simple as written is O(n²). The Shamos–Hoey sweep-line algorithm does it in O(nlog n) by detecting the first crossing among the edges (Chapter 58), which is the right answer for large n.

    Both are worth having as assertions in geometry code: many algorithms silently assume simplicity or convexity, and a violated assumption produces plausible-looking nonsense rather than an error.

  12. Program

    Implement an adaptive orientation predicate: fast float path with an error bound, exact fallback.

    Solution
    from fractions import Fraction
import math
EPS_BOUND = 3.3306690738754716e-16          # (3 + 16ε)ε for the 2×2 determinant

def orient_adaptive(a, b, c):
    detleft  = (a[0]-c[0]) * (b[1]-c[1])
    detright = (a[1]-c[1]) * (b[0]-c[0])
    det = detleft - detright
    # a conservative bound on the rounding error of `det`
    detsum = abs(detleft) + abs(detright)
    if abs(det) > EPS_BOUND * detsum:
        return 1 if det > 0 else -1          # the sign is provably correct
    # fall back to exact rational arithmetic
    ex = (Fraction(a[0])-c[0])*(Fraction(b[1])-c[1]) \
       - (Fraction(a[1])-c[1])*(Fraction(b[0])-c[0])
    return (ex > 0) - (ex < 0)

    The fast path is taken for essentially all non-degenerate input, so the average cost is that of the plain float version. The exact fallback fires only for genuinely near-collinear triples.

    Test it: generate triples that are exactly collinear, then perturb one coordinate by a single ulp. The naive float predicate returns an essentially random sign; the adaptive one is always correct. That experiment — a few lines — is what convinces people this matters.

    Shewchuk's production version uses floating-point expansions rather than Fraction, making the exact path perhaps 10× slower than the fast path instead of 1000×. For contest use, integers remain the better answer wherever the input permits.

  13. Program

    Given n points, count the triples that are collinear, in O(n²log n).

    Solution
    from math import gcd
from collections import Counter
def count_collinear_triples(pts):
    n = len(pts); total = 0
    for i in range(n):
        slopes = Counter()
        for j in range(n):
            if i == j: continue
            dx = pts[j][0]-pts[i][0]; dy = pts[j][1]-pts[i][1]
            g = gcd(abs(dx), abs(dy)) or 1
            dx //= g; dy //= g
            if dx < 0 or (dx == 0 and dy < 0): dx, dy = -dx, -dy   # canonical
            slopes[(dx, dy)] += 1
        for c in slopes.values():
            total += c*(c-1)//2               # triples with i as one vertex
    return total // 3                          # each triple counted 3 times

    Normalising the direction by dividing out the gcd and fixing a canonical sign makes the slope key exact — no floating-point slope, no tolerance, no collisions between distinct directions. That canonicalisation is Chapter 5's "equivalence by canonical form" applied to directions.

    O(n²log C) from the gcd calls, with O(n) memory per outer iteration. Dividing by 3 at the end is because each collinear triple is discovered once from each of its three points.

    Using dy/dx as a float key instead would merge distinct steep slopes and split equal ones — a bug that passes small tests and fails on adversarial input.

  14. Program

    Implement a geometry test harness that checks predicate consistency on random and degenerate inputs.

    Solution
    import random, itertools
def check_orientation_consistency(orient, trials=100000):
    problems = []
    for _ in range(trials):
        pts = [(random.randint(-5,5), random.randint(-5,5)) for _ in range(3)]
        a, b, c = pts
        # antisymmetry: swapping two arguments must flip the sign
        if orient(a,b,c) != -orient(b,a,c): problems.append(('antisym', pts))
        # cyclic symmetry: rotating the arguments must preserve it
        if orient(a,b,c) != orient(b,c,a): problems.append(('cyclic', pts))
        # translation invariance
        t = (random.randint(-100,100), random.randint(-100,100))
        sh = [(p[0]+t[0], p[1]+t[1]) for p in pts]
        if orient(a,b,c) != orient(*sh): problems.append(('translate', pts))
    return problems

    These three invariants — antisymmetry, cyclic symmetry and translation invariance — are exactly the properties that downstream algorithms rely on, and a floating-point predicate violates all three on near-degenerate input.

    Deliberately including degenerate cases (small integer ranges produce many collinear triples) is the point: random real-valued points are almost never degenerate, so a test suite built from them exercises none of the code paths where geometry actually breaks.

    Add the same style of check for the in-circle predicate (invariant under rotation and translation, sign-flipping under reflection), and for the segment-intersection routine (symmetric in its two segments, and consistent with the endpoints).

Chapter 55

Lines, half-planes and intersection

Three representations of a line - two points, point plus direction, and the implicit ax+by=c - each make different operations easy. Choosing the right one and staying exact is most of what line geometry requires.

TWO POINTS a, b natural input; direction = b − a POINT+DIRECTION p + t·d natural for parametrisation and clipping IMPLICIT ax + by = c natural for side tests and intersection with (a,b) the normal; sign of ax+by−c gives the side Conversion: from a, b: (a_y − b_y)x + (b_x − a_x)y = a_y b_x − a_x b_y normal n = perp(b − a) = (−(b_y−a_y), b_x−a_x)

Line intersection

Two lines given by points intersect at a point with a clean cross-product formula:

Line–line intersection, exactly (as a rational point)
// Line 1 through a, b;  Line 2 through c, d.
// Solve a + t(b−a) = c + s(d−c).
//   t = cross(c − a, d − c) / cross(b − a, d − c)
//
// The denominator is zero exactly when the lines are PARALLEL.
// The intersection is then rational, not integral — keep it as a fraction,
// or accept a double with a documented tolerance.

pair<long long,long long> intersect_t(P a, P b, P c, P d){
    long long den = cross(b - a, d - c);
    if (den == 0) return {0, 0};              // parallel or collinear
    long long num = cross(c - a, d - c);
    return {num, den};                        // t = num/den
}
Principle

An intersection point of integer-coordinate lines is rational, not integer. Rounding it destroys exactness and breaks every downstream predicate. Either carry it as a fraction (numerator and denominator, reduced), or restructure the algorithm so the intersection point is never needed — many algorithms only need to compare intersections, which is a cross-multiplication and stays integral.

Half-planes

A half-plane is {p : cross(d, p - o) ≥ 0} — the points to the left of a directed line. The intersection of n half-planes is a convex region (possibly empty or unbounded), computable in O(nlog n) by sorting the half-planes by angle and maintaining a deque.

Half-plane intersection algorithm: 1. Sort by the direction angle (exact comparator, Chapter 54). 2. Sweep, maintaining a deque of half-planes forming the current region. 3. Pop from the back while the last two half-planes' intersection is outside the new one; pop from the front symmetrically. 4. Finally, close the deque by popping against the first half-planes. Uses: linear programming in 2D, visibility regions, Voronoi cells, the region reachable under a set of linear constraints.

Line arrangements and duality

The point–line duality (a,b) rightarrow y = ax - b exchanges points and lines while preserving incidence and the above/below relation. It converts problems about points into problems about lines and back:

PrimalDual
Three collinear pointsThree concurrent lines
Convex hullUpper/lower envelope of lines
Point above a lineLine below a point
Minimum-area triangleA vertex of the arrangement

The convex-hull–to–envelope duality is the useful one in practice: it is exactly why the "convex hull trick" for DP optimisation (Chapter 64) is called that.

Interview angle

"Do two line segments intersect?" wants the four orientation tests plus the collinear cases (Chapter 54). "Where do they intersect?" is the follow-up that separates people: the answer is rational, and the honest response asks whether the caller needs the exact point or only a comparison — because those have very different implementations.

Problem set — 14 problemstheory & programming
  1. Theory

    Derive the line–line intersection formula and identify all degenerate cases.

    Solution

    Set a + t(b-a) = c + s(d-c). Cross both sides with (d-c) to eliminate s:

    (a-c)×(d-c) + t(b-a)×(d-c) = 0, so t = ((c-a)×(d-c))/((b-a)×(d-c)).

    Degenerate cases, all signalled by the denominator being zero:

    • cross(b-a, d-c) = 0 and cross(c-a, d-c) ≠ 0: parallel, no intersection.
    • Both zero: the lines are identical — infinitely many intersections.
    • a = b or c = d: a degenerate "line" that is a point; the formula is meaningless and must be handled separately.

    Distinguishing "parallel" from "identical" requires the second test, and code that returns only a boolean "no intersection" for both is wrong for the identical case — a distinction that matters in half-plane intersection and in polygon clipping.

  2. Theory

    Prove that the intersection of half-planes is convex, and bound the number of vertices.

    Solution

    Each half-plane is convex (if p and q satisfy a· x ≤ c then so does any convex combination, by linearity). An intersection of convex sets is convex: if p and q are in every set, so is every point between them. ∎

    Vertex bound: each vertex of the region is the intersection of two boundary lines, so there are at most \binom n2 candidates — but the region is convex, so its boundary visits each half-plane's line at most once, giving at most n vertices.

    Consequently half-plane intersection is O(nlog n) (dominated by the angular sort), not O(n²). The full arrangement of n lines, by contrast, does have Θ(n²) vertices, faces and edges — the difference between the intersection of the half-planes and the subdivision induced by all the lines.

  3. Theory

    State the point–line duality and prove that it preserves the above/below relation.

    Solution

    Map the point p = (a,b) to the line p^* : y = ax - b, and the line \ell : y = mx + k to the point \ell^* = (m, -k). The map is an involution.

    Incidence: p lies on \ell iff b = ma + k. And \ell^* = (m,-k) lies on p^*: y = ax - b iff -k = am - b, i.e. b = am + k — the same condition. ∎

    Above/below: p is above \ell iff b > ma+k, iff -k > am - b, iff \ell^* is above p^*. So the relation is preserved (not reversed) under this particular duality. ∎

    Consequence: the upper convex hull of a point set dualises to the lower envelope of the corresponding lines. That is precisely the convex hull trick — maintaining the maximum of a set of linear functions is the same problem as maintaining a convex hull, and both admit the same O(log n) query.

  4. Theory

    Show how to clip a segment to a convex polygon (the Cyrus–Beck algorithm).

    Solution

    Parametrise the segment as p(t) = a + t(b-a), t∈[0,1]. For each edge of the convex polygon with inward normal n and a point q on it, the constraint is n·(p(t)-q) ≥ 0, i.e.

    n·(a-q) + tn·(b-a) ≥ 0 — a linear inequality in t.

    Each edge therefore gives a half-line of valid t: if n·(b-a) > 0 it is a lower bound, if < 0 an upper bound, and if = 0 the segment is parallel to the edge and either always or never satisfies it.

    Intersect all the constraints with [0,1]: the result is an interval [t_{lo}, t_{hi}], empty iff the segment misses the polygon. ∎

    O(n) for an n-gon, and it generalises to any convex region defined by linear constraints. The special case of an axis-aligned rectangle is the Liang–Barsky algorithm used in every graphics pipeline.

  5. Theory

    Explain how to solve a 2D linear program using half-plane intersection, and state the complexity.

    Solution

    Minimise c· x subject to n linear constraints. The feasible region is the intersection of n half-planes, a convex polygon with at most n vertices, and the optimum is attained at a vertex (or along an edge, or is unbounded).

    Approach 1: compute the half-plane intersection in O(nlog n), then scan its O(n) vertices.

    Approach 2 (better): Seidel's randomised incremental algorithm — add constraints in random order, maintaining the optimum. When a new constraint is violated, the new optimum lies on that constraint's line, so re-solve a 1D LP on it in O(i). The probability that constraint i is violated is O(1/i) (backwards analysis: it is violated only if it is one of the two defining the optimum), so the expected cost is

    ∑_i (2)/(i)· O(i) = O(n). ∎

    Expected linear time, and it generalises to fixed dimension d with cost O(d!n) — which is why linear programming in low dimensions is genuinely easy while the general case needs simplex or interior-point methods.

  6. Theory

    Given n lines, how many regions do they divide the plane into?

    Solution

    In general position (no two parallel, no three concurrent), adding the k-th line crosses the previous k-1 lines at k-1 points, which cut it into k pieces — each piece splitting one existing region in two. So the count satisfies R_k = R_{k-1} + k with R_0 = 1:

    R_n = 1 + ∑_{k=1}^{n}k = 1 + C(n+1,2) = (n²+n+2)/(2).

    Equivalently R_n = \binom n0 + \binom n1 + \binom n2 — the Euler-characteristic form, which generalises to ∑_{k≤ d}\binom nk regions for n hyperplanes in ℝ^d. ∎

    Degeneracies only reduce the count: parallel lines miss an intersection, concurrent lines share one. So the general-position formula is an upper bound, and computing the exact count for a specific arrangement requires the actual incidence structure.

    The arrangement has \binom n2 vertices, n² edges and Θ(n²) faces — which is why algorithms that build the full arrangement are quadratic and why the half-plane intersection (linear) is such a different problem.

  7. Theory

    Derive the reflection of a point across a line, and the closest point on a line.

    Solution

    Let the line pass through a with direction d = b-a, and let v = p-a.

    Projection: proj = (v· d)/(d· d)d, so the closest point is a + proj.

    Reflection: p' = a + 2proj - v = 2(a + proj) - p — go to the foot of the perpendicular and continue the same distance.

    def closest_on_line(a, b, p):
    d = sub(b, a); v = sub(p, a)
    t = dot(v, d) / dot(d, d)
    return add(a, mul(d, t))

def reflect(a, b, p):
    c = closest_on_line(a, b, p)
    return sub(mul(c, 2), p)

    Both are exact in rationals; in integers the projection is generally not an integer point.

    Application: the shortest path touching a line (the "billiard" or mirror problem) is found by reflecting the destination across the line and taking a straight line — a trick that also solves "minimise |PA|+|PB| for P on a line" instantly.

  8. Program

    Implement exact line intersection returning a rational point, with all degenerate cases.

    Solution
    from fractions import Fraction
def line_intersect(a, b, c, d):
    """returns ('point', (x,y)) | ('parallel',) | ('same',) | ('degenerate',)"""
    if a == b or c == d: return ('degenerate',)
    r = (b[0]-a[0], b[1]-a[1])
    s = (d[0]-c[0], d[1]-c[1])
    den = r[0]*s[1] - r[1]*s[0]
    ac  = (c[0]-a[0], c[1]-a[1])
    if den == 0:
        return ('same',) if ac[0]*r[1] - ac[1]*r[0] == 0 else ('parallel',)
    t = Fraction(ac[0]*s[1] - ac[1]*s[0], den)
    return ('point', (a[0] + t*r[0], a[1] + t*r[1]))

    Returning a tagged result rather than a nullable point forces the caller to handle the three geometric cases, which is where these routines are usually misused.

    Fraction keeps the answer exact. If the caller only needs to compare two intersection points (as in a sweep line), skip the fraction entirely and cross-multiply — that stays in integers and is far faster.

    Test with: crossing lines, parallel distinct, identical, a shared point, and degenerate inputs. Each is a separate branch and each occurs in real data.

  9. Program

    Implement half-plane intersection in O(nlog n) and use it to find the area of a feasible region.

    Solution
    from collections import deque
def half_plane_intersection(planes):
    """each plane: (point, direction); the region is to the LEFT of each"""
    planes.sort(key=lambda h: angle_key(h[1]))
    dq = deque()
    for h in planes:
        while len(dq) >= 2 and not left_of(h, inter(dq[-2], dq[-1])): dq.pop()
        while len(dq) >= 2 and not left_of(h, inter(dq[0],  dq[1])):  dq.popleft()
        if dq and cross(dq[-1][1], h[1]) == 0:            # same direction
            if left_of(dq[-1], h[0]): continue            # h is redundant
            dq.pop()
        dq.append(h)
    while len(dq) >= 3 and not left_of(dq[0],  inter(dq[-2], dq[-1])): dq.pop()
    while len(dq) >= 3 and not left_of(dq[-1], inter(dq[0],  dq[1])):  dq.popleft()
    if len(dq) < 3: return []                             # empty or unbounded
    return [inter(dq[i], dq[(i+1) % len(dq)]) for i in range(len(dq))]

    Three subtleties account for most bugs here. The parallel same-direction case must keep only the tighter constraint. The final closing loop is required because the deque's two ends must be checked against each other. And an unbounded region produces fewer than three half-planes surviving — which must be reported, not treated as empty.

    Add a large bounding box (four half-planes at ±10⁹) up front to guarantee boundedness; then a genuinely unbounded feasible region shows up as a polygon touching the box, which is usually what you want anyway.

  10. Program

    Implement Seidel's randomised algorithm for 2D linear programming.

    Solution
    import random
def lp2d(constraints, cx, cy):
    """maximise cx·x + cy·y subject to a·x + b·y <= c"""
    random.shuffle(constraints)
    # start at a large bounding box vertex in the objective direction
    best = (BIG if cx > 0 else -BIG, BIG if cy > 0 else -BIG)
    for i, (a, b, c) in enumerate(constraints):
        if a*best[0] + b*best[1] <= c: continue          # still feasible
        # the new optimum lies ON this line: solve a 1D LP along it
        best = solve_1d(constraints[:i], (a, b, c), cx, cy)
        if best is None: return None                      # infeasible
    return best

    Why it is linear: by backwards analysis, after processing i constraints the optimum is determined by at most 2 of them, so a randomly-ordered constraint i is violated with probability ≤ 2/i. The re-solve costs O(i), so the expected total is ∑_i \frac2i· O(i) = O(n). ∎

    The shuffle is essential — with adversarial ordering the algorithm is Θ(n²), and the input order in a real problem is very often adversarial by accident (sorted, or grouped by source).

    The 1D subproblem is intersecting intervals on a line, which is a scan for the tightest lower and upper bounds — a few lines, and the place where infeasibility is detected.

  11. Program

    Clip a polygon against a convex polygon (Sutherland–Hodgman) and against a half-plane.

    Solution
    def clip_halfplane(poly, a, b):
    """keep the part of `poly` to the LEFT of the directed line a→b"""
    out = []
    n = len(poly)
    for i in range(n):
        cur, nxt = poly[i], poly[(i+1) % n]
        c1 = cross(a, b, cur)
        c2 = cross(a, b, nxt)
        if c1 >= 0: out.append(cur)
        if (c1 > 0) != (c2 > 0) and c1 != c2:
            out.append(line_point(a, b, cur, nxt))       # the crossing point
    return out

def clip_convex(subject, window):
    for i in range(len(window)):
        subject = clip_halfplane(subject, window[i], window[(i+1) % len(window)])
        if not subject: break
    return subject

    Sutherland–Hodgman clips against one edge at a time, so it is O(nm) for an n-gon against an m-gon. It requires the window to be convex; the subject may be any simple polygon, though a concave subject can produce degenerate connecting edges.

    The output vertices are rational. For an area computation that is fine (the shoelace formula handles fractions), but feeding the result back into an integer-coordinate algorithm requires care.

    For convex-against-convex, the O(n+m) rotating-calipers merge is better and is what computational-geometry libraries use.

  12. Program

    Use duality to convert a "maximum points on a line" problem into an arrangement problem.

    Solution
    # Primal: given n points, find the line containing the most of them.
# Dual:   each point (a,b) → line y = ax − b.  Collinear points become
#         CONCURRENT lines, so the answer is the arrangement vertex of
#         highest degree.
def max_collinear_dual(points):
    lines = [(a, -b) for a, b in points]      # y = ax + (−b)
    from collections import Counter
    best = 0
    for i in range(len(lines)):
        cnt = Counter()
        for j in range(len(lines)):
            if i == j: continue
            m1, k1 = lines[i]; m2, k2 = lines[j]
            if m1 == m2: continue              # parallel: no intersection
            # the intersection x-coordinate, as an exact fraction
            from fractions import Fraction
            cnt[Fraction(k2 - k1, m1 - m2)] += 1
        best = max(best, max(cnt.values(), default=0) + 1)
    return best

    Both the primal (group by slope from each point, Chapter 54 problem 13) and the dual (group by intersection x-coordinate) are O(n²log n) — the duality does not improve this particular problem, and that is worth knowing.

    Where duality genuinely helps: problems asking about all lines through pairs of points, or about the levels of an arrangement (the k-th smallest line at each x), where the dual formulation admits a sweep that the primal does not. And the minimum-area triangle among n points is solved in O(n²) by sweeping the dual arrangement — the primal has no comparable algorithm.

  13. Program

    Solve: given n points and a query line, count the points on each side, in O(log n) after preprocessing.

    Solution
    # Preprocess: build the convex layers, or use a partition tree.
# Simple practical approach for many queries: sort by angle around a pivot
# and answer with binary search — O(n log n) preprocessing, O(log n) per query
# for lines through the pivot.  For ARBITRARY lines, use a partition tree:
#
#   Matoušek's simplicial partition gives O(n) space and O(√n) query time
#   for half-plane range counting — provably near-optimal.
#
# For offline queries, the dual is better:
#   each point → a line;  each query line → a point;
#   "points below the query line" = "dual lines above the dual point",
#   answerable by a sweep over the arrangement.

    The honest answer is that O(log n) per query is not achievable for arbitrary half-plane counting with subquadratic space — the known lower bounds put the trade-off at roughly Q(n)· S(n) = Ω(n), so O(√n) query with O(n) space (partition trees) or O(log n) query with O(n²) space (the full arrangement with a point-location structure) are the two ends.

    Recognising that a problem's stated bound is impossible is itself a useful skill. In practice the answers are: precompute the arrangement if queries vastly outnumber points; use a partition tree if space matters; or process offline with a sweep if all queries are known in advance, which is usually the case in a contest.

  14. Program

    Implement a robust "point on segment" and "segments overlap" test, and fuzz it against a brute-force rational check.

    Solution
    from fractions import Fraction
import random
def on_segment(a, b, p):
    return (cross(a, b, p) == 0
            and min(a[0],b[0]) <= p[0] <= max(a[0],b[0])
            and min(a[1],b[1]) <= p[1] <= max(a[1],b[1]))

def brute_on_segment(a, b, p):
    """exact: is p = a + t(b−a) for some t in [0,1]?"""
    if a == b: return p == a
    dx, dy = b[0]-a[0], b[1]-a[1]
    if dx: t = Fraction(p[0]-a[0], dx)
    else:  t = Fraction(p[1]-a[1], dy)
    return 0 <= t <= 1 and a[0] + t*dx == p[0] and a[1] + t*dy == p[1]

for _ in range(200000):
    a, b, p = [(random.randint(-3,3), random.randint(-3,3)) for _ in range(3)]
    assert on_segment(a,b,p) == brute_on_segment(a,b,p), (a,b,p)

    The small coordinate range is deliberate: it produces a high density of degenerate cases — collinear triples, coincident points, zero-length segments, axis-aligned segments — which are exactly the inputs where geometry code fails and which random real-valued points never generate.

    The brute-force version is obviously correct but slow and awkward; the fast version is subtle. Fuzzing one against the other over 200,000 degenerate-rich cases is a far stronger guarantee than any set of hand-written test cases, and it takes three lines to set up.

Chapter 56

Polygons: area, centroid and point location

The shoelace formula computes a polygon's signed area in one pass, and its sign tells you the orientation. Point-in-polygon is a ray cast whose whole difficulty is degenerate cases, and Pick's theorem links area to lattice points exactly.

SHOELACE (signed area, vertices in order): 2A = Σ_{i} (x_i·y_{i+1} − x_{i+1}·y_i) indices mod n A > 0 ⟺ counterclockwise |A| = the area, always Works for ANY simple polygon, convex or not. CENTROID (of the area, not the vertices): C_x = (1/(6A)) Σ (x_i + x_{i+1})(x_i·y_{i+1} − x_{i+1}·y_i) C_y = (1/(6A)) Σ (y_i + y_{i+1})(x_i·y_{i+1} − x_{i+1}·y_i) PERIMETER: Σ |v_{i+1} − v_i| — the only one needing square roots

The shoelace formula is a sum of triangle areas from the origin, with signs cancelling the parts outside the polygon. That is why it works for non-convex polygons and why the sign encodes orientation — it is Chapter 45's determinant summed around the boundary.

Point in polygon

Ray casting, with the degenerate cases handled
bool inside(const vector<P>& poly, P p){
    int n = poly.size();
    bool in = false;
    for (int i = 0, j = n-1; i < n; j = i++){
        P a = poly[j], b = poly[i];
        if (on_segment(a, b, p)) return true;         // ON the boundary
        // does the upward ray from p cross edge (a,b)?
        // the half-open test [min, max) avoids double-counting vertices
        if ((a.y > p.y) != (b.y > p.y)){
            // x-coordinate of the crossing, compared without division
            long long t = (b.x - a.x) * (p.y - a.y) - (p.x - a.x) * (b.y - a.y);
            if ((b.y > a.y) ? (t > 0) : (t < 0)) in = !in;
        }
    }
    return in;
}
Principle

The correctness of ray casting rests entirely on the half-open comparison (a.y > p.y) != (b.y > p.y). It counts an edge exactly when the ray passes its lower endpoint but not its upper one — so a ray through a vertex crosses exactly one of the two incident edges, and a horizontal edge is never counted. Every other formulation needs special cases; this one needs none.

Pick's theorem

For a simple polygon with INTEGER vertices: A = I + B/2 − 1 A = area, I = interior lattice points, B = boundary lattice points Boundary points on the edge from a to b: gcd(|Δx|, |Δy|) (counting one endpoint per edge gives the total B around the polygon)

So I = A - B/2 + 1 counts interior lattice points in O(nlog C) — no enumeration, however large the polygon. Combined with the shoelace formula it is entirely exact.

Interview angle

"Compute a polygon's area" expects the shoelace formula in one pass with no triangulation. The follow-up worth volunteering: use twice the area as an integer and divide only at the end, so integer input gives an exact answer — polygon areas are always half-integers, and returning 2A avoids floating point entirely.

Problem set — 14 problemstheory & programming
  1. Theory

    Prove the shoelace formula.

    Solution

    Triangulate the polygon by connecting every vertex to the origin. The signed area of triangle (O, v_i, v_{i+1}) is \frac12(x_iy_{i+1}-x_{i+1}y_i) (Chapter 54).

    Summing around the boundary, the triangles outside the polygon are traversed in the opposite orientation and contribute negatively, cancelling exactly the parts counted spuriously. The net is the polygon's signed area. ∎

    A cleaner argument is Green's theorem: A = \frac12\oint(xdy - ydx), and evaluating the line integral along each straight edge gives exactly the shoelace term. That version makes the "any simple polygon" generality obvious, since Green's theorem needs only a simple closed curve.

    The formula is translation invariant despite involving the origin — shifting all vertices by t changes each term but not the sum, which is a good invariant to assert in tests.

  2. Theory

    Prove Pick's theorem for a triangle, then sketch the general case.

    Solution

    Additivity: if a polygon is split into two by a diagonal, and Pick's formula holds for each part, it holds for the whole. Let the diagonal contain d interior lattice points plus its two endpoints. Then I = I_1+I_2+d and B = B_1+B_2-2d-2, and

    A_1+A_2 = (I_1+\tfrac{B_1}2-1)+(I_2+\tfrac{B_2}2-1) = I + \tfrac B2 - 1 ✓.

    Base cases: for a lattice rectangle with sides w, h the formula gives (w-1)(h-1) + (2w+2h)/(2) - 1 = wh ✓. A right triangle is half a rectangle, and the diagonal's lattice points make the halving work out. A general lattice triangle decomposes into a rectangle minus right triangles.

    General polygon: every simple polygon can be triangulated with diagonals, and additivity propagates the result. ∎

    Pick's theorem is specific to two dimensions — the analogous statement fails in 3D (the Reeve tetrahedra have the same lattice-point counts but different volumes), which is why Ehrhart theory (Chapter 52) is the right generalisation.

  3. Theory

    Count the lattice points on the segment from (x_1,y_1) to (x_2,y_2).

    Solution

    The lattice points strictly between the endpoints are those of the form (x_1,y_1) + t(Δ x,Δ y) with t∈(0,1) rational and both coordinates integral. Writing g = gcd(|Δ x|,|Δ y|), the primitive step is (Δ x/g, Δ y/g), so there are exactly g-1 interior lattice points and g+1 including both endpoints. ∎

    For a polygon, summing g over all edges counts each vertex once (as the endpoint of one edge), giving

    B = ∑_{edges}gcd(|Δ x|,|Δ y|).

    This is exactly the boundary count Pick's theorem needs, computable in O(nlog C). The degenerate case Δ x = Δ y = 0 (a repeated vertex) gives gcd(0,0) = 0 by convention, which is the right answer for a zero-length edge.

  4. Theory

    Explain why the half-open comparison in ray casting handles vertices and horizontal edges correctly.

    Solution

    The test (a.y > p.y) != (b.y > p.y) treats the edge's y-interval as half-open: an edge is considered iff exactly one endpoint is strictly above p_y.

    • A vertex at the ray's height: the two edges meeting there share that vertex. If the polygon passes through the level (one edge up, one down), exactly one edge has its upper endpoint above and is counted — one crossing, correct. If the polygon merely touches the level (a local max or min), both edges are on the same side, neither is counted — zero crossings, also correct.
    • A horizontal edge has a_y = b_y, so the two comparisons agree and it is never counted — correct, since a horizontal edge at the ray's level does not constitute a crossing.

    Every other formulation (using ≥, or comparing to a midpoint) requires enumerating these cases explicitly. This one gets them all from a single asymmetry, which is why it is the standard. ∎

  5. Theory

    Derive the centroid formula for a polygon and explain why it differs from the average of the vertices.

    Solution

    The centroid of the area is (1)/(A)\int\int_P xdA. Decomposing into triangles from the origin, triangle i has area a_i = \frac12(x_iy_{i+1}-x_{i+1}y_i) and centroid \frac13(O + v_i + v_{i+1}). Weighting by signed area:

    C = (1)/(A)∑_i a_i·\frac{v_i+v_{i+1}}{3} = (1)/(6A)∑_i (v_i+v_{i+1})(x_iy_{i+1}-x_{i+1}y_i). ∎

    Why not the vertex average: the vertex average weights every vertex equally, which is the centroid of point masses at the vertices — a different object. A square with one side subdivided into 100 vertices has the same area centroid but a wildly different vertex average.

    Three distinct centroids exist for a polygon: of the vertices, of the boundary (weighted by edge length), and of the area. Problems rarely say which, and they differ; the area centroid is almost always the intended one.

  6. Theory

    Given a convex polygon and a query point, describe an O(log n) test and explain why non-convex polygons need O(n).

    Solution

    For a convex polygon, binary search on the fan from v_0 (Chapter 54 problem 5): O(log n).

    For a non-convex polygon, no such monotone structure exists — the boundary can wind arbitrarily, so a query point's status is not determined by a logarithmic number of orientation tests against the vertices. Ray casting is O(n) per query.

    But with preprocessing, point location in any planar subdivision is O(log n) per query using O(n) space: build a trapezoidal decomposition (randomised incremental, expected O(nlog n)) or Kirkpatrick's triangulation hierarchy. So the O(n) is a statement about the unpreprocessed case only.

    The practical rule: one query, ray cast; many queries against a fixed polygon, build a trapezoidal map or, for a monotone polygon, a simple chain decomposition giving O(log n) with much less machinery.

  7. Theory

    Prove that every simple polygon can be triangulated using n-3 diagonals, producing n-2 triangles.

    Solution

    Existence of a diagonal: take the leftmost vertex v (lowest, breaking ties). Its two neighbours a and b form a triangle avb. If no other vertex lies inside avb, then ab is a diagonal. Otherwise take the vertex inside avb farthest from line ab; the segment from v to it is a diagonal. ∎

    Induction: a diagonal splits the polygon into two simple polygons with k+1 and n-k+1 vertices. By induction they use k-2 and n-k-1 diagonals, and adding the splitting one gives n-3. Triangle count follows from Chapter 3's internal-node identity, or directly by induction. ∎

    Algorithms: ear clipping is O(n²) and simple; monotone-polygon decomposition plus triangulation is O(nlog n) and standard; Chazelle's algorithm is O(n) and famously unimplementable.

    Corollary (the art gallery theorem): 3-colour the triangulation's vertices; the least-used colour class has at most ⌊ n/3⌋ vertices and guards the whole polygon.

  8. Program

    Implement the shoelace formula, centroid and perimeter, returning exact values where possible.

    Solution
    from fractions import Fraction
import math
def area2(poly):
    """returns TWICE the signed area — an exact integer for integer input"""
    n = len(poly); s = 0
    for i in range(n):
        x1, y1 = poly[i]; x2, y2 = poly[(i+1) % n]
        s += x1*y2 - x2*y1
    return s

def centroid(poly):
    a2 = area2(poly)
    if a2 == 0: return None                     # degenerate polygon
    cx = cy = Fraction(0)
    n = len(poly)
    for i in range(n):
        x1, y1 = poly[i]; x2, y2 = poly[(i+1) % n]
        cr = x1*y2 - x2*y1
        cx += Fraction((x1 + x2) * cr)
        cy += Fraction((y1 + y2) * cr)
    return (cx / (3*a2), cy / (3*a2))

def perimeter(poly):
    n = len(poly)
    return sum(math.dist(poly[i], poly[(i+1) % n]) for i in range(n))

    Returning area2 rather than the area keeps integer input exact — polygon areas are half-integers, so twice the area is always an integer. Divide by 2 only when producing output.

    The centroid is rational and Fraction keeps it exact. The perimeter is the only quantity genuinely requiring floating point, since square roots of integers are irrational.

    Test invariants: area is translation-invariant; reversing the vertex order negates area2; the centroid of a rectangle is its middle; and the centroid must lie inside a convex polygon.

  9. Program

    Implement point-in-polygon by ray casting and by the winding number; compare on a self-intersecting polygon.

    Solution
    def ray_cast(poly, p):
    n = len(poly); inside = False
    for i in range(n):
        a, b = poly[i], poly[(i+1) % n]
        if on_segment(a, b, p): return 'boundary'
        if (a[1] > p[1]) != (b[1] > p[1]):
            t = cross(a, b, p)
            if (b[1] > a[1]) == (t > 0): inside = not inside
    return 'inside' if inside else 'outside'

def winding_number(poly, p):
    n = len(poly); wn = 0
    for i in range(n):
        a, b = poly[i], poly[(i+1) % n]
        if a[1] <= p[1]:
            if b[1] > p[1] and cross(a, b, p) > 0: wn += 1
        else:
            if b[1] <= p[1] and cross(a, b, p) < 0: wn -= 1
    return wn

    For a simple polygon the two agree: winding number is ±1 inside and 0 outside.

    For a self-intersecting polygon they differ, and the difference is meaningful. Ray casting implements the even–odd rule (a doubly-wound region counts as outside); the winding number implements the non-zero rule (it counts as inside). Both are used in graphics — SVG's fill-rule lets you choose — and neither is more correct; they answer different questions.

    Constructing a pentagram and querying its centre demonstrates the divergence immediately: even–odd says outside, non-zero says inside.

  10. Program

    Use Pick's theorem to count lattice points inside a polygon with coordinates up to 10⁹.

    Solution
    from math import gcd
def lattice_points(poly):
    n = len(poly)
    a2 = abs(area2(poly))                       # 2A, exact integer
    B = sum(gcd(abs(poly[i][0] - poly[(i+1)%n][0]),
                abs(poly[i][1] - poly[(i+1)%n][1])) for i in range(n))
    # Pick: A = I + B/2 − 1  ⟹  I = (2A − B + 2)/2
    I = (a2 - B + 2) // 2
    return I, B, I + B

    Exact and O(nlog C) — completely independent of the polygon's size, so a triangle with vertices at 10⁹ containing 10^{17} lattice points is handled instantly.

    Preconditions: the polygon must be simple (Pick's theorem fails for self-intersecting ones) and have integer vertices. Assert both; the second is easy to violate when the polygon came from an intersection computation (Chapter 55).

    The division by 2 is exact because 2A - B is always even for a lattice polygon — a small fact worth asserting, since a violation indicates non-integer vertices or a non-simple polygon.

  11. Program

    Implement ear-clipping triangulation of a simple polygon.

    Solution
    def triangulate(poly):
    n = len(poly)
    idx = list(range(n))
    if area2(poly) < 0: idx.reverse()            # ensure counterclockwise
    tris = []
    guard = 0
    while len(idx) > 3:
        found = False
        for k in range(len(idx)):
            i0, i1, i2 = idx[k-1], idx[k], idx[(k+1) % len(idx)]
            a, b, c = poly[i0], poly[i1], poly[i2]
            if cross(a, b, c) <= 0: continue      # reflex vertex, not an ear
            if any(point_in_triangle(poly[j], a, b, c)
                   for j in idx if j not in (i0, i1, i2)): continue
            tris.append((i0, i1, i2))
            idx.pop(k); found = True; break
        assert found, "no ear found — polygon is not simple"
        guard += 1
    tris.append(tuple(idx))
    return tris

    O(n²) — each of n-2 ear removals scans for an ear and checks containment. The two-ears theorem guarantees an ear always exists for a simple polygon with n\ge4, so the assertion is a genuine simplicity check rather than defensive padding.

    Both conditions are required: convexity of the vertex (cross > 0) and emptiness of the triangle. A convex vertex whose triangle contains another vertex is not an ear, and skipping that check produces overlapping triangles on non-convex input.

    For production use, monotone decomposition gives O(nlog n); ear clipping is chosen for its simplicity and because it handles holes with a standard bridging preprocessing step.

  12. Program

    Compute the area of the union of n axis-aligned rectangles in O(nlog n).

    Solution
    # Sweep line over x, maintaining the total covered y-length with a
# "count and cover" segment tree over the compressed y-coordinates.
def rectangle_union_area(rects):
    events = []
    ys = set()
    for x1, y1, x2, y2 in rects:
        events.append((x1, +1, y1, y2))
        events.append((x2, -1, y1, y2))
        ys.add(y1); ys.add(y2)
    ys = sorted(ys)
    tree = CoverTree(ys)                        # supports add(y1,y2,±1), covered()
    events.sort()
    area = 0; prev_x = events[0][0]
    for x, delta, y1, y2 in events:
        area += tree.covered() * (x - prev_x)
        tree.add(y1, y2, delta)
        prev_x = x
    return area

    The segment tree stores, per node, a coverage count and the covered length of its interval. Because ranges are only ever added and removed in matched pairs, no lazy propagation is needed — a node with positive count reports its full length, otherwise it reports the sum of its children. That specialisation is what makes this classic structure so short.

    O(nlog n). The same sweep computes the union's perimeter (track the number of boundary segments), the area covered at least k times (store per-count lengths), and the maximum overlap depth.

    For non-axis-aligned polygons the analogous problem is much harder and is solved by a general polygon-clipping library (Vatti, Greiner–Hormann) rather than a sweep.

  13. Program

    Given a polygon and a line, compute the area on each side of the line.

    Solution
    def area_split_by_line(poly, a, b):
    """returns (area left of a→b, area right)"""
    left  = clip_halfplane(poly, a, b)           # Chapter 55
    right = clip_halfplane(poly, b, a)           # the reversed line
    return abs(area2(left))/2, abs(area2(right))/2

    Clipping to each half-plane and taking areas is correct for a convex polygon, where each half is a single connected piece.

    For a non-convex polygon the line may cut it into several components, and Sutherland–Hodgman produces a single vertex list with degenerate connecting edges along the cut line. The shoelace formula still gives the correct total area, because those degenerate edges enclose zero area — so the computation works even though the polygon returned is not a faithful representation of the region.

    That is worth knowing precisely: the area is right, the polygon is not. If you need the actual components, use a proper polygon-clipping algorithm that returns a list of loops.

    Application: binary search on the line's offset to find the cut that bisects the area — a common contest problem, and the ham-sandwich theorem's one-dimensional case.

  14. Program

    Verify Pick's theorem by brute force on random small lattice polygons.

    Solution
    import random
from math import gcd
def brute_lattice_count(poly, lim=12):
    I = B = 0
    n = len(poly)
    for x in range(-lim, lim+1):
        for y in range(-lim, lim+1):
            p = (x, y)
            on = any(on_segment(poly[i], poly[(i+1)%n], p) for i in range(n))
            if on: B += 1
            elif ray_cast(poly, p) == 'inside': I += 1
    return I, B

for _ in range(500):
    poly = random_simple_lattice_polygon(lim=8)
    I, B = brute_lattice_count(poly)
    a2 = abs(area2(poly))
    assert a2 == 2*I + B - 2, (poly, a2, I, B)

    Generating random simple lattice polygons is itself the hard part: pick random points and take the convex hull for a guaranteed-simple convex case, or use the 2-opt "uncross" heuristic (repeatedly swap crossing edges) to make a random permutation simple.

    The assertion in the form 2A = 2I + B - 2 keeps everything integral — no division, no rounding, an exact equality that either holds or does not.

    Running it on deliberately non-simple polygons shows the theorem failing, which is a good way to internalise that the simplicity hypothesis is load-bearing rather than technical.

Chapter 57

Convex hull

The smallest convex set containing the points, computable in O(n log n) by sorting and two linear scans. It is the gateway to diameter, width, minimum enclosing shapes, and the convex hull trick for DP.

The convex hull of a point set is the smallest convex polygon containing all of them — equivalently the intersection of all half-planes containing the set, or the set of all convex combinations.

Gift wrapping (Jarvis march) O(nh) h = hull size; good when h is tiny Graham scan O(n log n) sort by angle, then one stack pass ANDREW'S MONOTONE CHAIN O(n log n) sort by (x,y), two passes — preferred Chan's algorithm O(n log h) optimal, output-sensitive, intricate Quickhull O(n log n) expected, O(n²) worst Lower bound: Ω(n log n) by reduction from sorting (Chapter 13).

Andrew's monotone chain

The implementation to memorise
vector<P> hull(vector<P> p){
    sort(p.begin(), p.end());                     // by x, then y
    p.erase(unique(p.begin(), p.end()), p.end());
    int n = p.size(), k = 0;
    if (n < 3) return p;
    vector<P> h(2*n);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++){                  // lower hull
        while (k >= 2 && cross(h[k-2], h[k-1], p[i]) <= 0) k--;
        h[k++] = p[i];
    }
    for (int i = n-2, t = k+1; i >= 0; i--){      // upper hull
        while (k >= t && cross(h[k-2], h[k-1], p[i]) <= 0) k--;
        h[k++] = p[i];
    }
    h.resize(k-1);                                // drop the repeated start
    return h;                                     // counterclockwise
}

Two decisions in that code carry all the subtlety. Sorting by (x,y) rather than by angle avoids atan2 entirely and makes the algorithm exact for integer input. And the comparison <= 0 versus < 0 decides whether collinear boundary points are kept — <= 0 drops them, < 0 keeps them, and which you want depends on the problem.

Principle

Decide explicitly whether collinear points belong on the hull. For area and diameter they are harmless either way; for "how many points lie on the hull boundary" the answer changes; and for rotating calipers, keeping them can cause infinite loops. Choose, and write a comment saying which.

What the hull unlocks

ProblemMethodCost after the hull
Diameter (farthest pair)rotating calipersO(h)
Width (minimum strip)rotating calipersO(h)
Minimum-area bounding boxcalipers; a side lies on the hullO(h)
Maximum-distance pair to a lineternary search on the hullO(log h)
Point in hullbinary search on the fanO(log h)
Minkowski sum of convex setsmerge edge vectors by angleO(h_1+h_2)
DP optimisationconvex hull trick (Chapter 64)O(log n) per query

Rotating calipers
