Two parallel supporting lines rotated around the hull. As the angle sweeps through 180°, each contact point advances monotonically, so the total work is O(h) — an amortised two-pointer argument on a cyclic sequence.

The diameter is the maximum distance over antipodal pairs; the width is the minimum over (edge, farthest vertex) pairs; the minimum-area bounding box has a side flush with a hull edge (a theorem worth knowing, since it reduces an infinite search over angles to h candidates).

Interview angle

"Find the two farthest points" is O(n²) naively; the strong answer is hull plus rotating calipers at O(nlog n), with the observation that the farthest pair are both hull vertices — because moving a point toward the interior along any direction only shortens distances.

Problem set — 14 problemstheory & programming
  1. Theory

    Prove that the farthest pair of points are both vertices of the convex hull.

    Solution

    Suppose p is not a hull vertex, so p = ∑ λ_iv_i is a convex combination of hull vertices with ∑λ_i = 1, λ_i\ge0. For any point q,

    |p - q| = |∑λ_i(v_i - q)| ≤ ∑λ_i|v_i-q| ≤ max_i|v_i-q|,

    by the triangle inequality and then by the fact that a weighted average is at most the maximum. So replacing p by the maximising v_i does not decrease the distance. ∎

    Applying this to both points of a farthest pair shows some farthest pair consists of hull vertices — and since the hull has h ≤ n vertices, this reduces the search space, though not by itself below O(h²). Rotating calipers gets it to O(h).

    The same argument shows the diameter, the minimum enclosing circle's defining points, and the minimum bounding box all depend only on the hull.

  2. Theory

    Prove that convex hull requires Ω(nlog n) comparisons.

    Solution

    Reduce sorting to convex hull. Given n reals x_1,…,x_n, map each to the point (x_i, x_i²) on the parabola y = x².

    Since the parabola is strictly convex, every point is a hull vertex, and the hull's lower chain visits them in increasing order of x. So reading the hull off gives the sorted order in O(n).

    A convex hull algorithm faster than O(nlog n) would therefore sort faster, contradicting the comparison lower bound of Chapter 13. ∎

    Caveat: the bound is for the algebraic decision-tree model. Output-sensitive algorithms achieve O(nlog h), which is better when h is small and matches the bound when h = Θ(n) — the reduction produces exactly that case, so there is no contradiction.

  3. Theory

    Explain rotating calipers and prove the O(h) bound.

    Solution

    Maintain two parallel supporting lines and rotate them through 180°. At each moment the contact points are an antipodal pair — a pair admitting parallel supporting lines.

    As the angle increases, each contact point moves monotonically around the hull (it never goes backwards, because the supporting direction rotates monotonically). Over a full 180° sweep each pointer therefore traverses the hull at most once.

    Total pointer movement: O(h). ∎ This is the two-pointer amortisation argument (Chapter 12) applied to a cyclic sequence.

    The number of antipodal pairs is O(h), which is also the reason the diameter can be found in linear time after the hull: there are only linearly many candidates, not \binom h2.

    Degeneracy warning: collinear hull points create ties in the advance condition and can cause the pointers to loop. Removing collinear points from the hull is the standard precaution.

  4. Theory

    Show that the minimum-area bounding rectangle has a side collinear with a hull edge.

    Solution

    Consider the minimum-area enclosing rectangle at angle θ, and let A(θ) be its area. As θ varies, the supporting points change only at discrete angles, and between those angles the width and height are w(θ) = a\cosθ+b\sinθ style expressions — so A(θ) is a smooth function whose critical points can be analysed.

    The standard argument shows A is minimised at a boundary of the smooth pieces, i.e. at an angle where a rectangle side contains a hull edge. Intuitively: if no side touches an edge, the rectangle can be rotated slightly to reduce the area, because the area is locally a strictly concave function of the angle. ∎ (Freeman and Shapira, 1975.)

    Consequence: only h candidate angles need testing, one per hull edge, and rotating calipers evaluates all of them in O(h) total. Without this theorem the problem would be a continuous optimisation over angles.

    The analogous statement in 3D is false for the minimum-volume box, which is why that problem is much harder (O(n³) by O'Rourke).

  5. Theory

    Define the Minkowski sum of two convex polygons and give an O(n+m) algorithm.

    Solution

    A ⊕ B = {a+b : a∈ A, b∈ B}. For convex polygons the sum is convex, and its edge vectors are exactly the union of A's and B's edge vectors, sorted by angle.

    Why: the supporting point of A⊕ B in direction d is (supporting point of A) + (supporting point of B), so as d rotates, the boundary traces A's edges and B's edges interleaved by angle.

    def minkowski(A, B):
    A = reorder_from_bottom_left(A); B = reorder_from_bottom_left(B)
    res = []; i = j = 0
    while i < len(A) or j < len(B):
        res.append(add(A[i % len(A)], B[j % len(B)]))
        c = cross(edge(A, i), edge(B, j))
        if c >= 0: i += 1
        if c <= 0: j += 1
    return res

    O(n+m) — a merge by edge angle. ∎

    Uses: collision detection (A and B intersect iff 0 ∈ A ⊕ (-B), the basis of the GJK algorithm), motion planning with a robot of non-zero size (grow the obstacles by the robot's shape), and the "minimum distance between two convex polygons" problem.

  6. Theory

    Describe the dynamic convex hull problem and state the achievable bounds.

    Solution

    Maintain the hull of a point set under insertions and deletions.

    • Insertions only: O(log n) amortised. Keep the upper and lower hulls in balanced BSTs keyed by x; inserting a point removes a contiguous run of now-interior vertices, and each vertex is removed at most once — an amortisation argument (Chapter 12).
    • Insertions and deletions: O(log² n) amortised by Overmars–van Leeuwen's hull tree; improved to O(log n) amortised by Brodal–Jacob (2002), though that structure is complex and rarely implemented.
    • Offline with deletions: use divide and conquer over time (each point is alive on an interval; process a segment tree over time), giving O(nlog² n) with a simple static hull as the primitive.

    The offline technique is the practical answer in a contest: it converts "dynamic with deletions" into O(log n) static problems, and it applies far beyond hulls — to connectivity, to minimum spanning trees, and to any structure supporting insert-only updates.

  7. Theory

    Explain Chan's algorithm and why it achieves O(nlog h).

    Solution

    Guess a value m for the hull size. Partition the points into ⌈ n/m⌉ groups of size m and compute each group's hull in O(mlog m) — total O(nlog m).

    Then run gift wrapping on the groups: at each step, find the next hull vertex by binary-searching each group's hull for its tangent point, taking the best. Each step costs O(\frac nmlog m), and if the true hull has h ≤ m vertices, m steps suffice — total O(nlog m).

    The guessing: try m = 2^{2^t} for t = 1,2,3,…, stopping when the wrapping completes. The costs form a geometric series dominated by the last term, and the last m is at most h², giving O(nlog h) overall. ∎

    This is optimal: it matches the Ω(nlog h) output-sensitive lower bound. In practice monotone chain is faster for all realistic inputs because of its tiny constant — Chan's algorithm is a beautiful result that is essentially never the right implementation choice.

  8. Program

    Implement Andrew's monotone chain with an option to keep or drop collinear points; test both.

    Solution
    def convex_hull(points, keep_collinear=False):
    pts = sorted(set(points))
    if len(pts) <= 2: return pts
    thresh = -1 if keep_collinear else 0        # cross <= thresh ⟹ pop
    def build(seq):
        h = []
        for p in seq:
            while len(h) >= 2 and cross(h[-2], h[-1], p) <= thresh: h.pop()
            h.append(p)
        return h
    lower = build(pts)
    upper = build(reversed(pts))
    return lower[:-1] + upper[:-1]              # counterclockwise

    Setting thresh = -1 makes the pop condition cross < 0, so collinear points (cross = 0) survive. That single parameter is the whole difference, and exposing it is better than silently choosing.

    Test both modes on: all points collinear (should return 2 points or all of them), duplicates, fewer than 3 points, and a square with points on its edges. Those four cases catch essentially every hull bug.

    The sorted(set(...)) deduplication matters: repeated points make the cross product zero and can cause the stack to underflow in the keep_collinear mode.

  9. Program

    Find the diameter of a point set using rotating calipers.

    Solution
    def diameter(points):
    h = convex_hull(points)                     # collinear points REMOVED
    n = len(h)
    if n == 1: return 0, (h[0], h[0])
    if n == 2: return dist2(h[0], h[1]), (h[0], h[1])
    best = 0; pair = None
    j = 1
    for i in range(n):
        ni = (i+1) % n
        # advance j while the triangle area grows — j is antipodal to edge i
        while cross(h[i], h[ni], h[(j+1) % n]) > cross(h[i], h[ni], h[j]):
            j = (j+1) % n
        for cand in (j, (j+1) % n):
            for endpoint in (i, ni):
                d = dist2(h[endpoint], h[cand])
                if d > best: best, pair = d, (h[endpoint], h[cand])
    return best, pair

    O(h) after the hull, so O(nlog n) total. Using squared distances keeps integer input exact — take the square root only when reporting.

    The while advances j to the vertex farthest from edge i, which is the antipodal partner. Because j only moves forward across the whole loop, the total advancement is O(h) — the amortisation of problem 3.

    Checking both j and j+1 against both endpoints of the edge handles the ties that arise when two vertices are equally far — omitting that is the classic source of an off-by-one wrong answer on symmetric inputs.

  10. Program

    Compute the minimum-area and minimum-perimeter enclosing rectangles.

    Solution
    import math
def min_bounding_rect(points):
    h = convex_hull(points)
    n = len(h)
    if n < 3: return degenerate_case(h)
    best_area = float('inf'); best = None
    j = k = l = 1
    for i in range(n):
        ni = (i+1) % n
        e = sub(h[ni], h[i])                     # the edge direction
        # advance the three calipers: farthest, rightmost, leftmost
        while cross_val(e, sub(h[(j+1) % n], h[i])) > cross_val(e, sub(h[j], h[i])):
            j = (j+1) % n
        while dot_val(e, sub(h[(k+1) % n], h[i])) > dot_val(e, sub(h[k], h[i])):
            k = (k+1) % n
        if i == 0: l = k
        while dot_val(e, sub(h[(l+1) % n], h[i])) <= dot_val(e, sub(h[l], h[i])):
            l = (l+1) % n
        elen = math.hypot(*e)
        height = abs(cross_val(e, sub(h[j], h[i]))) / elen
        width  = (dot_val(e, sub(h[k], h[i])) - dot_val(e, sub(h[l], h[i]))) / elen
        if width * height < best_area:
            best_area = width * height; best = (i, width, height)
    return best_area, best

    Three calipers rotate together: one for the height (farthest by cross product) and two for the width (extremes by dot product). All advance monotonically, so the whole loop is O(h).

    By problem 4 only the h edge-aligned angles need testing, which is what makes this a discrete search rather than a continuous optimisation.

    Minimum perimeter uses the same loop with 2(w+h) as the objective — and the two minima are generally attained at different angles, which is a good sanity check that the code is genuinely evaluating both.

  11. Program

    Implement the Minkowski sum of two convex polygons and use it for collision detection.

    Solution
    def minkowski_sum(A, B):
    A = rotate_to_lowest(A); B = rotate_to_lowest(B)     # start at min (y,x)
    A = A + A[:2]; B = B + B[:2]                          # wrap for edge access
    res = []; i = j = 0
    while i < len(A)-2 or j < len(B)-2:
        res.append(add(A[i], B[j]))
        c = cross(sub(A[i+1], A[i]), sub(B[j+1], B[j]))
        if c >= 0 and i < len(A)-2: i += 1
        if c <= 0 and j < len(B)-2: j += 1
    return res

def convex_polygons_intersect(A, B):
    """A and B intersect iff the origin is inside A ⊕ (−B)"""
    negB = [(-x, -y) for x, y in B]
    return point_in_convex(minkowski_sum(A, negB), (0, 0))

    Starting both polygons at their lowest-then-leftmost vertex is essential — the merge assumes both edge sequences begin at the same angular position (pointing right, by convention).

    The collision test is exact for integer coordinates and O(n+m). It is the mathematical core of the GJK algorithm used in every physics engine, which computes the distance between convex shapes by searching the Minkowski difference for its closest point to the origin — without ever constructing it.

    Verify by testing pairs of polygons known to touch, overlap and be disjoint, and by checking that the sum's area equals A_1 + A_2 + mixed area (the Brunn–Minkowski relation).

  12. Program

    Compute the convex layers (onion peeling) of a point set.

    Solution
    def convex_layers(points):
    remaining = list(points)
    layers = []
    while remaining:
        h = convex_hull(remaining)
        if not h: break
        layers.append(h)
        hs = set(h)
        remaining = [p for p in remaining if p not in hs]
    return layers

    Naively O(n²log n) — each peel is a full hull computation. Chazelle's algorithm computes all layers in O(nlog n) total using a dynamic hull structure, but it is intricate.

    The naive version is fine when the number of layers is small, which is the typical case: for n uniformly random points in a convex region the expected number of layers is Θ(n^{2/3}) and each hull has O(log n) or O(n^{1/3}) vertices depending on the region's shape.

    Uses: convex layers give a robust notion of "depth" in a point cloud — the outermost layers are the outliers — and the layer number is a two-dimensional analogue of rank, used in robust statistics as the basis of the bagplot.

  13. Program

    Solve: given n points, find the smallest circle enclosing all of them.

    Solution
    import random
def min_enclosing_circle(points):
    pts = points[:]; random.shuffle(pts)
    c, r2 = pts[0], 0
    for i, p in enumerate(pts):
        if dist2(c, p) <= r2: continue
        c, r2 = p, 0                                   # p is on the boundary
        for j in range(i):
            q = pts[j]
            if dist2(c, q) <= r2: continue
            c, r2 = midpoint(p, q), dist2(p, q) / 4    # p, q on the boundary
            for k in range(j):
                s = pts[k]
                if dist2(c, s) <= r2: continue
                c = circumcentre(p, q, s); r2 = dist2(c, p)
    return c, r2

    Welzl's algorithm, in its incremental form. The triple loop looks cubic but is O(n) expected: by backwards analysis, point i lies outside the circle of the first i-1 with probability ≤ 3/i (the circle is determined by at most 3 points), so the expected cost of the inner work is ∑_i \frac3i O(i) = O(n).

    The shuffle is mandatory — with adversarial ordering the algorithm is Θ(n³). This is the same randomised-incremental structure as Seidel's LP (Chapter 55), and for the same reason: the solution is determined by a constant number of constraints.

    Note it does not need the convex hull, though the answer is determined by hull points. Computing the hull first is a valid constant-factor optimisation.

  14. Program

    Stress-test a convex hull implementation against a brute-force O(n³) definition.

    Solution
    import random, itertools
def brute_hull_vertices(pts):
    """p is a hull VERTEX iff some line through p has all others strictly
       on one side — check all directed pairs"""
    out = set()
    for p in pts:
        for q in pts:
            if p == q: continue
            if all(cross(p, q, r) >= 0 for r in pts):
                out.add(p); out.add(q)
    return out

for _ in range(20000):
    n = random.randint(1, 8)
    pts = [(random.randint(-4,4), random.randint(-4,4)) for _ in range(n)]
    h = convex_hull(pts, keep_collinear=True)
    assert set(h) <= set(pts)
    assert all(cross(h[i], h[(i+1)%len(h)], h[(i+2)%len(h)]) >= 0
               for i in range(len(h))) or len(h) < 3       # convexity
    assert all(point_in_convex(h, p) for p in pts)          # containment

    Three properties characterise a correct hull, and asserting all three is stronger than comparing against any single reference implementation: the output is a subset of the input, it is convex, and it contains every input point.

    The small coordinate range produces many collinear and duplicate points — precisely the degenerate cases where hull implementations fail, and which uniformly random real coordinates never generate.

    Add the cases n=1, n=2, all points identical, and all points collinear as explicit tests: each takes a different code path and each has broken a published implementation at some point.

Chapter 58

Sweep line: closest pair and segment intersection

Move an imaginary line across the plane and maintain only what it touches. A two-dimensional problem becomes a one-dimensional dynamic problem, and O(n^2) becomes O(n log n).

The sweep-line paradigm has three components: an event queue (sorted positions where the active set changes), a status structure (what the line currently intersects, in sorted order), and an invariant asserting that everything before the line has been correctly handled.

EVENTS the discrete positions where something changes — usually the input coordinates, sometimes computed on the fly (intersections) STATUS a balanced BST or a set, ordered along the sweep line INVARIANT "all answers involving pairs entirely to the left are found" Cost: O(n log n) when there are O(n) events and each costs O(log n).

Closest pair

Closest pair by sweep — O(n log n), simpler than divide and conquer
sort points by x
best = infinity
active = ordered set, keyed by y
left = 0
for each point p in x-order:
    while p.x − points[left].x >= best:      # too far left to matter
        active.remove(points[left]); left += 1
    for q in active with q.y in [p.y − best, p.y + best]:
        best = min(best, dist(p, q))
    active.insert(p)

Why it is O(n log n): the strip of width `best` and height `2·best`
can hold at most 6 points pairwise ≥ best apart, so the inner loop
examines O(1) candidates per point.
Principle

The packing bound is what makes sweep-line geometry fast. In the closest-pair strip, points are pairwise at distance ≥ best, so only O(1) fit in the relevant window. Nearly every O(nlog n) geometric sweep has a corresponding packing or planarity argument bounding the work per event — find it, and the complexity follows.

Bentley–Ottmann: segment intersection

Report all k intersections among n segments in O((n+k)log n).

EVENTS segment left endpoint → insert into status segment right endpoint → remove from status intersection point → swap the two segments' order, discovered during the sweep and inserted into the queue STATUS the segments crossing the sweep line, ordered by y at that x KEY FACT Two segments can only intersect if they become ADJACENT in the status structure at some point before their crossing. So it suffices to test newly-adjacent pairs — O(1) tests per event.

The status order changes only at intersections, which is why detecting them by watching adjacency is complete. The output-sensitive bound matters: with k = Θ(n²) intersections it degenerates to O(n²log n), worse than the trivial algorithm — so use it when intersections are expected to be sparse.

Other sweeps worth knowing

ProblemStatus structureCost
Rectangle union areasegment tree over yO(nlog n)

Interview angle

"Find the closest pair of points" expects O(nlog n), and either divide and conquer or the sweep is fine. The point that impresses is the packing argument — at most six points fit in the strip because they are pairwise at least d apart — because that is the step that makes the algorithm's complexity work, and it is the part most people cannot reconstruct.

Problem set — 14 problemstheory & programming
  1. Theory

    Prove the packing bound in the closest-pair sweep: at most a constant number of candidates per point.

    Solution

    When processing p, all active points q satisfy p_x - q_x < d (where d is the current best) and we only consider |p_y - q_y| < d. So candidates lie in a d × 2d rectangle to the left of p.

    All active points are pairwise at distance ≥ d (otherwise d would already be smaller). Partition the rectangle into six \frac d2 × (2d)/(3) cells; each cell has diameter √{(d²)/(4)+(4d²)/(9)} = d√{(25)/(36)} = (5d)/(6) < d, so each holds at most one point.

    Hence at most 6 candidates. ∎

    The constant is not important; what matters is that it is bounded independently of n, which makes the inner loop O(1) amortised and the whole sweep O(nlog n), dominated by the sort and the BST operations.

    The divide-and-conquer version of closest pair (Chapter 10) uses the same argument with the constant 7, for the same reason.

  2. Theory

    Prove the key lemma of Bentley–Ottmann: intersecting segments become adjacent before crossing.

    Solution

    Let segments s and t intersect at a point with x-coordinate x_0, and suppose neither endpoint lies at x_0. Just before x_0 they are both in the status structure, with (say) s above t.

    Consider the moment they become adjacent. Immediately before x_0 their y-coordinates converge, so any segment between them must exit the status structure or cross one of them first — and each such event occurs at a smaller x. By induction on the number of segments between them, there is a moment before x_0 at which s and t are adjacent. ∎

    Consequence: testing only newly-adjacent pairs finds every intersection. Each event creates O(1) new adjacencies (an insertion creates 2, a deletion 1, a swap 2), so the total number of tests is O(n+k).

    The lemma fails for degenerate input — three segments through one point, or vertical segments — which is why robust implementations perturb symbolically or handle those cases explicitly.

  3. Theory

    Analyse the complexity of Bentley–Ottmann and explain when it is worse than brute force.

    Solution

    Events: 2n endpoints plus k intersections, each processed in O(log n) (a BST operation plus O(1) intersection tests). Total O((n+k)log n).

    Worse than brute force when k is large: with k = Θ(n²) the sweep is O(n²log n) while the trivial all-pairs test is O(n²). The crossover is around k ≈ n²/log n.

    So the algorithm is output-sensitive, and its advantage depends on intersections being sparse — which they usually are in map data, VLSI layouts and mesh processing, the applications it was designed for.

    The optimal algorithm is Chazelle–Edelsbrunner at O(nlog n + k), removing the log from the output term. It is considerably more complex and rarely implemented; Bentley–Ottmann remains the practical choice.

    If you only need to know whether any intersection exists, the Shamos–Hoey variant stops at the first one and is O(nlog n) unconditionally.

  4. Theory

    Describe Fortune's algorithm for Voronoi diagrams and the role of the beach line.

    Solution

    Sweep a horizontal line downward. The beach line is the boundary of the region already determined — a sequence of parabolic arcs, one per site above the sweep line, where each parabola is the locus of points equidistant from its site and the sweep line.

    Two event types:

    • Site event: the sweep reaches a new site, inserting a new arc into the beach line and splitting an existing one.
    • Circle event: an arc shrinks to zero width, meaning three sites become co-circular — this creates a Voronoi vertex.

    There are n site events and O(n) circle events (each creates a vertex, and a planar graph on n sites has O(n) vertices by Euler's formula), each costing O(log n). Total O(nlog n), which is optimal. ∎

    The insight that makes it work is that the beach line is monotone in x, so it can live in a balanced BST — which is not obvious, since the Voronoi diagram itself has no such ordering.

    In practice, computing the Delaunay triangulation (the dual) by randomised incremental insertion is simpler to implement and equally fast, and the Voronoi diagram is read off from it.

  5. Theory

    Design a sweep for the skyline problem: given n buildings as (l, r, h), output the outline.

    Solution

    Events: (l, +h) and (r, -h) for each building. Sweep left to right maintaining a multiset of active heights.

    At each event x, update the multiset, then look at its maximum. If the maximum changed, emit the key point (x, new max).

    events = sorted([(l, -h) for l,r,h in bs] + [(r, h) for l,r,h in bs])
# note: -h for starts so that at the same x, taller starts come FIRST
# and ends come after starts, which avoids spurious key points

    O(nlog n). The event ordering is the whole difficulty: at a shared x-coordinate, starts must precede ends (so a building starting where another ends does not create a dip), and among starts the taller must come first (so no spurious key point is emitted). Encoding start heights as negative achieves both with a plain sort.

    The multiset needs max and erase one occurrence — a std::multiset, a heap with lazy deletion, or a counting map. Lazy deletion is simplest: push to a max-heap and pop stale entries when they surface.

  6. Theory

    Explain how to compute the area of the union of n rectangles and generalise to "covered at least k times".

    Solution

    Sweep over x. The status is a segment tree over the compressed y-coordinates, storing per node a coverage count and the length covered at least once. Adding a rectangle's y-range increments the count on O(log n) nodes; the covered length is recomputed bottom-up.

    Between consecutive events, the covered length times the x-gap contributes to the area. O(nlog n).

    No lazy propagation is needed because every range increment is eventually matched by a decrement, so a node's count is always accurate for its own interval — a specialisation that makes the code much shorter than a general segment tree.

    For "at least k times": store per node an array of lengths covered exactly 0,1,…,k-1 times plus "k or more". The merge is a shift by the node's own count. Cost becomes O(nklog n) — fine for small k, and this is the standard solution to "area covered by at least k rectangles".

  7. Theory

    Describe an angular sweep for computing the visibility polygon from a point.

    Solution

    Sort all segment endpoints by angle around the viewpoint. Sweep a ray through 360°, maintaining a BST of the segments the ray currently crosses, ordered by distance from the viewpoint.

    At each event (a segment starting or ending relative to the ray), insert or remove it; the visible point in the current direction is on the nearest segment, which is the BST's minimum.

    Emit a vertex whenever the nearest segment changes. O(nlog n). ∎

    The subtlety is the BST ordering: two segments' distance order can only change where they cross, and if no segments cross (the usual case for a simple polygon's edges) the order is stable within the sweep, so a plain comparator works. With crossing segments the comparator is not a valid ordering and the structure must be rebuilt or the segments split at their intersections first.

    Applications: field-of-view in games, radio coverage, the art-gallery problem, and shadow computation. The same sweep with "farthest" instead of "nearest" gives the region visible from outside.

  8. Program

    Implement closest pair by sweep line and verify against brute force.

    Solution
    from sortedcontainers import SortedList
import math
def closest_pair(points):
    pts = sorted(points)
    active = SortedList(key=lambda p: (p[1], p[0]))
    best = float('inf'); pair = None
    left = 0
    for p in pts:
        d = math.isqrt(int(best)) + 1 if best < float('inf') else 0
        while best < float('inf') and p[0] - pts[left][0] >= math.sqrt(best):
            active.remove(pts[left]); left += 1
        lo = active.bisect_left((p[0], p[1] - math.sqrt(best) if best < float('inf') else -10**18))
        for q in active[lo:]:
            if best < float('inf') and q[1] - p[1] > math.sqrt(best): break
            d2 = (p[0]-q[0])**2 + (p[1]-q[1])**2
            if d2 < best: best, pair = d2, (p, q)
        active.add(p)
    return best, pair

    Working with squared distances keeps integer input exact, though the strip bounds then need a square root — an alternative is to keep both best2 and its integer square root, updating the latter only when best2 changes.

    Verify against the O(n²) brute force on 20,000 random small instances, including duplicate points (distance 0) and all-collinear points. The duplicate case is worth testing explicitly: best becomes 0 and the strip has zero width, which must not cause an infinite loop.

  9. Program

    Implement Bentley–Ottmann to report all segment intersections.

    Solution
    import heapq
def bentley_ottmann(segments):
    events = []
    for i, (a, b) in enumerate(segments):
        if a > b: a, b = b, a
        heapq.heappush(events, (a, 0, i))          # 0 = left endpoint
        heapq.heappush(events, (b, 2, i))          # 2 = right endpoint
    status = OrderedSegments()                      # BST keyed by y at sweep x
    found = set()
    while events:
        pt, kind, data = heapq.heappop(events)
        status.set_x(pt[0])
        if kind == 0:
            i = data; status.insert(i)
            for j in (status.above(i), status.below(i)):
                if j is not None: try_intersect(i, j, pt, events, found)
        elif kind == 2:
            i = data
            a, b = status.above(i), status.below(i)
            status.remove(i)
            if a is not None and b is not None:
                try_intersect(a, b, pt, events, found)
        else:                                       # kind == 1: intersection
            i, j = data
            status.swap(i, j)
            # test the two NEW adjacencies created by the swap
            ...
    return found

    The implementation difficulty is entirely in OrderedSegments: a BST whose comparator depends on the current sweep x. Every insertion and search must use a consistent x, and the swap at an intersection must be an exact reordering rather than a re-sort — otherwise the structure's invariant breaks.

    Degenerate cases that break naive implementations: vertical segments (undefined slope), three or more segments through one point (multiple simultaneous swaps), overlapping collinear segments (no well-defined order), and shared endpoints. Handling all four correctly is what makes production implementations long.

    For a contest, the O(n²) all-pairs test is usually the right answer unless n is large and k is known to be small.

  10. Program

    Solve the skyline problem with a sweep and a max-heap with lazy deletion.

    Solution
    import heapq
def skyline(buildings):
    events = []
    for l, r, h in buildings:
        events.append((l, -h, r))            # start: negative h sorts taller first
        events.append((r, 0, 0))             # end marker
    events.sort()
    result = []
    heap = [(0, float('inf'))]               # (−height, end); ground at 0
    for x, negh, r in events:
        while heap[0][1] <= x: heapq.heappop(heap)      # lazy deletion
        if negh: heapq.heappush(heap, (negh, r))
        cur = -heap[0][0]
        if not result or result[-1][1] != cur:
            result.append((x, cur))
    return result

    Lazy deletion avoids needing a heap with arbitrary removal: entries carry their end coordinate, and stale ones are popped when they reach the top and their building has ended. Each entry is pushed and popped once, so the total is O(nlog n).

    The sentinel (0, inf) represents ground level and guarantees the heap is never empty — removing it introduces an empty-heap check in three places.

    The event encoding (-h for starts, 0 for ends) makes a plain sort produce the correct order: at equal x, starts come before ends, and among starts the taller comes first. Getting that ordering right is the whole problem; the rest is bookkeeping.

  11. Program

    Compute the area of the union of n rectangles using a coverage segment tree.

    Solution
    class CoverTree:
    def __init__(self, ys):
        self.ys = ys; n = len(ys) - 1
        self.cnt = [0] * (4*n); self.cov = [0] * (4*n); self.n = n
    def _update(self, node, lo, hi, l, r, delta):
        if r <= lo or hi <= l: return
        if l <= lo and hi <= r:
            self.cnt[node] += delta
        else:
            mid = (lo+hi)//2
            self._update(2*node+1, lo, mid, l, r, delta)
            self._update(2*node+2, mid, hi, l, r, delta)
        if self.cnt[node] > 0:
            self.cov[node] = self.ys[hi] - self.ys[lo]      # fully covered
        elif hi - lo == 1:
            self.cov[node] = 0
        else:
            self.cov[node] = self.cov[2*node+1] + self.cov[2*node+2]

    The recomputation of cov after the recursion is the crux: a node with positive count reports its whole interval regardless of its children, and only when the count drops to zero do the children's contributions matter. Because increments and decrements are matched, the count is never negative and no lazy propagation is required.

    O(nlog n) total. Coordinate-compressing the y-values first is essential — the tree is over the 2n distinct y-coordinates, not over the coordinate range.

    Verify against a brute-force grid computation on small integer rectangles, including nested, identical and disjoint ones.

  12. Program

    Implement a sweep to find the maximum number of intervals overlapping at any point, and the k intervals achieving it.

    Solution
    def max_overlap(intervals):
    events = []
    for i, (l, r) in enumerate(intervals):
        events.append((l, 1, i))
        events.append((r, -1, i))          # half-open [l, r): ends sort first
    events.sort(key=lambda e: (e[0], e[1]))   # −1 before +1 at equal x
    cur = 0; best = 0; active = set(); best_set = set()
    for x, delta, i in events:
        if delta == 1: active.add(i); cur += 1
        else:          active.discard(i); cur -= 1
        if cur > best: best, best_set = cur, set(active)
    return best, best_set

    The tie-break (x, delta) with -1 < +1 implements half-open intervals: an interval ending exactly where another begins does not count as overlapping. Reversing it gives closed intervals. Which one is wanted is a specification question and is the most common source of off-by-one here.

    O(nlog n). Maintaining the active set makes it O(nlog n + output); if only the count is needed, drop the set and it becomes a two-line sweep.

    This is the minimum-number-of-rooms scheduling problem (Chapter 5), and by Dilworth's theorem the answer is also the size of the largest antichain in the interval order — three formulations of one sweep.

  13. Program

    Detect whether any two of n segments intersect, in O(nlog n) (Shamos–Hoey).

    Solution
    def any_intersection(segments):
    events = []
    for i, (a, b) in enumerate(segments):
        if a > b: a, b = b, a
        events.append((a, 0, i)); events.append((b, 1, i))
    events.sort()
    status = SortedList()                    # ordered by y at the sweep x
    for pt, kind, i in events:
        if kind == 0:
            pos = status.insert_and_locate(i, pt[0])
            for j in status.neighbours(pos):
                if segments_intersect(*segments[i], *segments[j]): return True
        else:
            a, b = status.neighbours_of(i)
            status.remove(i)
            if a is not None and b is not None:
                if segments_intersect(*segments[a], *segments[b]): return True
    return False

    Because it stops at the first intersection, no intersection events ever enter the queue — the sweep is O(nlog n) unconditionally, with none of Bentley–Ottmann's output sensitivity.

    This is the practical tool for testing whether a polygon is simple (Chapter 54 problem 11): run it on the polygon's edges, excluding adjacent-edge pairs which legitimately share an endpoint.

    The status comparator still depends on the sweep x, but since no swaps occur before the first intersection is found, the ordering remains valid throughout — which is precisely why this variant avoids the implementation difficulties of the full algorithm.

  14. Program

    Build a generic sweep-line framework and instantiate it for three different problems.

    Solution
    import heapq
class Sweep:
    def __init__(self, events, status, handle):
        self.q = list(events); heapq.heapify(self.q)
        self.status = status
        self.handle = handle
        self.output = []
    def run(self):
        while self.q:
            e = heapq.heappop(self.q)
            new_events = self.handle(e, self.status, self.output)
            for ne in (new_events or ()): heapq.heappush(self.q, ne)
        return self.output

# instantiate: interval overlap (status = counter),
#              rectangle union (status = CoverTree),
#              closest pair    (status = SortedList by y)

    Factoring out the loop makes the three components explicit — event queue, status, handler — and forces you to name them, which is the design discipline the paradigm rewards. The handler returning new events is what supports Bentley–Ottmann's dynamically-discovered intersection events.

    The framework is thin by design. Sweep-line problems differ almost entirely in their status structure and in the event ordering at ties, and both of those resist abstraction — which is why in practice most people write the loop inline. The value of writing it once is that it makes the tie-breaking rule a visible, testable parameter rather than an accident of a sort comparator.

Chapter 59

Circles, tangents and 3D geometry

Circles bring square roots and therefore genuine numerical care, but most predicates still reduce to comparing squared quantities exactly. The 3D extensions - planes, spheres, the triple product - follow the same pattern one dimension up.

Circle: |P − C| = r, or (x−cx)² + (y−cy)² = r² Point vs circle: compare (p−c)·(p−c) against r² EXACT for integers Two circles: d = |c₁ − c₂| d > r₁+r₂ separate d = r₁+r₂ externally tangent |r₁−r₂| < d < r₁+r₂ two intersection points d = |r₁−r₂| internally tangent d < |r₁−r₂| one inside the other, no intersection d = 0, r₁ = r₂ identical

Circle intersections

Circle–circle intersection by the radical line
// Circles (c1, r1), (c2, r2).  Let d = |c2 − c1|.
// The intersection points lie on the RADICAL LINE, perpendicular to c1c2 at
//   a = (d² + r1² − r2²) / (2d)      distance from c1 along the axis
//   h = √(r1² − a²)                  half the chord length
// Then:  base = c1 + a·(c2−c1)/d,  points = base ± h·perp((c2−c1)/d)

pair<P,P> circle_intersect(P c1, double r1, P c2, double r2){
    P dv = c2 - c1;
    double d2 = norm2(dv), d = sqrt(d2);
    double a = (d2 + r1*r1 - r2*r2) / (2*d);
    double h2 = r1*r1 - a*a;
    if (h2 < 0) return {};                       // no intersection
    P base = c1 + dv * (a/d);
    P off  = perp(dv) * (sqrt(h2)/d);
    return {base + off, base - off};
}

The radical axis of two circles is the locus of points with equal power |P-C|²-r². Subtracting the two circle equations eliminates the quadratic terms, leaving a line — which is why circle intersection reduces to line–circle intersection, and why three circles' radical axes are concurrent (the radical centre).

Principle

Keep everything squared for as long as possible. "Is P inside the circle", "which of two points is closer", and "do these circles intersect" are all comparisons of squared quantities and stay exact in integers. Take a square root only when a length must be output — never to make a decision.

Tangents

From a point P to circle (C, r), with d = |P − C| ≥ r: tangent length = √(d² − r²) the two tangent points lie on the circle of diameter PC (Thales) ⟹ they are the intersections of circle (C,r) with circle (midpoint(P,C), d/2) Between two circles: 4 tangent lines when separate (2 external, 2 internal) external: treat as tangent from a point to a circle of radius |r₁−r₂| internal: same with radius r₁+r₂

Three dimensions

Dot product a·b = |a||b|cos θ same as 2D Cross product a×b = a VECTOR, perpendicular to both |a×b| = area of the parallelogram Triple product a·(b×c) = det[a b c] = signed VOLUME of the parallelepiped = 0 ⟺ a, b, c are coplanar Plane: n·(P − P₀) = 0, or ax+by+cz = d with n = (a,b,c) distance from Q: |n·Q − d| / |n| side test: sign(n·Q − d) — the 3D orientation predicate Sphere: |P − C| = r. Sphere–plane intersection is a circle. Convex hull in 3D: O(n log n), with O(n) faces by Euler's formula V−E+F=2.
Interview angle

"Do two circles intersect?" should never involve a square root: compare d² against (r_1+r_2)² and (r_1-r_2)². Volunteering that — and noting it keeps integer input exact — turns a routine question into a demonstration of numerical judgement.

Problem set — 14 problemstheory & programming
  1. Theory

    Derive the circle–circle intersection formula and enumerate the degenerate cases.

    Solution

    Place c_1 at the origin and c_2 at (d,0). The two equations are x²+y² = r_1² and (x-d)²+y² = r_2². Subtracting eliminates y²:

    2dx - d² = r_1²-r_2², so x = (d²+r_1²-r_2²)/(2d),

    and y = ±√{r_1²-x²}. Rotating back gives the general formula. ∎

    Degenerate cases, all detectable by comparing d² exactly:

    • d = 0 and r_1 = r_2: identical circles, infinitely many points.
    • d = 0, r_1 ≠ r_2: concentric, none. (The formula divides by d — guard first.)
    • d² = (r_1+r_2)² or d² = (r_1-r_2)²: tangent, one point.
    • r_1² < x²: no real intersection.

    All the comparisons are on squared quantities, so with integer centres and radii the classification is exact even though the points are irrational.

  2. Theory

    Define the power of a point and prove that the radical axis of two circles is a line.

    Solution

    The power of P with respect to circle (C,r) is pow(P) = |P-C|² - r² — positive outside, zero on the circle, negative inside. It equals the squared tangent length from P.

    The radical axis is {P : pow_1(P) = pow_2(P)}:

    |P-C_1|²-r_1² = |P-C_2|²-r_2².

    Expanding, the |P|² terms cancel and what remains is linear in P — a line, perpendicular to C_1C_2. ∎

    Radical centre: three circles' three pairwise radical axes are concurrent, because a point on two of them has equal power to all three. This gives an elegant construction and is the basis of the "power diagram" (a weighted Voronoi diagram) used in mesh generation.

    When the circles intersect, the radical axis is the line through their two intersection points — which is why the intersection derivation of problem 1 works.

  3. Theory

    Derive the circumcircle of a triangle and state when it fails to exist.

    Solution

    The circumcentre is equidistant from all three vertices, so it lies on the perpendicular bisector of each side. Solving two of them:

    With a at the origin, b and c the other vertices, and D = 2(b_xc_y - b_yc_x):

    O_x = (c_y|b|² - b_y|c|²)/(D), O_y = (b_x|c|² - c_x|b|²)/(D).

    D = 2cross(b,c) is twice the orientation determinant, so it vanishes exactly when the three points are collinear — and then there is no circumcircle (or, projectively, a line). ∎

    The radius is R = (abc)/(4K) where a, b, c are the side lengths and K the area — a formula worth knowing because it computes R without finding the centre.

    The circumcentre is rational for integer input, so it can be kept exact as a fraction. The radius generally is not, which is why the in-circle predicate (Chapter 45) is formulated as a determinant rather than as a distance comparison.

  4. Theory

    Find the tangent lines from an external point to a circle.

    Solution

    Let d = |P-C| with d > r. The tangent length is L = √{d²-r²} (Pythagoras, since the radius is perpendicular to the tangent at the touch point).

    The tangent points are at distance r from C and at distance L from P — so they are the intersections of circle (C,r) with circle (P,L), solvable by problem 1.

    Equivalently (Thales): the tangent points lie on the circle with diameter PC, since the angle \angle CTP is a right angle. So intersect (C,r) with the circle centred at the midpoint of PC with radius d/2. ∎

    The angle between PC and each tangent is \arccos(r/d), giving a direct rotation-based construction that avoids a second circle intersection.

    Degenerate cases: d = r gives one tangent (P is on the circle), d < r gives none. Both are detected by comparing d² with r² exactly.

  5. Theory

    Count and construct the common tangents of two circles in every configuration.

    Solution
    separate (d > r₁+r₂) 4 tangents (2 external, 2 internal) externally tangent (d = r₁+r₂) 3 (the internal pair merges) intersecting 2 (external only) internally tangent 1 one inside the other 0 identical infinitely many

    External tangents: shrink both circles by min(r_1,r_2); one becomes a point, and the problem reduces to tangents from a point to a circle of radius |r_1-r_2|. Then translate the resulting lines back outward.

    Internal tangents: the same construction with radius r_1+r_2, which corresponds to reflecting one circle's radius.

    Both reductions turn a two-circle problem into problem 4, which is why that one is the primitive worth implementing carefully.

    All six cases are distinguished by comparing d² against (r_1± r_2)² — exactly, with no square roots.

  6. Theory

    Derive the 3D orientation predicate and explain its geometric meaning.

    Solution

    For four points a, b, c, d:

    orient3d(a,b,c,d) = (b-a)·\big((c-a)×(d-a)\big) = \det\begin{smallmatrix}b_x-a_x & c_x-a_x & d_x-a_x\\ b_y-a_y & c_y-a_y & d_y-a_y\\ b_z-a_z & c_z-a_z & d_z-a_z\end{smallmatrix}.

    This is six times the signed volume of the tetrahedron abcd. Its sign says whether d is above or below the plane through a, b, c (with "above" meaning the side the normal (b-a)×(c-a) points to), and zero means the four points are coplanar. ∎

    It is the direct analogue of the 2D orientation test, and it plays the same role: 3D convex hull, Delaunay tetrahedralisation and point location all reduce to its sign.

    Magnitude bound: for coordinates in [-C,C] the determinant is at most 48C³, so 64-bit integers are exact only to C ≈ 6×10⁵ — considerably tighter than the 2D case, and a common source of overflow in 3D code.

  7. Theory

    Explain the "lifting to a paraboloid" trick that turns Delaunay triangulation into a 3D convex hull.

    Solution

    Map each planar point (x,y) to (x,y,x²+y²) on the paraboloid z = x²+y².

    Key fact: a circle in the plane lifts to a plane in 3D, and "inside the circle" becomes "below the plane". So the in-circle predicate becomes a 3D orientation test:

    incircle(a,b,c,d) = orient3d(\hat a,\hat b,\hat c,\hat d) where \hat{} denotes the lift.

    Consequence: the lower convex hull of the lifted points projects exactly to the Delaunay triangulation, because a triangle is Delaunay iff its circumcircle is empty iff the corresponding lifted plane has all other lifted points above it. ∎

    This reduces a 2D problem to a 3D hull, unifies the algorithms, and explains why the in-circle determinant has the form it does (Chapter 45 problem 14) — the x²+y² column is the lift.

    The same trick in one dimension higher relates 3D Delaunay to 4D hulls, and the general statement is that Delaunay in ℝ^d is a hull in ℝ^{d+1}.

  8. Program

    Implement exact circle predicates: point in circle, circle intersection classification, using only integer arithmetic.

    Solution
    def point_vs_circle(p, c, r):
    """−1 inside, 0 on, +1 outside — exact for integer input"""
    d2 = (p[0]-c[0])**2 + (p[1]-c[1])**2
    return (d2 > r*r) - (d2 < r*r)

def circle_relation(c1, r1, c2, r2):
    d2 = (c1[0]-c2[0])**2 + (c1[1]-c2[1])**2
    s = (r1 + r2)**2
    t = (r1 - r2)**2
    if d2 > s:  return 'separate'
    if d2 == s: return 'externally tangent'
    if d2 > t:  return 'intersecting'
    if d2 == t: return 'identical' if d2 == 0 and r1 == r2 else 'internally tangent'
    return 'contained'

    Every comparison is between integers, so the classification is exact — no epsilon, no ambiguity at tangency. That matters because tangency is precisely where a floating-point version gives the wrong answer, and tangency is precisely what test-setters include.

    The d2 == 0 and r1 == r2 check for identical circles must come before the internal-tangent case, since concentric equal circles satisfy d² = (r_1-r_2)² = 0.

    The intersection points are irrational and require floating point or a symbolic representation — but no decision in this function does.

  9. Program

    Compute the intersection points of two circles and of a line and a circle, with numerical care.

    Solution
    import math
def line_circle(a, b, c, r):
    """intersections of segment/line ab with circle (c, r)"""
    d = (b[0]-a[0], b[1]-a[1])
    f = (a[0]-c[0], a[1]-c[1])
    A = d[0]*d[0] + d[1]*d[1]
    B = 2*(f[0]*d[0] + f[1]*d[1])
    C = f[0]*f[0] + f[1]*f[1] - r*r
    disc = B*B - 4*A*C
    if disc < 0: return []
    sq = math.sqrt(disc)
    # numerically stable quadratic: avoid subtracting nearly-equal numbers
    q = -0.5 * (B + math.copysign(sq, B))
    t1, t2 = q/A, C/q if q != 0 else 0.0
    return sorted({t1, t2})

    The stable quadratic formula is the point. The naive \frac{-B±√{B²-4AC}}{2A} suffers catastrophic cancellation for one root when B² \gg 4AC — exactly the near-tangent case. Computing the larger root first and obtaining the other as C/(Aq) (from t_1t_2 = C/A) keeps both accurate.

    The discriminant is exact for integer input, so the existence test is reliable; only the point coordinates are approximate.

    For a segment rather than a line, clamp t to [0,1] and discard roots outside — and note that a tangent gives a double root, which the set collapses to one.

  10. Program

    Find all common tangent lines of two circles.

    Solution
    import math
def common_tangents(c1, r1, c2, r2):
    out = []
    d2 = (c2[0]-c1[0])**2 + (c2[1]-c1[1])**2
    for sign1 in (1, -1):                      # external then internal
        r = r2*sign1 - r1
        if d2 < r*r - 1e-12: continue
        h = math.sqrt(max(0.0, d2 - r*r))
        for sign2 in (1, -1):
            # the tangent line is  nx·x + ny·y = c
            nx = ((c2[0]-c1[0])*r + (c2[1]-c1[1])*h*sign2) / d2
            ny = ((c2[1]-c1[1])*r - (c2[0]-c1[0])*h*sign2) / d2
            out.append((nx, ny, nx*c1[0] + ny*c1[1] + r1))
            if h == 0: break                   # tangent circles: one line
    return out

    The unified formulation handles all four tangents with two sign parameters: sign1 selects external versus internal, sign2 selects which of the pair. Shrinking by r_1 reduces both cases to tangents from a point, as in problem 5.

    The h == 0 break prevents emitting a duplicate line at tangency — which is how the counts 3 and 1 in the classification table arise.

    Verify by checking that each returned line is at distance exactly r_1 from c_1 and r_2 from c_2 (up to tolerance), and that the number returned matches the exact classification from problem 8.

  11. Program

    Compute the area of intersection of two circles, and of a circle with a polygon.

    Solution
    import math
def circle_circle_area(c1, r1, c2, r2):
    d = math.dist(c1, c2)
    if d >= r1 + r2: return 0.0
    if d <= abs(r1 - r2): return math.pi * min(r1, r2)**2
    a1 = math.acos((d*d + r1*r1 - r2*r2) / (2*d*r1))
    a2 = math.acos((d*d + r2*r2 - r1*r1) / (2*d*r2))
    return r1*r1*(a1 - math.sin(2*a1)/2) + r2*r2*(a2 - math.sin(2*a2)/2)

def circle_polygon_area(c, r, poly):
    """sum of signed circular-triangle areas, one per polygon edge"""
    total = 0.0
    n = len(poly)
    for i in range(n):
        total += circle_triangle_area(c, r, poly[i], poly[(i+1) % n])
    return abs(total)

    The two-circle formula sums two circular segments, each being a sector minus a triangle. The acos arguments must be clamped to [-1,1] — rounding can push them microscopically outside and produce a NaN that silently poisons the result.

    The circle–polygon area uses the same shoelace decomposition as Chapter 56: sum the signed area of the region between the circle and each edge's triangle from the centre. Each term is either a triangle, a sector, or a mixture depending on how the edge cuts the circle — a case analysis of about 20 lines that is worth writing once and keeping.

    Verify against Monte Carlo integration: sample points in a bounding box and count how many fall in both shapes. Agreement to three digits with 10⁶ samples confirms the case analysis.

  12. Program

    Implement 3D vector operations and the orientation predicate, with an overflow analysis.

    Solution
    struct P3 { long long x, y, z; };
P3 sub(P3 a, P3 b){ return {a.x-b.x, a.y-b.y, a.z-b.z}; }
long long dot(P3 a, P3 b){ return a.x*b.x + a.y*b.y + a.z*b.z; }
P3 cross(P3 a, P3 b){
    return {a.y*b.z - a.z*b.y, a.z*b.x - a.x*b.z, a.x*b.y - a.y*b.x};
}
__int128 orient3d(P3 a, P3 b, P3 c, P3 d){
    P3 u = sub(b,a), v = sub(c,a), w = sub(d,a);
    return (__int128)u.x*(v.y*w.z - v.z*w.y)
         - (__int128)u.y*(v.x*w.z - v.z*w.x)
         + (__int128)u.z*(v.x*w.y - v.y*w.x);
}

    Overflow analysis: with coordinates in [-C,C], the differences are ≤ 2C, the 2×2 minors are ≤ 8C², and the full determinant is ≤ 48C³. For int64 that requires C \lesssim 6×10⁵; the __int128 accumulator in the outer products raises it to C \lesssim 4×10^{11}.

    Note the inner minors are still computed in long long and must not overflow on their own — at C = 10⁶ they reach 8×10^{12}, safe; at C = 10⁹ they reach 8×10^{18}, marginal. Casting them too is the safe choice.

    This kind of bound should be computed and written in a comment above every geometric predicate — it is the difference between code that is exact and code that is exact on the test data.

  13. Program

    Compute the convex hull of points in 3D and verify Euler's formula.

    Solution
    # Incremental 3D hull: maintain a set of faces; for each new point,
# delete the faces it can "see" and cone the resulting horizon to it.
def hull3d(points):
    faces = initial_tetrahedron(points)
    for p in points[4:]:
        visible = [f for f in faces if orient3d(*f, p) > 0]
        if not visible: continue                    # inside the hull
        horizon = boundary_edges(visible)
        faces = [f for f in faces if f not in visible]
        faces += [(e[0], e[1], p) for e in horizon]
    return faces

# verification
V = len({v for f in faces for v in f})
E = len({tuple(sorted(e)) for f in faces for e in edges_of(f)})
F = len(faces)
assert V - E + F == 2                              # Euler's formula
assert E == 3*F // 2                               # every face is a triangle
assert F <= 2*V - 4                                # the triangulated bound

    Randomised incremental insertion gives O(nlog n) expected. The three assertions are the right correctness checks: Euler's formula must hold for any convex polyhedron, and with all faces triangular 2E = 3F, which combine to F ≤ 2V-4 and E ≤ 3V-6.

    Those bounds also answer the complexity question: a 3D hull has O(n) faces, so the output size is linear — unlike 4D and above, where the hull can have Θ(n^{⌊ d/2⌋}) faces and output-sensitivity becomes essential.

    Degeneracies (four coplanar points, all points coplanar) need explicit handling; the initial tetrahedron construction must search for four non-coplanar points and report failure if none exist.

  14. Program

    Solve: given n circles, compute the area of their union.

    Solution
    import math
def circles_union_area(circles):
    """Green's theorem: integrate around the boundary of the union."""
    total = 0.0
    for i, (c, r) in enumerate(circles):
        # find the arcs of circle i NOT covered by any other circle
        events = []
        covered_fully = False
        for j, (c2, r2) in enumerate(circles):
            if i == j: continue
            d = math.dist(c, c2)
            if d + r <= r2: covered_fully = True; break     # i is inside j
            if d >= r + r2 or d + r2 <= r: continue          # no overlap
            ang = math.atan2(c2[1]-c[1], c2[0]-c[0])
            half = math.acos(max(-1.0, min(1.0, (d*d + r*r - r2*r2)/(2*d*r))))
            events.append((ang - half, ang + half))          # the covered arc
        if covered_fully: continue
        for a, b in uncovered_arcs(events):
            total += arc_contribution(c, r, a, b)            # Green's term
    return total

    Green's theorem turns the area into a boundary integral: A = \frac12\oint(xdy - ydx). Each uncovered arc contributes a closed-form term (a sector plus a triangle), so the whole computation is O(n²log n) — for each circle, sort and merge the covered arc intervals.

    The two containment checks (d + r <= r2 and d + r2 <= r) must come before the arc computation, since acos's argument is out of range in those cases — and clamping it, as the code does, silently produces a wrong arc rather than an error.

    Verify with Monte Carlo, and with the two-circle formula of problem 11 as an exact special case. Circle-union area is a problem where a subtly wrong case analysis produces answers that look plausible, so independent verification is not optional.

IX. Graphs, Games and Optimisation
Chapter 60

Counting trees: Cayley, Prufer and the matrix-tree theorem

There are n^(n-2) labelled trees on n vertices, and the bijective proof - the Prufer sequence - is also an encoding, a random-tree generator, and a way to count trees with prescribed degrees.

CAYLEY'S FORMULA: the number of labelled trees on n vertices is n^{n−2} n = 1: 1 n = 2: 1 n = 3: 3 n = 4: 16 n = 5: 125 Rooted labelled trees: n^{n−1} (choose a root as well) Forests of k rooted trees on n vertices: k·n^{n−k−1} Trees with prescribed degrees d₁..d_n: the multinomial (n−2)! / ∏(dᵢ − 1)! — vertex i appears dᵢ − 1 times in the Prüfer code

The Prüfer sequence

A bijection between labelled trees on {1,…,n} and sequences in {1,…,n}^{n-2}. Since there are n^{n-2} such sequences, Cayley's formula follows immediately.

Encode and decode
ENCODE:  repeat n−2 times:
             take the LEAF with the smallest label
             append its neighbour to the sequence
             delete the leaf

DECODE:  degree[v] = 1 + (number of times v appears in the sequence)
         repeat for each element a of the sequence:
             take the smallest leaf v (degree 1, not yet used)
             add edge (v, a);  degree[v]−−;  degree[a]−−
         join the last two remaining vertices

Both directions run in O(n log n) with a heap, or O(n) with a pointer trick.
Principle

A vertex of degree d appears exactly d-1 times in the Prüfer sequence. That single fact turns every "count trees with degree constraints" question into a multiset-permutation count — and it is why leaves (degree 1) never appear at all.

The matrix-tree theorem

For a graph with Laplacian L = D - A, every cofactor of L counts the spanning trees (Chapter 45). For weighted graphs the same determinant computes ∑_T∏_{e∈ T}w_e.

Spanning trees of K_n: n^{n−2} (Cayley) Spanning trees of K_{m,n}: m^{n−1}·n^{m−1} Spanning trees of the cycle C_n: n Spanning trees of a graph: any cofactor of L, O(n³) Directed spanning trees (arborescences) rooted at r: the Tutte matrix-tree theorem — delete row/column r from the in-degree Laplacian and take the determinant

Counting other tree-like objects

ObjectCount
Labelled trees on n verticesn^{n-2}
Labelled rooted treesn^{n-1}
Labelled forests, k trees, given rootskn^{n-k-1}
Binary trees with n nodes (unlabelled)C_n (Catalan, Chapter 32)
Unlabelled rooted treesno closed form; ~ 0.44·2.956^n n^{-3/2}
Functional graphs on n nodesn^n
Spanning trees of a graphmatrix-tree determinant
Interview angle

"How many trees on n labelled vertices?" — n^{n-2}, and the proof worth naming is the Prüfer bijection rather than the determinant, because the bijection is constructive: it also gives you an O(n) encoding, a uniform random-tree generator, and the degree-constrained count, all from the same map.

Problem set — 14 problemstheory & programming
  1. Theory

    Prove that the Prüfer encoding is a bijection.

    Solution

    Well-defined: a tree with n\ge2 vertices has at least two leaves, so the encoding never gets stuck, and it produces exactly n-2 symbols.

    Injective: the decoding is deterministic. From the sequence, \deg(v) = 1 + count(v), so the leaves are exactly the vertices absent from the sequence, and the smallest is uniquely determined at each step. Following the decoding reconstructs the tree uniquely.

    Surjective: given any sequence, the decoding produces a graph with n-1 edges. It is acyclic because each step attaches a vertex that is then removed and never reappears, so no cycle can close. An acyclic graph with n-1 edges on n vertices is a tree. ∎

    Hence trees correspond bijectively to n^{n-2} sequences — Cayley's formula, proved constructively.

  2. Theory

    Prove that a vertex of degree d appears exactly d-1 times in its Prüfer sequence.

    Solution

    Induct on n. Let v be the smallest leaf removed first, with neighbour u.

    • v has degree 1 and, being removed immediately, is never appended — it appears 0 times ✓.
    • u is appended once, and in the remaining tree its degree is \deg(u)-1, so by induction it appears \deg(u)-2 more times, totalling \deg(u)-1 ✓.
    • Any other vertex w has the same degree in the smaller tree and appears \deg(w)-1 times by induction ✓.

    The base case n=2 has an empty sequence and both degrees 1. ∎

    Corollary: the number of labelled trees with prescribed degrees d_1,…,d_n (summing to 2n-2) is the number of sequences with vertex i appearing d_i-1 times — the multinomial ((n-2)!)/(∏(d_i-1)!).

  3. Theory

    Derive the number of spanning trees of K_{m,n}.

    Solution

    By the matrix-tree theorem, compute a cofactor of the Laplacian. For K_{m,n} the Laplacian is

    L = \begin{smallmatrix}nI_m & -J_{m× n}\\ -J_{n× m} & mI_n\end{smallmatrix}.

    Its eigenvalues are 0 (once), m+n (once), n with multiplicity m-1, and m with multiplicity n-1. By the eigenvalue form of the matrix-tree theorem (the number of spanning trees is \frac1{m+n}∏_{nonzero}λ_i):

    \tau(K_{m,n}) = \frac{(m+n)· n^{m-1}· m^{n-1}}{m+n} = m^{n-1}n^{m-1}. ∎

    Check K_{1,n} (a star): 1^{n-1}n^0 = 1 ✓. Check K_{2,2} (a 4-cycle): 2^1·2^1 = 4 ✓, matching \tau(C_4) = 4.

    The eigenvalue formula \tau = \frac1n∏_{i\ge2}λ_i is often easier than a cofactor when the graph is symmetric enough for the spectrum to be known.

  4. Theory

    Count the labelled forests on n vertices consisting of k trees with specified roots.

    Solution

    The answer is kn^{n-k-1}.

    Proof by a generalised Prüfer argument: add a new vertex n+1 joined to all k roots. This gives a tree on n+1 vertices in which n+1 has degree exactly k. By problem 2, such trees correspond to Prüfer sequences of length n-1 in which the symbol n+1 appears exactly k-1 times.

    Choosing the positions and the other symbols: C(n-1,k-1)n^{n-k}. Dividing by the C(n,k) ways the roots could have been chosen and re-normalising yields kn^{n-k-1} for specified roots. ∎

    Check k=1: 1· n^{n-2} ✓ (Cayley, with a distinguished root that does not matter since the tree is unrooted). Check k=n: n· n^{-1} = 1 ✓ (n isolated vertices, one forest).

    This is the standard tool for "count the ways to connect components" problems.

  5. Theory

    Use the generalised Cayley formula to count the ways to add edges connecting given components into a tree.

    Solution

    Given k components with sizes a_1,…,a_k summing to n, the number of ways to add k-1 edges making the whole thing a tree is

    n^{k-2}∏_{i=1}^{k}a_i.

    Why: contract each component to a single vertex. The resulting structure is a labelled tree on k vertices, of which there are k^{k-2} — but each edge of that tree can attach to any vertex within its component, contributing a factor. Careful counting via the degree-constrained Prüfer formula gives the stated product. ∎

    Check k=2: n^0a_1a_2 = a_1a_2 ✓ — any pair of endpoints, one from each component.

    Check all a_i = 1 (so k=n): n^{n-2}·1 = n^{n-2} ✓, recovering Cayley.

    This formula answers "how many ways to make the graph connected with the minimum number of edges", which is a common contest question.

  6. Theory

    Explain the matrix-tree theorem for directed graphs (arborescences).

    Solution

    An arborescence rooted at r is a spanning tree with all edges directed toward r (or away, depending on convention).

    Tutte's theorem: build the Laplacian L = D_{out} - A where D_{out} is the out-degree diagonal matrix. Delete row r and column r; the determinant of what remains counts the arborescences oriented toward r.

    Unlike the undirected case, different roots give different counts — so "the cofactor" is not root-independent here, and which row and column to delete is part of the specification.

    BEST theorem combines this with Eulerian circuits: the number of Eulerian circuits in a connected digraph with all in-degrees equal to out-degrees is

    ec(G) = \tau_r(G)∏_v(\deg^+(v)-1)!,

    where \tau_r is the arborescence count from any root — one of the few problems where counting is polynomial while the corresponding Hamiltonian question is #P-hard.

  7. Theory

    Derive the number of unlabelled rooted trees asymptotically, and explain why there is no closed form.

    Solution

    Let T(x) = ∑ t_nx^n count unlabelled rooted trees. A tree is a root with a multiset of subtrees, so by Pólya's multiset construction (Chapter 34):

    T(x) = x\exp(∑_{k\ge1}(T(x^k))/(k)).

    The T(x^k) terms account for repeated identical subtrees and make the equation non-algebraic — unlike the labelled case T = xe^T, which Lagrange inversion solves exactly (Chapter 53).

    Asymptotics (Otter, 1948): t_n ~ Cα^n n^{-3/2} with α ≈ 2.9557653 and C ≈ 0.4399240, obtained by singularity analysis of the functional equation. Both constants are believed to be transcendental and have no closed form. ∎

    Values: 1, 1, 2, 4, 9, 20, 48, 115, 286 — computable to thousands of terms by iterating the functional equation, but never in closed form.

    The contrast with the labelled case is instructive: removing labels destroys the exponential structure and replaces a clean formula with a numerically-defined constant.

  8. Program

    Implement Prüfer encoding and decoding in O(n), and verify they are inverse.

    Solution
    def prufer_encode(adj, n):
    deg = [len(adj[v]) for v in range(n)]
    ptr = next(v for v in range(n) if deg[v] == 1)
    leaf = ptr
    code = []
    for _ in range(n - 2):
        nxt = next(u for u in adj[leaf] if deg[u] > 0 or u > leaf)
        # (in practice, track the single remaining neighbour explicitly)
        code.append(nxt)
        deg[nxt] -= 1
        if deg[nxt] == 1 and nxt < ptr:
            leaf = nxt                          # the new smallest leaf
        else:
            ptr += 1
            while deg[ptr] != 1: ptr += 1
            leaf = ptr
        deg[leaf] = 0
    return code

def prufer_decode(code, n):
    deg = [1]*n
    for v in code: deg[v] += 1
    ptr = next(v for v in range(n) if deg[v] == 1)
    leaf = ptr
    edges = []
    for v in code:
        edges.append((leaf, v))
        deg[v] -= 1
        if deg[v] == 1 and v < ptr: leaf = v
        else:
            ptr += 1
            while deg[ptr] != 1: ptr += 1
            leaf = ptr
        deg[leaf] = 0
    edges.append((leaf, n-1))
    return edges

    The O(n) trick is the ptr pointer: it only ever moves forward, so the total work across all iterations is O(n) rather than the O(nlog n) a heap would cost. The new leaf is either the vertex just decremented (if it is smaller than the pointer) or the next one the pointer finds.

    Verify by round-tripping all n^{n-2} trees for n\le6 (1296 trees at n=6) and confirming the encode–decode composition is the identity and that every code is produced exactly once.

  9. Program

    Generate a uniformly random labelled tree on n vertices, and a random tree with prescribed degrees.

    Solution
    import random
def random_tree(n):
    if n == 1: return []
    if n == 2: return [(0, 1)]
    code = [random.randrange(n) for _ in range(n-2)]
    return prufer_decode(code, n)

def random_tree_with_degrees(degs):
    """degs must sum to 2n − 2, each ≥ 1"""
    n = len(degs)
    assert sum(degs) == 2*n - 2 and all(d >= 1 for d in degs)
    code = []
    for v, d in enumerate(degs): code += [v]*(d-1)
    random.shuffle(code)
    return prufer_decode(code, n)

    Uniformity is immediate from the bijection: a uniform random sequence gives a uniform random tree. This is far better than the alternatives — random edge addition with cycle rejection is slow and non-uniform if done carelessly, and a random permutation-based construction gives only path-like trees.

    The degree-constrained version is equally direct: the multiset of code symbols is determined by the degrees, so shuffling it uniformly samples uniformly among trees with those degrees.

    Verify uniformity for n=4: generate 10⁶ trees and check that all 16 appear about 62{,}500 times each, with a chi-square test.

  10. Program

    Count spanning trees of a graph modulo a prime using the matrix-tree theorem.

    Solution
    MOD = 10**9+7
def spanning_tree_count(n, edges):
    L = [[0]*n for _ in range(n)]
    for u, v in edges:
        L[u][u] += 1; L[v][v] += 1
        L[u][v] -= 1; L[v][u] -= 1
    M = [[L[i][j] % MOD for j in range(1, n)] for i in range(1, n)]
    return det_mod(M, MOD)

    O(n³), so n\le500 is comfortable — for a count that can be astronomically large (500^{498} for K_{500}).

    Multi-edges are handled correctly by the construction (each parallel edge increments the degree and decrements the off-diagonal), and they genuinely multiply the tree count. Self-loops must be discarded — they contribute to no spanning tree and would corrupt the degree.

    Validate on the three cases whose answers are known independently: K_n → n^{n-2}, C_n → n, and any tree → 1. Those exercise the sign conventions and the row/column deletion.

    For an exact integer answer rather than a residue, use Bareiss (Chapter 45) or several primes plus CRT with the Hadamard bound.

  11. Program

    Count the ways to connect k given components into a spanning tree.

    Solution
    MOD = 10**9+7
def ways_to_connect(component_sizes):
    k = len(component_sizes)
    n = sum(component_sizes)
    if k == 1: return 1
    prod = 1
    for a in component_sizes: prod = prod * a % MOD
    return prod * pow(n, k-2, MOD) % MOD

    The formula n^{k-2}∏ a_i from problem 5. O(k + log n).

    Edge cases: k=1 needs a special case, since n^{-1} is meaningless as written (though the modular inverse happens to give the right answer, relying on that is fragile). k=2 gives a_1a_2, which is a good hand-checkable case.

    The typical problem statement is "a graph has some edges; count the ways to add the minimum number of edges to connect it". Run a union-find to get the component sizes, then apply this formula — two lines of real work, and the formula is the entire difficulty.

    Verify by brute force for n\le7: enumerate all C(\binom n2,k-1) edge sets of the right size and count how many connect the components.

  12. Program

    Enumerate all spanning trees of a small graph, and count them for a large one.

    Solution
    from itertools import combinations
def all_spanning_trees(n, edges):
    out = []
    for subset in combinations(range(len(edges)), n-1):
        dsu = DSU(n); ok = True
        for i in subset:
            if not dsu.unite(*edges[i]): ok = False; break
        if ok: out.append(subset)
    return out

    Brute force is C(m,n-1) — feasible only for tiny graphs, but the right way to validate the matrix-tree implementation.

    For genuine enumeration there are output-sensitive algorithms (Kapoor–Ramesh) running in O(N + V + E) for N spanning trees, based on exchanging one edge at a time. But since N can be n^{n-2}, enumeration is rarely what you want — the count, a random sample, or the minimum is.

    Random sampling uniformly from spanning trees is elegant: Wilson's algorithm (loop-erased random walks) or Aldous–Broder produce a uniform spanning tree in expected O(cover time), connecting this chapter to Chapter 41's random walks.

  13. Program

    Compute the number of labelled forests with exactly k trees, for all k, in O(n²).

    Solution
    MOD = 10**9+7
def forests_by_component_count(n):
    """F[k] = number of labelled forests on n vertices with exactly k trees"""
    C = binomial_table(n)
    rooted = [0]*(n+1)
    for i in range(1, n+1): rooted[i] = pow(i, i-1, MOD)   # rooted trees on i
    F = [[0]*(n+1) for _ in range(n+1)]
    F[0][0] = 1
    for i in range(1, n+1):
        for k in range(1, i+1):
            # the component containing vertex 1 has size j
            for j in range(1, i-k+2):
                F[i][k] = (F[i][k] + C[i-1][j-1] * pow(j, j-2, MOD)
                                   * F[i-j][k-1]) % MOD
    return F[n]

    O(n³) as written; the standard trick of fixing vertex 1's component makes each term unambiguous and avoids overcounting by a factor of k!.

    The O(n²) version uses the EGF: forests are sets of trees, so \hat{F}(x,u) = e^{u\hat{T}(x)} and the coefficient of u^k is \hat{T}^k/k! — computable by the power-series toolkit of Chapter 53 in O(nlog n) per k.

    Sanity check: F[1] = n^{n-2} (Cayley), F[n] = 1 (all isolated), and ∑_k F[k] is the total number of labelled forests — OEIS A001858: 1, 1, 2, 7, 38, 291.

  14. Program

    Verify Cayley's formula and the degree-constrained count by exhaustive enumeration for small n.

    Solution
    from itertools import combinations, product
from math import factorial
def enumerate_trees(n):
    verts = list(range(n))
    all_edges = list(combinations(verts, 2))
    trees = []
    for subset in combinations(all_edges, n-1):
        dsu = DSU(n)
        if all(dsu.unite(u, v) for u, v in subset): trees.append(subset)
    return trees

for n in range(1, 8):
    trees = enumerate_trees(n)
    assert len(trees) == (n**(n-2) if n >= 2 else 1), n
    # degree-constrained check
    from collections import Counter
    by_deg = Counter()
    for t in trees:
        d = [0]*n
        for u, v in t: d[u] += 1; d[v] += 1
        by_deg[tuple(d)] += 1
    for degs, cnt in by_deg.items():
        expected = factorial(n-2)
        for d in degs: expected //= factorial(d-1)
        assert cnt == expected, (degs, cnt, expected)

    At n=7 there are C(21,6) = 54{,}264 edge subsets to test, yielding 7^5 = 16{,}807 trees — fast enough, and it validates both Cayley's formula and the multinomial degree count simultaneously.

    The degree check is the stronger test: it verifies the refined statement of problem 2, which a bug in the Prüfer implementation would violate even if the total count happened to be right.

Chapter 61

Matchings, Hall's theorem and combinatorial duality

Every max-min theorem in combinatorics has the same shape: the largest "packing" equals the smallest "covering". Konig, Hall, Dilworth and Menger are four faces of that one statement, and each turns a hard-looking question into a matching computation.

HALL'S THEOREM A bipartite graph has a perfect matching saturating the left side iff |N(S)| ≥ |S| for every S ⊆ Left. KÖNIG'S THEOREM In a bipartite graph: max matching = min vertex cover (and hence max independent set = n − max matching) DILWORTH In a finite poset: min chain cover = max antichain MIRSKY (dual) min antichain cover = longest chain MENGER max edge-disjoint s–t paths = min s–t edge cut (and the vertex version, with vertex cuts) All are special cases of MAX-FLOW MIN-CUT (Chapter 62), which is itself a special case of LP DUALITY.

Hall's condition

The condition is necessary trivially: if |N(S)| < |S| the vertices of S have too few partners. Sufficiency is the theorem, and the standard proof is by induction on |L| with two cases — either every proper non-empty subset has strict slack (|N(S)| > |S|), in which case match any edge and recurse; or some S has |N(S)| = |S|, in which case split the problem at S.

Principle

Hall's condition has 2^{|L|} instances, so it is a certificate, not an algorithm: you verify a specific violating set, or you find a matching. To decide, run a matching algorithm — and if it fails, the algorithm hands you the violating set (the reachable vertices from an unmatched one along alternating paths).

Augmenting paths

Berge's lemma: a matching M is maximum iff there is no augmenting path — a path alternating between non-matching and matching edges, with both endpoints unmatched. Flipping such a path increases the matching by one.

Kuhn's algorithm: O(V·E), simple and fast in practice
bool try_kuhn(int v, vector<bool>& used){
    for (int to : adj[v]){
        if (used[to]) continue;
        used[to] = true;
        if (match_r[to] == -1 || try_kuhn(match_r[to], used)){
            match_r[to] = v;
            return true;
        }
    }
    return false;
}
// for each left vertex: reset `used`, try to augment.  O(V·E) total.
// Hopcroft–Karp finds many shortest augmenting paths per phase: O(E√V).
ProblemAlgorithmCost
Bipartite maximum matchingKuhn / Hopcroft–KarpO(VE) / O(E√V)
Bipartite min-cost perfect matchingHungarian algorithmO(n³)
General graph maximum matchingBlossom (Edmonds)O(V³) or O(E√V)
Minimum path cover on a DAGn - max matchingO(E√V)
Maximum antichain in a posetDilworth via matchingO(n³) + matching
Maximum independent set (bipartite)n - max matching (König)O(E√V)

The last row is worth emphasising: maximum independent set is NP-hard in general and polynomial on bipartite graphs, purely because of König's theorem. Recognising bipartiteness is therefore often the whole solution.

Interview angle

"Assign n tasks to n workers minimising total cost" is the Hungarian algorithm at O(n³). "Can every task be assigned?" is Hall's condition, decided by a matching. And "what is the minimum number of workers who together can cover every task?" is König's minimum vertex cover — same computation, different reading.

Problem set — 14 problemstheory & programming
  1. Theory

    Prove Hall's theorem.

    Solution

    Necessity: if S is matched injectively into N(S), then |N(S)| ≥ |S|.

    Sufficiency, by induction on |L|. Two cases:

    • Every non-empty proper S ⊂neq L has |N(S)| ≥ |S|+1. Pick any edge (u,v) and match it. In the remaining graph, any S has lost at most one neighbour, so |N'(S)| ≥ |N(S)|-1 ≥ |S| — Hall's condition still holds, and induction finishes.
    • Some S has |N(S)| = |S| exactly. By induction match S into N(S) perfectly.
