    Explain why signed right shift rounds toward negative infinity and what to use for truncating division.

    Solution

    Arithmetic right shift copies the sign bit, so x \gg 1 computes ⌊ x/2⌋ — rounding down. For x = -7: -7 \gg 1 = -4, while -7/2 = -3 in C (which truncates toward zero).

    So \gg and / differ for negative operands, and replacing x/2 by x>>1 is only safe for non-negative x.

    Which do you want? Floor division is usually the mathematically correct one — it makes x mod m non-negative, which is what modular arithmetic needs (Chapter 14). Truncating division is what C gives you.

    long long floordiv(long long a, long long b){
    long long q = a / b;
    if ((a % b != 0) && ((a < 0) != (b < 0))) q--;
    return q;
}

    Python's // and % already floor, which is why Python code translates to C++ incorrectly at exactly these points — one of the most common porting bugs in competitive programming.

  5. Theory

    Derive a bit-parallel algorithm for the longest common subsequence.

    Solution

    Hyyrö's bit-vector LCS: represent one row of the LCS DP table as a bitmask, where bit j records whether dp[i][j] > dp[i][j-1] (a "step" in the row).

    For each character of the second string, update the whole row with a constant number of word operations:

    for each character c of B:
    u = V & Match[c]                    // positions where c matches
    V = (V + u) | (V - u)               // the carry propagation does the DP

    The addition's carry chain performs exactly the "take the max of the left and upper neighbours" propagation that the DP requires — arithmetic carry as a parallel prefix operation. ∎

    O(nm/64) instead of O(nm). At n = m = 10⁴ that is 1.5×10⁶ word operations instead of 10⁸.

    The same idea gives bit-parallel edit distance (Myers' algorithm) and approximate string matching (Shift-Or / Bitap), all exploiting that a carry chain is a free prefix-scan.

  6. Theory

    Show how to compute the XOR of 0,1,…,n in O(1).

    Solution

    Look at the XOR of four consecutive integers starting at a multiple of 4:

    4k ⊕ (4k+1) ⊕ (4k+2) ⊕ (4k+3) = 0,

    because the low two bits cycle through 00,01,10,11 (XOR 0) and the high bits appear four times (XOR 0). So the prefix XOR depends only on n mod 4:

    n mod 4 = 0 → n n mod 4 = 1 → 1 n mod 4 = 2 → n + 1 n mod 4 = 3 → 0

    ∎ Then \bigoplus_{i=l}^{r} i = f(r)⊕ f(l-1).

    This is the standard tool for "XOR of a range" queries and appears constantly in problems that ask for the XOR of a huge arithmetic-like range. The analogous sum has the closed form n(n+1)/2; the XOR's is this period-4 pattern.

  7. Theory

    Explain the SOS (sum over subsets) transform and its complexity.

    Solution

    Given f on all 2^n masks, compute F[m] = ∑_{s⊆ m}f[s] for every m.

    Naively this is O(3^n) by submask enumeration. The SOS transform does it in O(2^n n) by processing one bit at a time:

    for i in range(n):
    for m in range(1 << n):
        if m >> i & 1: F[m] += F[m ^ (1 << i)]

    Why it works: after processing bits 0..i, F[m] equals the sum over submasks that agree with m on bits above i and are arbitrary below. Inducting on i gives the full subset sum at the end. ∎

    It is a multidimensional prefix sum over the hypercube {0,1}^n — the direct analogue of a 2D prefix sum, done one dimension at a time. The inverse (Möbius) transform is the same loop with -=.

    At n=20: 2^{20}×20 = 2×10⁷ versus 3^{20} = 3.5×10⁹ — the difference between feasible and not.

  8. Program

    Implement popcount four ways and benchmark them.

    Solution
    // 1. hardware instruction
int pc_builtin(uint64_t x){ return __builtin_popcountll(x); }

// 2. Kernighan — O(popcount)
int pc_kernighan(uint64_t x){ int c = 0; while (x){ x &= x-1; c++; } return c; }

// 3. SWAR (divide and conquer) — O(log width), branchless
int pc_swar(uint64_t x){
    x -= (x >> 1) & 0x5555555555555555ULL;
    x = (x & 0x3333333333333333ULL) + ((x >> 2) & 0x3333333333333333ULL);
    x = (x + (x >> 4)) & 0x0F0F0F0F0F0F0F0FULL;
    return (x * 0x0101010101010101ULL) >> 56;
}

// 4. table lookup, 8 bits at a time
int pc_table(uint64_t x){
    int c = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < 8; i++){ c += TBL[x & 0xFF]; x >>= 8; }
    return c;
}

    Typical relative timings: builtin 1×, SWAR 3×, table 6×, Kernighan 2–20× depending on the popcount. The builtin compiles to a single POPCNT instruction on any x86-64 since 2008 and on ARMv8.

    SWAR is worth understanding: each step sums adjacent pairs, then nibbles, then bytes, and the final multiply-and-shift sums the eight byte counts in one operation — a parallel prefix computation done with ordinary arithmetic.

    Kernighan wins when the popcount is very small (a sparse mask) and loses badly when it is large.

  9. Program

    Implement subset enumeration, submask enumeration and same-popcount enumeration, and verify the counts.

    Solution
    def all_subsets(n):
    return range(1 << n)

def submasks(m):
    s = m
    while True:
        yield s
        if s == 0: break
        s = (s - 1) & m

def same_popcount(k, n):
    """all n-bit masks with exactly k set bits, increasing"""
    if k == 0: yield 0; return
    x = (1 << k) - 1
    while x < (1 << n):
        yield x
        c = x & -x
        r = x + c
        x = r | (((x ^ r) >> 2) // c)

from math import comb
assert sum(1 for m in all_subsets(12) for _ in submasks(m)) == 3**12
assert sum(1 for _ in same_popcount(5, 12)) == comb(12, 5)

    The two assertions verify the two counting facts: submask pairs number 3^n, and same-popcount masks number \binom nk. Both are exact and catch any off-by-one in the loop termination.

    The if s == 0: break placement in submasks is what includes the empty set; testing that 0 in submasks(m) for every m is worth an explicit assertion.

  10. Program

    Implement the SOS transform and use it to count, for each mask, the number of array elements that are submasks of it.

    Solution
    def sos_transform(f, n):
    F = f[:]
    for i in range(n):
        for m in range(1 << n):
            if m >> i & 1: F[m] += F[m ^ (1 << i)]
    return F

def count_submask_elements(values, n):
    cnt = [0] * (1 << n)
    for v in values: cnt[v] += 1
    return sos_transform(cnt, n)          # F[m] = #{v : v ⊆ m}

# the SUPERSET version: iterate the other way
def sos_superset(f, n):
    F = f[:]
    for i in range(n):
        for m in range(1 << n):
            if not (m >> i & 1): F[m] += F[m | (1 << i)]
    return F

    O(2^n n). The superset version flips the condition and the direction — both are needed, and confusing them is the usual bug.

    Applications: counting pairs with a &amp; b = 0 (for each a, the count of b that are submasks of lnot a), subset-sum convolution (Chapter 30), and any "for each mask, aggregate over its submasks" query.

    Verify against the naive O(3^n) double loop for n\le12 — that also demonstrates the speed difference concretely.

  11. Program

    Implement a Fenwick tree and explain its index arithmetic in terms of bit tricks.

    Solution
    class Fenwick:
    def __init__(self, n): self.n = n; self.t = [0]*(n+1)
    def add(self, i, v):
        i += 1
        while i <= self.n:
            self.t[i] += v
            i += i & -i                  # move to the next covering node
    def prefix(self, i):
        i += 1; s = 0
        while i > 0:
            s += self.t[i]
            i -= i & -i                  # strip the lowest set bit
        return s

    The structure: node i covers the range (i - (i&amp;{-i}), i] — a block whose length is the lowest set bit of i. So i -= i & -i walks from i down through a decomposition of [1,i] into O(popcount(i)) disjoint blocks, and i += i & -i walks up through all the nodes whose block contains i.

    Both loops run at most log n times, and the whole structure is one array of size n+1 — no pointers, no recursion, excellent cache behaviour. That is why a Fenwick tree beats a segment tree by a factor of 3–5 in practice despite the same asymptotics.

    The bit trick is the data structure: the tree shape is exactly the binary representation of the indices, which is why the code is six lines with no explicit tree at all.

  12. Program

    Use bitsets to compute the transitive closure and to speed up a subset-sum DP.

    Solution
    # transitive closure — O(n³/64)
reach = [1 << i for i in range(n)]              # each vertex reaches itself
for k in range(n):
    for i in range(n):
        if reach[i] >> k & 1: reach[i] |= reach[k]

# subset-sum feasibility — O(n·S/64)
possible = 1                                     # bit s set ⟺ sum s achievable
for a in items:
    possible |= possible << a
    possible &= (1 << (S+1)) - 1                # keep only sums ≤ S
print((possible >> target) & 1)

    Python's arbitrary-precision integers are bitsets, and <<, |, & operate word-parallel internally — so this idiom gives the 64× speed-up with no extra machinery.

    The subset-sum line possible |= possible << a is the entire DP: shifting by a represents "also take this item", and OR-ing merges the two options. At n = 100 and S = 10⁵ this is 100×10⁵/64 = 1.5×10⁶ word operations — instant, versus 10⁷ for the boolean-array version.

    In C++ use std::bitset<S> for a compile-time size or a vector<uint64_t> with a hand-written shift.

  13. Program

    Write bit-twiddling routines for: reversing bits, next power of two, and integer log base 2.

    Solution
    uint32_t reverse_bits(uint32_t x){
    x = ((x >> 1) & 0x55555555) | ((x & 0x55555555) << 1);
    x = ((x >> 2) & 0x33333333) | ((x & 0x33333333) << 2);
    x = ((x >> 4) & 0x0F0F0F0F) | ((x & 0x0F0F0F0F) << 4);
    x = ((x >> 8) & 0x00FF00FF) | ((x & 0x00FF00FF) << 8);
    return (x >> 16) | (x << 16);
}

uint64_t next_pow2(uint64_t x){
    if (x <= 1) return 1;
    return 1ULL << (64 - __builtin_clzll(x - 1));
}

int ilog2(uint64_t x){ return 63 - __builtin_clzll(x); }   // x > 0 required

    Bit reversal is a butterfly network: swap adjacent bits, then pairs, then nibbles, and so on — log_2 w steps. It is exactly the permutation the FFT needs (Chapter 50), and the same structure explains why that permutation is its own inverse.

    next_pow2 uses x-1 so that an exact power of two maps to itself — the classic off-by-one. Guard x=0 separately, since clz(0) is undefined.

    ilog2 must never be implemented as (int)log2((double)x): for large x the floating-point result can be off by one ulp at exact powers of two, giving a wrong answer that survives most testing (Chapter 11 problem 13).

  14. Program

    Write a test harness verifying bit-trick identities exhaustively over 16-bit values.

    Solution
    for x in range(1 << 16):
    # lowest set bit
    if x:
        assert x & -x == 1 << (x & -x).bit_length() - 1
        assert (x & (x-1)) == x - (x & -x)
    # power of two
    assert ((x != 0) and (x & (x-1)) == 0) == (bin(x).count('1') == 1)
    # popcount agreement across implementations
    assert pc_kernighan(x) == pc_swar(x) == bin(x).count('1')
    # bit reversal is an involution
    assert reverse_bits16(reverse_bits16(x)) == x
    # next power of two
    if x: assert next_pow2(x) >= x and next_pow2(x) < 2*x

for m in range(1 << 12):
    subs = list(submasks(m))
    assert len(subs) == 1 << bin(m).count('1')
    assert all(s & m == s for s in subs)
    assert len(set(subs)) == len(subs)

    Exhaustive testing over 16 bits is 65,536 cases — instant, and it is a proof for that width (Chapter 2: a finite domain fully enumerated is verified, not merely tested).

    The identities that generalise to 64 bits do so structurally, so a 16-bit exhaustive check plus a 64-bit random check is strong coverage. The exception is anything involving INT_MIN or width-specific constants, which need explicit 64-bit tests.

    Keeping this harness is worthwhile: bit tricks are exactly the kind of code that is copied, adapted, and silently broken.

Chapter 66

IEEE 754 floating point and error analysis

Floating-point numbers are a logarithmically-spaced finite subset of the reals, and arithmetic on them is exact-then-rounded. Almost every surprising result follows from that one fact plus the loss of associativity.

IEEE 754 double: 1 sign bit | 11 exponent bits | 52 mantissa bits value = (−1)^s × 1.m × 2^{e−1023} (normalised) ≈ 15.95 decimal digits; machine epsilon ε = 2⁻⁵² ≈ 2.22×10⁻¹⁶ range ≈ 10^{±308}; subnormals extend down to ≈ 5×10⁻³²⁴ SPECIAL VALUES ±0 two zeros; 0.0 == −0.0 is TRUE but 1/0.0 ≠ 1/−0.0 ±∞ from overflow or x/0 NaN from 0/0, ∞−∞, √(negative); NaN != NaN is TRUE THE FUNDAMENTAL GUARANTEE fl(a ⊕ b) = (a ⊕ b)(1 + δ) with |δ| ≤ ε — each operation is computed exactly, then rounded once.

What breaks

0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3 0.1 has no exact binary representation (a + b) + c != a + (b + c) addition is NOT associative a + b − b != a catastrophic cancellation x == y is fragile use a tolerance — but see below sorting with a float comparator can violate the strict weak ordering if NaN is present (Chapter 5) — undefined behaviour in C++

Integers up to 2^{53} are represented exactly in a double, so integer arithmetic in floating point is safe below that — and silently wrong above it. That threshold, about 9×10^{15}, is why JavaScript's Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER exists and why 64-bit IDs must not be passed through JSON as numbers.

Catastrophic cancellation

The quadratic formula, wrong and right
// WRONG when b² much larger than 4ac: one root loses all its digits
x1 = (-b + sqrt(b*b - 4*a*c)) / (2*a);
x2 = (-b - sqrt(b*b - 4*a*c)) / (2*a);

// RIGHT: compute the well-conditioned root, then use x1*x2 = c/a
double q = -0.5 * (b + copysign(sqrt(b*b - 4*a*c), b));
x1 = q / a;
x2 = c / q;

// a = 1, b = 1e8, c = 1:
//   naive x1 = 0.0        (all significant digits lost)
//   stable x1 = -1e-8     (correct)
Principle

Subtracting nearly-equal quantities destroys significant digits — the relative error of the difference is the absolute error divided by a tiny result. The fix is always algebraic: rewrite so the subtraction never happens. √{x+1}-√x becomes 1/(√{x+1}+√x); 1-\cos x becomes 2\sin²(x/2); e^x-1 becomes expm1(x).

Comparing floats

ABSOLUTE tolerance |a − b| < eps fails for large values RELATIVE tolerance |a − b| < eps·max(|a|,|b|) fails near zero COMBINED |a − b| <= eps·max(1,|a|,|b|) usually right ULP comparison compare the integer bit patterns — exact, scale-free NONE of these is an equivalence relation (Chapter 5): tolerance comparison is not transitive, so it must never be a sort key or a hash key. Snap to a grid instead: round(x/eps).
Interview angle

"Why is 0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3?" — because 0.1 and 0.2 are not exactly representable in binary, so each is rounded, and the sum of the rounded values rounds to a double slightly above 0.3. The follow-up worth volunteering: the same happens in decimal with 1/3, so this is not a flaw in binary but a consequence of any finite radix.

Problem set — 14 problemstheory & programming
  1. Theory

    Explain exactly why 0.1+0.2 ≠ 0.3, giving the stored values.

    Solution

    0.1 in binary is 0.00011 — infinitely repeating, like 1/3 in decimal. The nearest double is

    0.1000000000000000055511151231257827…

    Similarly 0.2 rounds slightly up. Their exact sum is 0.3000000000000000166533…, which rounds to the double 0.30000000000000004440892…

    But the double nearest the literal 0.3 is 0.29999999999999998889776… — one ulp below. Hence the inequality. ∎

    The general fact: a fraction p/q in lowest terms is exactly representable in base b iff every prime factor of q divides b. In binary only powers of 2 qualify, so 0.5 and 0.25 are exact while 0.1 and 0.3 are not.

  2. Theory

    Show that floating-point addition is not associative, with a maximally bad example.

    Solution

    Take a = 10^{20}, b = -10^{20}, c = 1.

    (a+b)+c = 0 + 1 = 1, but a+(b+c) = 10^{20} + (-10^{20}+1) = 0, since -10^{20}+1 rounds back to -10^{20} (the 1 is far below the ulp at that magnitude). ∎

    Consequences:

    • Summing an array gives different results in different orders. Kahan or pairwise summation reduces the error from O(nε) to O(ε) and O(εlog n).
    • Parallel reduction is non-deterministic unless the order is pinned — a genuine reproducibility problem in scientific computing and ML training.
    • Compilers may not reorder float arithmetic without -ffast-math, precisely because it changes results.

    Multiplication is also non-associative, but far milder: relative errors compose rather than cancel.

  3. Theory

    Derive the error bound for summing n floats, and explain Kahan summation.

    Solution

    Naive left-to-right summation incurs a relative error ≤ε per step, accumulating to

    |error| ≤ nε∑|x_i| + O(ε²).

    The ∑|x_i| factor is the problem: with cancellation the true sum can be tiny while ∑|x_i| is huge, so the relative error is unbounded.

    Kahan summation tracks the lost low bits:

    s = c = 0.0
for x in xs:
    y = x - c
    t = s + y
    c = (t - s) - y        # the part of y that was LOST
    s = t

    The bound improves to 2ε∑|x_i| — independent of n. ∎

    Warning: the compiler must not simplify (t - s) - y to zero, which it is mathematically entitled to do. Avoid -ffast-math, or use pairwise summation, which gives O(εlog n) with no such fragility and is what NumPy uses.

  4. Theory

    Explain why tolerance comparison is not an equivalence relation, and what to use instead.

    Solution

    Define x ~ y \iff |x-y| < ε. Reflexive and symmetric, but not transitive: with ε = 1, 0\sim0.6 and 0.6\sim1.2 but 0\not\sim1.2. ∎

    Consequences: it cannot be

    • a sort comparator — the strict weak ordering fails, and std::sort then has undefined behaviour that can read out of bounds;
    • a hash-map key — equal-by-tolerance values hash differently;
    • a grouping key — the "groups" depend on comparison order.

    The fix is to snap to a grid: k = round(x/ε), then compare or hash the integer k. That is an equivalence relation — the kernel of a function (Chapter 5) — at the cost of separating two values that straddle a grid boundary.

    For exact geometric predicates the real answer is to avoid floats entirely (Chapter 54).

  5. Theory

    Define the condition number and compute it for subtraction.

    Solution

    The relative condition number of f at x is κ(x) = |xf'(x)/f(x)| — the factor by which a relative input error is amplified.

    For subtraction f(a,b) = a-b: perturbing a by a relative \delta changes the result by a\delta, a relative change of a\delta/(a-b). So

    κ = (|a|+|b|)/(|a-b|),

    which is enormous when a≈ b — the analytic statement of catastrophic cancellation. ∎

    Addition of same-sign numbers has κ=1 (perfectly conditioned); multiplication and division have κ=1 in each argument; √{} has κ=1/2 and reduces error.

    So the only genuinely dangerous elementary operation is subtraction of nearly-equal quantities — which is why every stability fix in this chapter is about avoiding one.

  6. Theory

    Explain subnormal numbers and why they can cause a 100× slowdown.

    Solution

    Subnormals have a zero exponent field and an implicit leading 0 rather than 1, filling the gap between 0 and the smallest normal ≈2.2×10^{-308}, down to ≈5×10^{-324} with progressively fewer significant bits.

    Their purpose is gradual underflow: without them x-y could be zero for distinct x and y, breaking the guarantee that x≠ y \Rightarrow x-y\ne0.

    The performance problem: many CPUs handle subnormals in microcode or trap to a slow path, costing 100–200 cycles instead of 4. A DSP loop whose values decay into the subnormal range slows by two orders of magnitude with no other symptom.

    Mitigations: set the FTZ (flush-to-zero) and DAZ (denormals-are-zero) CPU flags, as audio and game engines routinely do; or add a tiny DC offset. Modern x86 since Skylake handles most subnormal operations at full speed, so the problem is less acute — but it still bites on older hardware and some ARM cores.

  7. Theory

    Explain why NaN != NaN and enumerate what it breaks.

    Solution

    NaN represents "not a number". IEEE 754 specifies that every comparison involving NaN except != returns false, so NaN == NaN is false. The rationale: NaN is not a value, and making all ordered comparisons false lets isnan(x) be written as x != x.

    What it breaks:

    • Sorting: a < comparator is not a strict weak ordering with NaN present — std::sort has undefined behaviour and can crash or corrupt memory.
    • Containers: a NaN key can never be found again, since lookup uses equality.
    • Negation: !(a < b) is not a >= b when NaN is involved — both are false, so De Morgan-style rewriting of float comparisons is unsound (Chapter 1 problem 8).
    • Min/max: std::min(NaN, x) depends on argument order.

    Defence: check for NaN at data boundaries and assert its absence before sorting. One NaN silently poisons every aggregate computed downstream.

  8. Program

    Implement Kahan and pairwise summation; compare errors against exact rational summation.

    Solution
    from fractions import Fraction
import math
def naive_sum(xs):
    s = 0.0
    for x in xs: s += x
    return s

def kahan_sum(xs):
    s = c = 0.0
    for x in xs:
        y = x - c
        t = s + y
        c = (t - s) - y
        s = t
    return s

def pairwise_sum(xs):
    if len(xs) <= 128: return naive_sum(xs)
    m = len(xs) // 2
    return pairwise_sum(xs[:m]) + pairwise_sum(xs[m:])

exact = float(sum(Fraction(x) for x in xs))
for name, f in (("naive", naive_sum), ("kahan", kahan_sum),
                ("pairwise", pairwise_sum), ("fsum", math.fsum)):
    print(name, abs(f(xs) - exact) / abs(exact))

    On 10⁶ values of widely differing magnitudes, typical relative errors: naive 10^{-10}, pairwise 10^{-15}, Kahan 10^{-16}, math.fsum exact (full-precision accumulation, correctly rounded).

    Fraction gives the exact answer for comparison — which is what makes this a measurement rather than a comparison of two approximations.

    Try the adversarial input [1e100, 1.0, -1e100]: naive gives 0.0, Kahan gives 0.0 (it cannot recover a value already lost from the running sum), and fsum gives 1.0. That distinguishes "compensated" from "exact".

  9. Program

    Write a stable quadratic solver and demonstrate the naive version failing.

    Solution
    import math
def quadratic_naive(a, b, c):
    d = math.sqrt(b*b - 4*a*c)
    return ((-b + d)/(2*a), (-b - d)/(2*a))

def quadratic_stable(a, b, c):
    disc = b*b - 4*a*c
    if disc < 0: return None
    sq = math.sqrt(disc)
    q = -0.5 * (b + math.copysign(sq, b))
    return (q/a, c/q) if q != 0 else (0.0, 0.0)

a, b, c = 1.0, 1e8, 1.0
print(quadratic_naive(a, b, c))    # small root comes out 0.0 or garbage
print(quadratic_stable(a, b, c))   # (-1e+08, -1e-08) — both correct

    With b = 10⁸, √{b²-4ac} ≈ b - 2×10^{-8}, so -b + √{·} subtracts two numbers agreeing in 16 digits — every significant digit is lost.

    The stable version computes the root away from the cancellation (copysign ensures the addition never cancels) and obtains the other from x_1x_2 = c/a.

    Verify by substituting both roots back: |ax²+bx+c| should be at rounding-error level for both, which the naive version fails dramatically for the small root.

  10. Program

    Implement ULP-based comparison and contrast with absolute and relative tolerances.

    Solution
    import struct
def ulp_diff(a, b):
    """number of representable doubles between a and b"""
    ia = struct.unpack('<q', struct.pack('<d', a))[0]
    ib = struct.unpack('<q', struct.pack('<d', b))[0]
    if ia < 0: ia = (1 << 63) - ia          # map to a monotone integer order
    if ib < 0: ib = (1 << 63) - ib
    return abs(ia - ib)

def almost_equal(a, b, max_ulps=4, abs_eps=1e-300):
    if a == b: return True
    if abs(a - b) <= abs_eps: return True    # handles ±0 and near-zero
    return ulp_diff(a, b) <= max_ulps

    Reinterpreting a double's bits as a signed integer gives a monotone map, so the integer difference counts the representable values between them — a scale-free closeness measure.

    Why it is better: an absolute tolerance is wrong for large values (10^{20} and 10^{20}+1 are the same double); a relative tolerance is wrong near zero. ULP comparison is correct in both regimes, with the small absolute guard handling the crossing of zero.

    Still not transitive, so it remains unusable as a sort or hash key — a better predicate, not a repair of the underlying non-equivalence.

  11. Program

    Demonstrate order-dependence of summation and quantify the spread.

    Solution
    import random
from fractions import Fraction
xs = [random.uniform(-1e6, 1e6) for _ in range(10000)]
exact = float(sum(Fraction(x) for x in xs))
results = set()
for _ in range(1000):
    ys = xs[:]; random.shuffle(ys)
    results.add(naive_sum(ys))
print(len(results), min(results), max(results), exact)
print("spread in ulps:", ulp_diff(min(results), max(results)))

    Typically hundreds of distinct results spread over thousands of ulps. Sorting by increasing magnitude before summing markedly reduces the error (small values are added while the running sum is still small); decreasing magnitude makes it worse.

    The practical consequence: parallel reductions, GPU kernels and multi-threaded aggregations are non-deterministic in their last digits unless the reduction order is pinned — the same program on the same data giving different answers on different thread counts.

    Fixes: pin the order, use compensated summation, or accumulate in a wider type (long double, __float128).

  12. Program

    Write stable versions of √{x+1}-√x, 1-\cos x and ln(1+x).

    Solution
    import math
def sqrt_diff(x):
    # sqrt(x+1) - sqrt(x) = 1/(sqrt(x+1) + sqrt(x))  — no subtraction at all
    return 1.0 / (math.sqrt(x+1) + math.sqrt(x))

def one_minus_cos(x):
    # 1 - cos x = 2 sin^2(x/2)
    s = math.sin(x/2)
    return 2*s*s

def log1p_stable(x):
    return math.log1p(x)          # the library function; never write log(1+x)

    Each rewrite eliminates a subtraction of nearly-equal quantities. At x = 10^{16} the naive √{x+1}-√x gives exactly 0.0 while the stable form gives 5×10^{-9}, correct to full precision.

    At x = 10^{-8}, 1-\cos x naively gives 0.0 (since \cos x rounds to 1.0) while 2\sin²(x/2) gives 5×10^{-17}.

    The standard library provides log1p, expm1, hypot, fma and cbrt precisely because the obvious formulas are unstable. Use them — writing log(1+x) or sqrt(x*x+y*y) by hand is a numerical bug, not a style preference.

  13. Program

    Implement exact float-to-decimal conversion and verify round-tripping.

    Solution
    from fractions import Fraction
import struct, random
def exact_decimal(x):
    """the EXACT value of a double — usually 700+ digits"""
    return Fraction(x)                        # Fraction(float) is exact

for _ in range(10**6):
    bits = random.getrandbits(64)
    x = struct.unpack('<d', struct.pack('<Q', bits))[0]
    if x != x or math.isinf(x): continue
    assert float(repr(x)) == x                # shortest round-trip

    Every finite double has an exact decimal representation (since 2^{-k} terminates in decimal), typically 700+ digits for small values — Fraction(0.1) displays the exact stored value.

    The shortest round-tripping representation is a different, harder problem, solved by Steele–White's Dragon4 and now Ryu and Grisu: the shortest decimal string that parses back to the same double. 17 significant digits always suffice; the shortest is usually 15–17.

    Round-tripping 10⁶ random bit patterns verifies this exhaustively — and it is exactly the property that lets you serialise a double to text and back without loss, which naive %.15g formatting does not guarantee.

  14. Program

    Write an audit that detects float-related bugs: NaN, infinities, excessive dynamic range, subnormals.

    Solution
    import math
def audit_floats(values, name=""):
    problems = []
    n_nan = sum(1 for v in values if v != v)
    n_inf = sum(1 for v in values if math.isinf(v))
    if n_nan: problems.append(f"{name}: {n_nan} NaN values")
    if n_inf: problems.append(f"{name}: {n_inf} infinities")
    finite = [v for v in values if math.isfinite(v)]
    nonzero = [abs(v) for v in finite if v]
    if nonzero:
        mx, mn = max(nonzero), min(nonzero)
        if mx/mn > 1e15:
            problems.append(f"{name}: dynamic range {mx/mn:.1e} exceeds double "
                            "precision — expect cancellation")
        if any(v < 2.2e-308 for v in nonzero):
            problems.append(f"{name}: subnormal values present (slow path)")
    return problems

    Three checks that catch most real problems: NaN or infinity entering the data, a dynamic range exceeding what a double holds simultaneously (guaranteeing cancellation in any sum), and subnormals (a performance trap).

    Run it at every data boundary — after parsing, after a numerical routine, before serialising. One NaN entering a pipeline silently poisons every aggregate downstream, and catching it at the boundary is vastly cheaper than debugging the aggregate.

    Add a review rule that no float is used as a dictionary or sort key without snapping (problem 4) — a grep can enforce it.

Chapter 67

Numerical methods: root finding, integration, optimisation

When a closed form does not exist, iterate. The three questions for any numerical method are the same: does it converge, how fast, and what does it cost per step - and the answers are usually a trade between robustness and speed.

ROOT FINDING convergence per-step cost Bisection linear, factor 2 1 evaluation, ALWAYS works False position linear (usually) 1 evaluation Secant superlinear, φ≈1.618 1 evaluation Newton QUADRATIC 1 evaluation + 1 derivative Brent's method superlinear 1 evaluation, robust — the default Quadratic convergence means the correct digits DOUBLE each step: 10⁻¹ → 10⁻² → 10⁻⁴ → 10⁻⁸ → 10⁻¹⁶ four steps from one digit to full Bisection needs ~50 steps to go from 10⁻¹ to 10⁻¹⁶.

Bisection and Newton

The two ends of the robustness/speed trade
double bisect(function<double(double)> f, double lo, double hi){
    // REQUIRES a sign change: f(lo) and f(hi) must have opposite signs
    for (int i = 0; i < 200; i++){          // fixed count, not an epsilon test
        double mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;    // NOT (lo+hi)/2 — that can overflow
        if ((f(mid) < 0) == (f(lo) < 0)) lo = mid; else hi = mid;
    }
    return lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
}

double newton(function<double(double)> f, function<double(double)> df,
              double x, int iters = 50){
    for (int i = 0; i < iters; i++){
        double d = df(x);
        if (d == 0) break;                  // flat: Newton is undefined
        double nx = x - f(x)/d;
        if (nx == x) break;                 // converged to machine precision
        x = nx;
    }
    return x;
}
Principle

Bisection always converges given a sign change, at one bit per step. Newton converges quadratically or not at all — it can cycle, diverge, or run off to infinity from a bad start. The production answer is a hybrid: take a Newton step, and if it leaves the bracketing interval, fall back to bisection. That is Brent's method, and it is what every library uses.

Integration

Trapezoid ∫ ≈ h[f₀/2 + f₁ + ... + f_{n−1} + f_n/2] error O(h²) Simpson ∫ ≈ (h/3)[f₀ + 4f₁ + 2f₂ + 4f₃ + ... + f_n] error O(h⁴) — exact for cubics, despite being derived from parabolas Gauss–Legendre with n nodes exact for degree 2n−1 Romberg Richardson-extrapolate the trapezoid rule error O(h^{2k}) Monte Carlo error O(1/√N) — independent of DIMENSION (Chapter 36) Adaptive: split an interval and recurse where the error estimate is large.

Newton in more than one place

Newton's method is not only for scalar roots. The same "linearise and solve" step gives:

SettingNewton step
Scalar rootx arrow x - f(x)/f'(x)
Integer square rootx arrow (x + n/x)/2
Reciprocal without divisionx arrow x(2 - ax)
Power series inverseB arrow B(2 - AB) (Chapter 53)
Modular inverse mod 2^kx arrow x(2-ax) mod 2^{2k} (Chapter 17)
Systems of equationsx arrow x - J^{-1}F(x)
Optimisationx arrow x - H^{-1}\nabla f

The reciprocal iteration is why hardware dividers and gmp compute 1/a by Newton on f(x) = 1/x - a — it needs only multiplication, and the precision doubles each step, so a full-precision reciprocal costs about the same as one multiplication at the final size.

Interview angle

"Compute a square root without the library" expects Newton: x arrow (x+n/x)/2, quadratic convergence, about 5 iterations from a decent start. The follow-up worth pre-empting: for an integer square root, floating point is wrong above 2^{53} and you must finish with an integer Newton step plus a correction loop.

Problem set — 14 problemstheory & programming
  1. Theory

    Prove that Newton's method converges quadratically near a simple root.

    Solution

    Let r be a simple root (f(r)=0, f'(r)\ne0) and e_n = x_n - r. Taylor-expand about x_n:

    0 = f(r) = f(x_n) - e_nf'(x_n) + \tfrac12e_n²f''(\xi).

    Dividing by f'(x_n) and rearranging with x_{n+1} = x_n - f(x_n)/f'(x_n):

    e_{n+1} = (f''(\xi))/(2f'(x_n))e_n².

    So |e_{n+1}| ≤ C|e_n|² with C ≈ |f''(r)/(2f'(r))| — quadratic. ∎

    At a multiple root f'(r)=0 and convergence degrades to linear with rate 1-1/m for multiplicity m. The repair is the modified iteration x arrow x - mf/f', or Newton applied to f/f', which restores quadratic convergence without knowing m.

    The proof is local: it says nothing about whether the iteration reaches the neighbourhood at all, which is the subject of problem 2.

  2. Theory

    Give three distinct ways Newton's method can fail, with examples.

    Solution
    • Zero derivative: f(x) = x³-2x+2 from x_0=0 cycles between 0 and 1 forever — a period-2 orbit, not divergence.
    • Divergence: f(x) = x^{1/3} has root 0, but Newton gives x_{n+1} = -2x_n — the iterate doubles away from the root every step.
    • Overshoot to a different basin: for a polynomial with several roots, a step from near a local extremum can land arbitrarily far away. The basins of attraction form a fractal (the Newton fractal), so an arbitrarily small change in the start can change which root you find.

    The unifying cause: Newton assumes the function is well-approximated by its tangent over the whole step, which fails when f' is small or f'' is large relative to the step.

    The defence is bracketing: maintain an interval known to contain a root, and reject any Newton step leaving it — falling back to bisection. That gives guaranteed convergence with Newton's speed whenever Newton behaves.

  3. Theory

    Derive Simpson's rule and explain why it is exact for cubics.

    Solution

    Fit a parabola through (a,f(a)), (m,f(m)), (b,f(b)) with m=(a+b)/2, and integrate it exactly:

    \int_a^b f ≈ (b-a)/(6)(f(a)+4f(m)+f(b)).

    Why cubics too: the error term involves f''' integrated against a weight that is odd about the midpoint, so it integrates to zero. Formally the error is

    -((b-a)^5)/(2880)f^{(4)}(\xi) — depending on the fourth derivative, so any cubic is integrated exactly. ∎

    This is the general phenomenon for symmetric quadrature rules: an even number of nodes placed symmetrically gains one extra degree of exactness for free.

    Gauss–Legendre pushes this to the limit: choosing both the nodes and the weights optimally gives exactness up to degree 2n-1 with n nodes — twice what a fixed-node rule achieves.

  4. Theory

    Explain Richardson extrapolation and derive Romberg integration.

    Solution

    If a method has error expansion A(h) = A + c_1h^p + c_2h^{2p}+···, then combining two step sizes eliminates the leading term:

    (2^pA(h/2) - A(h))/(2^p-1) = A + O(h^{2p}).

    Romberg applies this repeatedly to the trapezoid rule (which has p=2 and only even powers of h, by Euler–Maclaurin):

    R[0][k] = trapezoid with 2^k intervals R[j][k] = (4^j·R[j−1][k] − R[j−1][k−1]) / (4^j − 1)

    The first extrapolation gives exactly Simpson's rule; the second gives Boole's; and R[k][k] has error O(h^{2k+2}). ∎

    Practically: 5–6 levels reach machine precision for a smooth integrand, using about 64 function evaluations. Each level reuses all previous evaluations, so nothing is wasted.

    The catch: the error expansion must exist, which requires the integrand to be smooth. For a function with a singularity or a kink, Romberg extrapolates a non-existent expansion and can be worse than the plain trapezoid rule.

  5. Theory

    Compare deterministic quadrature with Monte Carlo and identify the crossover dimension.

    Solution

    A product rule with n nodes per dimension uses n^d evaluations in d dimensions and achieves error O(n^{-k}) = O(N^{-k/d}) for a degree-k-exact rule with N=n^d total points.

    Monte Carlo achieves O(N^{-1/2}) — independent of d.

    Crossover: N^{-k/d} = N^{-1/2} when d = 2k. For Simpson (k=4) that is d = 8; for trapezoid (k=2), d=4. ∎

    So beyond about 4–8 dimensions, Monte Carlo wins — and the gap widens exponentially. That is the "curse of dimensionality", and it is why high-dimensional integrals in physics, finance and Bayesian statistics are all done by sampling.

    Quasi-Monte Carlo (Sobol or Halton low-discrepancy sequences) improves the rate to O((log N)^d/N) — better than N^{-1/2} for moderate d, and the practical choice in finance where d ≈ 100 but the effective dimension is much lower.

  6. Theory

    Explain why the secant method's convergence order is φ, the golden ratio.

    Solution

    The secant method replaces f'(x_n) by the finite difference through the last two points. Its error satisfies

    e_{n+1} ≈ Ce_ne_{n-1}.

    Positing |e_{n+1}| ~ K|e_n|^p and substituting gives |e_n|^p ~ |e_n|·|e_n|^{1/p}, so p = 1 + 1/p, i.e. p²-p-1 = 0 and

    p = (1+√5)/(2) = φ ≈ 1.618. ∎

    Why it can still beat Newton: Newton has order 2 but needs two evaluations per step (f and f'). Comparing per-evaluation, secant achieves φ ≈ 1.618 against Newton's √2 ≈ 1.414. So when the derivative costs as much as the function — which is typical — secant is faster.

    Newton wins when the derivative is cheap (a polynomial evaluated by Horner gives f and f' in one pass, Chapter 49) or available analytically at no cost.

  7. Theory

    Derive the integer square root by Newton and prove the termination condition.

    Solution

    For ⌊√n⌋ use the integer iteration

    x_{k+1} = ⌊(x_k + ⌊ n/x_k⌋)/(2)⌋.

    Claim: from any x_0 ≥ ⌊√n⌋, the sequence decreases until it reaches ⌊√n⌋ and then either stays or oscillates by one.

    Why: by AM–GM, (x+n/x)/(2) ≥ √n for all x>0, so every iterate after the first is ≥⌊√n⌋. And while x > ⌊√n⌋ the step strictly decreases. So the standard loop condition "stop when the next value is ≥ the current" terminates exactly at the floor. ∎

    def isqrt(n):
    if n < 2: return n
    x = 1 << ((n.bit_length() + 1) // 2)        # a good starting bound
    while True:
        y = (x + n // x) // 2
        if y >= x: return x
        x = y

    Roughly loglog n iterations from that start. Never use int(math.sqrt(n)): for n > 2^{53} the double cannot represent n exactly and the result can be off by one — silently, and only for specific inputs.

  8. Program

    Implement bisection, Newton, secant and Brent; compare iteration counts on several functions.

    Solution
    def bisect(f, lo, hi, iters=200):
    flo = f(lo)
    for _ in range(iters):
        mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2
        fm = f(mid)
        if (fm < 0) == (flo < 0): lo, flo = mid, fm
        else: hi = mid
    return lo + (hi - lo) / 2

def secant(f, x0, x1, iters=100, tol=1e-15):
    f0, f1 = f(x0), f(x1)
    for _ in range(iters):
        if f1 == f0: break
        x2 = x1 - f1 * (x1 - x0) / (f1 - f0)
        if abs(x2 - x1) < tol * max(1.0, abs(x2)): return x2
        x0, f0, x1, f1 = x1, f1, x2, f(x2)
    return x1

    Typical iteration counts to 10^{-15} on f(x)=x²-2 from a reasonable start: bisection 52, secant 7, Newton 5, Brent 6.

    Then run them on the pathological cases of problem 2 (x³-2x+2 from 0, and x^{1/3}): bisection and Brent still converge, Newton and secant fail. That contrast is the whole argument for using a hybrid method by default.

    Use lo + (hi-lo)/2 rather than (lo+hi)/2 — the latter can overflow for large bounds and is less accurate near the interval's endpoints.

  9. Program

    Implement adaptive Simpson integration with an error estimate.

    Solution
    def simpson(f, a, b):
    m = (a + b) / 2
    return (b - a) / 6 * (f(a) + 4*f(m) + f(b))

def adaptive_simpson(f, a, b, eps=1e-10, whole=None, depth=50):
    if whole is None: whole = simpson(f, a, b)
    m = (a + b) / 2
    left, right = simpson(f, a, m), simpson(f, m, b)
    if depth <= 0 or abs(left + right - whole) <= 15 * eps:
        return left + right + (left + right - whole) / 15    # Richardson
    return (adaptive_simpson(f, a, m, eps/2, left,  depth-1)
          + adaptive_simpson(f, m, b, eps/2, right, depth-1))

    The 15 comes from the error expansion: halving the interval reduces the O(h^4) error by 2^4 = 16, so |L+R-W| ≈ 15× the error of L+R. Adding (L+R-W)/15 is a free Richardson extrapolation to O(h^6).

    The depth guard is essential: a discontinuous or oscillatory integrand can recurse forever, and without a limit the program hangs rather than returning a poor answer.

    Adaptivity concentrates the evaluations where the function is difficult — integrating 1/√x on [0,1], it spends nearly all its budget near 0 and returns 2.0 to 9 digits, where a uniform rule would need millions of points.

  10. Program

    Implement Romberg integration and show the convergence table.

    Solution
    def romberg(f, a, b, levels=8):
    R = [[0.0]*(levels) for _ in range(levels)]
    h = b - a
    R[0][0] = h/2 * (f(a) + f(b))
    for k in range(1, levels):
        h /= 2
        # reuse all previous evaluations; add only the new midpoints
        s = sum(f(a + (2*i-1)*h) for i in range(1, 2**(k-1) + 1))
        R[k][0] = R[k-1][0]/2 + h*s
        for j in range(1, k+1):
            R[k][j] = R[k][j-1] + (R[k][j-1] - R[k-1][j-1]) / (4**j - 1)
    return R[levels-1][levels-1], R

    Printing the table shows the columns converging at increasing rates. For \int_0^1 e^x: column 0 gains 2 digits per row, column 1 gains 4, column 2 gains 6 — reaching machine precision by row 5 with 33 function evaluations.

    The R[k][0] recurrence reuses every previous evaluation, so doubling the resolution costs only the new midpoints. Recomputing the trapezoid rule from scratch each level would double the total work.

    Run it on |x| over [-1,1] to see the failure mode: the kink breaks the Euler–Maclaurin expansion, and the extrapolated columns are worse than the plain trapezoid rule. That is the caveat in problem 4 made visible.

  11. Program

    Implement an exact integer square root and cube root, and verify against brute force.

    Solution
    def isqrt(n):
    if n < 0: raise ValueError
    if n < 2: return n
    x = 1 << ((n.bit_length() + 1) // 2)
    while True:
        y = (x + n // x) // 2
        if y >= x: return x
        x = y

def icbrt(n):
    if n < 0: return -icbrt(-n)
    if n < 2: return n
    x = 1 << ((n.bit_length() + 2) // 3)
    while True:
        y = (2*x + n // (x*x)) // 3
        if y >= x: return x
        x = y

for n in range(10**6):
    r = isqrt(n)
    assert r*r <= n < (r+1)*(r+1)
for n in range(0, 10**18, 10**11):
    r = icbrt(n)
    assert r**3 <= n < (r+1)**3

    The assertions state the defining property directly — r²≤ n<(r+1)² — which is stronger and clearer than comparing against a floating-point reference.

    The cube-root iteration is Newton on x³-n: x arrow (2x + n/x²)/3. The same pattern gives any integer k-th root with x arrow ((k-1)x + n/x^{k-1})/k.

    Compare against int(n ** (1/3)) for n near 10^{18}: the floating-point version is off by one for many inputs, and Python's math.isqrt (added in 3.8) exists precisely because of this.

  12. Program

    Solve a system of non-linear equations with multivariate Newton.

    Solution
    import numpy as np
def newton_system(F, J, x0, iters=50, tol=1e-12):
    x = np.array(x0, dtype=float)
    for _ in range(iters):
        Fx = np.array(F(x), dtype=float)
        if np.linalg.norm(Fx) < tol: return x
        Jx = np.array(J(x), dtype=float)
        # SOLVE, do not invert — Chapter 44
        dx = np.linalg.solve(Jx, -Fx)
        x = x + dx
        if np.linalg.norm(dx) < tol * max(1.0, np.linalg.norm(x)): return x
    return x

    Each step solves JΔ x = -F at O(n³) — using solve rather than forming J^{-1}, which is both slower and less accurate (Chapter 44 problem 13).

    Convergence is quadratic near a solution where J is non-singular, and the same failure modes as the scalar case apply, amplified: a near-singular Jacobian makes the step enormous.

    Practical safeguards: a line search (accept the step only if ‖F‖ decreases, else halve it), and a Levenberg–Marquardt damping (J^TJ+λ I)Δ x = -J^TF that interpolates between Newton (λ\to0) and gradient descent (λ large). Quasi-Newton methods (Broyden, BFGS) approximate J from successive evaluations, avoiding the derivative entirely.

  13. Program

    Compare deterministic and Monte Carlo integration as the dimension grows.

    Solution
    import random, math, itertools
def product_rule(f, d, n):
    """trapezoid product rule: n^d evaluations"""
    h = 1.0/n
    total = 0.0
    for idx in itertools.product(range(n+1), repeat=d):
        w = 1.0
        for i in idx: w *= 0.5 if i in (0, n) else 1.0
        total += w * f([i*h for i in idx])
    return total * h**d

def monte_carlo(f, d, N):
    return sum(f([random.random() for _ in range(d)]) for _ in range(N)) / N

f = lambda x: math.exp(-sum(v*v for v in x))
for d in (1, 2, 4, 8, 16):
    print(d, product_rule(f, d, 8), monte_carlo(f, d, 8**min(d,5)))

    At d=1 the product rule is far more accurate for the same budget. By d=8 it needs 9^8 = 43 million evaluations for the same nodes-per-dimension, and Monte Carlo with a fraction of that is competitive. Beyond d≈10 the product rule is simply infeasible.

    That is the curse of dimensionality made concrete: the same accuracy per dimension costs exponentially more total work, while Monte Carlo's O(N^{-1/2}) does not notice the dimension at all.

    Add a Sobol sequence for comparison and observe the quasi-Monte Carlo rate sitting between the two.

  14. Program

    Implement gradient descent with a line search and compare to Newton on a badly-conditioned quadratic.

    Solution
    import numpy as np
def gradient_descent(f, grad, x0, iters=10000, tol=1e-10):
    x = np.array(x0, dtype=float)
    for i in range(iters):
        g = np.array(grad(x))
        if np.linalg.norm(g) < tol: return x, i
        t = 1.0                                    # backtracking line search
        fx = f(x)
        while f(x - t*g) > fx - 0.5*t*g.dot(g) and t > 1e-20:
            t *= 0.5
        x = x - t*g
    return x, iters

# f(x, y) = x² + 100y²  — condition number 100
f    = lambda v: v[0]**2 + 100*v[1]**2
grad = lambda v: [2*v[0], 200*v[1]]

    Gradient descent on this needs hundreds of iterations, zig-zagging across the narrow valley; Newton converges in one step, because the function is its own quadratic model.

    The convergence rate of gradient descent is ((κ-1)/(κ+1))^2 per step for a quadratic with condition number κ — so κ=100 gives a factor of 0.96 per step, needing about 400 iterations for 10^{-8}.

    The practical middle ground: L-BFGS approximates the Hessian from a few recent gradients, achieving near-Newton convergence at gradient-descent cost per step, and is what most optimisation libraries use for smooth problems. For very high dimensions where even that is too much memory, momentum and Adam approximate the same effect stochastically.

Chapter 68

Information theory: entropy and coding bounds

Entropy is the average number of bits needed to identify an outcome, and it is a hard floor on compression. The same quantity bounds decision-tree depth, database index size and the number of comparisons a sort requires.

H(X) = −Σ p(x) log₂ p(x) entropy, in BITS H = 0 a certain outcome carries no information H = log₂ n uniform over n outcomes — the maximum H(fair coin) = 1 H(p=0.9) = 0.469 H(fair die) = log₂6 ≈ 2.585 JOINT H(X,Y) = −Σ p(x,y) log p(x,y) CONDITIONAL H(Y|X) = H(X,Y) − H(X) ≤ H(Y), with equality iff independent MUTUAL INFO I(X;Y) = H(X) + H(Y) − H(X,Y) = H(Y) − H(Y|X) ≥ 0 KL DIVERGENCE D(p‖q) = Σ p log(p/q) ≥ 0 not symmetric, not a metric

The source coding theorem

Shannon: any uniquely decodable code for a source with entropy H has expected length ≥ H bits per symbol, and a code with expected length < H+1 exists.

The lower bound comes from Kraft's inequality: a prefix code with lengths \ell_i exists iff ∑ 2^{-\ell_i}\le1. Minimising ∑ p_i\ell_i subject to that gives \ell_i = -log_2 p_i — and Gibbs' inequality shows no other choice does better.

Huffman coding: optimal, and greedy
Repeatedly merge the two least-frequent symbols into a node whose
frequency is their sum.  The resulting tree's depths are the code lengths.

  O(n log n) with a heap;  O(n) if the frequencies arrive sorted.

OPTIMALITY (exchange argument, Chapter 2):
  In some optimal tree the two least-frequent symbols are siblings at the
  greatest depth — if not, swapping them there does not increase the cost.
  Merging them is therefore safe, and induction finishes.

Expected length:  H ≤ L < H + 1.   The gap is because code lengths are
INTEGERS; arithmetic coding removes it, reaching H + ε.
Principle

Entropy is a floor, not a target. No lossless compressor beats H bits per symbol for that model — so all compression progress comes from better models, not better coders. LZ77 exploits repetition, PPM and context mixing exploit conditional structure, and each lowers the effective entropy rather than beating the bound.

Where the same bound appears

QuestionInformation bound
Comparison sortinglog_2(n!) ≈ nlog_2 n comparisons (Chapter 13)
Searching a sorted arraylog_2 n comparisons
Identifying 1 of n outcomeslog_2 n yes/no questions
Weighing puzzles (3 outcomes/query)log_3 N weighings
Lossless compressionH bits per symbol
Storing a set of k from nlog_2\binom nk bits
Bloom filter (with error ε)nlog_2(1/ε) bits — beats exact storage
Twenty Questions20 bits, so 10⁶ objects

The Bloom filter row is the interesting one: allowing a false-positive rate ε drops the requirement from log_2C(U,n) bits to 1.44nlog_2(1/ε) — independent of the universe size. That is the information-theoretic reason approximate membership is so much cheaper than exact.

Interview angle

"How many weighings to find the odd coin among 12?" is ⌈log_3 24⌉ = 3, because each weighing has three outcomes and there are 24 answers (which coin, and heavy or light). Deriving the bound before constructing the scheme is the mark of understanding — and it immediately tells you 13 coins is the true maximum.

Problem set — 14 problemstheory & programming
  1. Theory

    Prove that entropy is maximised by the uniform distribution.

    Solution

    By Gibbs' inequality (or Jensen applied to the concave log), for any distribution p on n outcomes and the uniform q:

    D(p‖q) = ∑ p_ilog(p_i)/(1/n) = log n - H(p) ≥ 0,

    with equality iff p = q. So H(p)≤log_2 n with equality exactly for the uniform distribution. ∎

    The non-negativity of KL divergence follows from Jensen: -D(p‖q) = ∑ plog(q/p) ≤ log∑ p·(q/p) = log 1 = 0.

    Interpretation: uncertainty is greatest when nothing is known, and any structure — any deviation from uniform — reduces the bits needed. That is exactly why compression works: real data is far from uniform.

  2. Theory

    State and prove Kraft's inequality.

    Solution

    Kraft: a binary prefix code with lengths \ell_1,…,\ell_n exists iff ∑_i 2^{-\ell_i}\le1.

    (⟹) Embed the code in an infinite binary tree. A codeword of length \ell occupies a node at depth \ell, and the prefix property means no codeword is an ancestor of another — so their subtrees are disjoint. A depth-\ell subtree contains a fraction 2^{-\ell} of the leaves at any deeper level, and disjointness forces the fractions to sum to at most 1.

    (⟸) Sort the lengths increasing and assign codewords greedily in binary-counter order, each time skipping past the subtree just consumed. The inequality guarantees there is always room. ∎

    Consequence: minimising ∑ p_i\ell_i subject to Kraft gives \ell_i = -log_2 p_i by Lagrange multipliers, and the resulting cost is exactly H. Rounding up to integers gives Shannon–Fano coding with L < H+1.

    McMillan's theorem extends the inequality to all uniquely decodable codes, not just prefix ones — so prefix codes lose nothing.

  3. Theory

    Prove that Huffman coding is optimal.

    Solution

    Lemma: some optimal prefix code has the two least-frequent symbols x, y as siblings at maximum depth.

    Why: in an optimal tree, the two deepest leaves are siblings (an unpaired deepest leaf could be moved up). If they are not x and y, swap them with x and y — the cost change is (p_x-p_a)(\ell_a-\ell_x)\le0 since p_x≤ p_a and \ell_a≥\ell_x. So the swap does not increase the cost. ∎

    Induction: merging x and y into a symbol of weight p_x+p_y reduces the alphabet by one, and the cost of any tree relates to the merged tree's cost by exactly p_x+p_y — a constant. So an optimal tree for the merged problem yields an optimal tree for the original. ∎

    This is an exchange argument (Chapter 2 problem 8), the standard shape for proving a greedy algorithm optimal.

    Note the limits: Huffman is optimal among symbol codes with integer lengths. Its redundancy is at most p_{max}+0.086 bits per symbol, which is significant for skewed alphabets — a symbol with probability 0.9 needs 0.15 bits but gets 1.

  4. Theory

    Show that the comparison-sort lower bound is an entropy argument.

    Solution

    A sorting algorithm must distinguish n! permutations. Each comparison yields at most 1 bit (two outcomes), so at least log_2(n!) comparisons are needed — the decision-tree bound of Chapter 13.

    As entropy: the output is uniform over n! possibilities, so H = log_2(n!) bits must be extracted, and each comparison supplies at most H(outcome) ≤ 1 bit. ∎

    The entropy framing generalises immediately:

    • If the input is partially sorted, the output entropy is lower and fewer comparisons suffice — which is exactly what adaptive sorts like Timsort exploit.
    • A comparison with a biased outcome distribution supplies less than 1 bit, so an algorithm making predictable comparisons is wasteful.
    • Three-way comparisons supply log_2 3 bits, giving the bound log_3(n!) — which is why ternary comparisons help.

    Radix sort escapes because reading a b-bit key supplies b bits at once, not 1.

  5. Theory

    Compute the entropy of English text at several model orders and interpret the numbers.

    Solution
    Uniform over 27 symbols log₂27 = 4.75 bits/char Order-0 (letter frequencies) ≈ 4.14 bits/char Order-1 (given the previous) ≈ 3.56 Order-2 ≈ 3.3 Order-3 ≈ 3.1 Shannon's human experiments ≈ 1.0–1.3 bits/char Modern neural language models ≈ 0.6–1.0 bits/char

    Each additional order of context lowers the conditional entropy, because H(X|Y)≤ H(X) always (conditioning never increases entropy).

    Interpretation: gzip achieves about 2 bits/char on English, PPM and modern context-mixing compressors about 1.5, and large language models under 1. The gap between 4.14 and 1.0 is entirely a modelling gap — the coder is already optimal for its model.

    This is the practical content of the chapter's Principle box: compression research is model research. Shannon's 1951 estimate of 1 bit/char, obtained by having humans guess the next letter, was a prediction of what a perfect model could achieve — and it took 60 years to approach it.

  6. Theory

    Derive the optimal Bloom filter parameters from an information-theoretic viewpoint.

    Solution

    With m bits, n items and k hash functions, a bit is 0 with probability (1-1/m)^{kn}≈ e^{-kn/m}, so the false-positive rate is

    ε ≈ (1-e^{-kn/m})^k.

    Minimising over k gives k^* = \frac mnln2 and ε = 2^{-k^*}, hence

    m = -(nlnε)/((ln2)²) ≈ 1.44nlog_2(1/ε) bits.

    ≈ 9.6 bits per element for ε = 1%. ∎

    The information-theoretic bound for approximate membership is nlog_2(1/ε) bits, so a Bloom filter is within a factor of 1/ln2 = 1.44 of optimal. Cuckoo filters and quotient filters close most of that gap.

    The striking part is what is absent: the universe size U. Exact membership needs log_2\binom Un ≈ nlog_2(U/n) bits, which grows with U. Accepting a 1% error makes the cost independent of how large the keys are — which is why Bloom filters are used for URLs, hashes and arbitrary strings alike.

  7. Theory

    Define mutual information and explain its use in feature selection and decision trees.

    Solution

    I(X;Y) = H(X)-H(X|Y) = H(Y)-H(Y|X) = D(p_{XY}‖p_Xp_Y) — the reduction in uncertainty about X from learning Y, symmetric and non-negative, zero exactly when X and Y are independent.

    Decision trees: at each node choose the feature maximising I(label;feature) — the "information gain" criterion of ID3 and C4.5. It is exactly "which question tells me the most".

    Feature selection: rank features by I(label;feature), or better by conditional mutual information given the already-selected ones, which avoids picking redundant features.

    The bias worth knowing: raw information gain favours high-cardinality features (an ID column perfectly determines the label and has maximal gain, while generalising not at all). C4.5's gain ratio divides by H(feature) to correct for this — an entropy-based fix for an entropy-based flaw.

  8. Program

    Compute the entropy of a data stream at several model orders.

    Solution
    from collections import Counter, defaultdict
import math
def entropy(counts):
    total = sum(counts.values())
    return -sum(c/total * math.log2(c/total) for c in counts.values() if c)

def conditional_entropy(text, order):
    """H(next | previous `order` symbols)"""
    ctx = defaultdict(Counter)
    for i in range(order, len(text)):
        ctx[text[i-order:i]][text[i]] += 1
    total = sum(sum(c.values()) for c in ctx.values())
    return sum(sum(c.values())/total * entropy(c) for c in ctx.values())

for k in range(5):
    print(k, conditional_entropy(text, k))

    The values decrease with the order, and multiplying by the length gives a lower bound on the compressed size achievable with that model.

    Watch for overfitting: at high orders most contexts are seen once, so the measured conditional entropy tends to 0 — not because the text is predictable but because the model has memorised it. The honest measure holds out data, or adds a smoothing term (Chapter 36's Laplace smoothing).

    Comparing length× H_k against gzip's output size on the same text is illuminating: gzip typically lands between the order-2 and order-3 bounds.

  9. Program

    Implement Huffman coding and compare its length to the entropy bound.

    Solution
    import heapq
from collections import Counter
def huffman(freqs):
    h = [(f, i, s) for i, (s, f) in enumerate(freqs.items())]
    heapq.heapify(h)
    nxt = len(h)
    parent = {}
    while len(h) > 1:
        f1, _, a = heapq.heappop(h)
        f2, _, b = heapq.heappop(h)
        node = ('node', a, b)
        heapq.heappush(h, (f1+f2, nxt, node)); nxt += 1
    _, _, root = h[0]
    codes = {}
    def walk(node, prefix=""):
        if isinstance(node, tuple) and node[0] == 'node':
            walk(node[1], prefix + "0"); walk(node[2], prefix + "1")
        else:
            codes[node] = prefix or "0"          # single-symbol edge case
    walk(root)
    return codes

codes = huffman(freqs)
total = sum(freqs.values())
L = sum(freqs[s]/total * len(c) for s, c in codes.items())
print("Huffman:", L, "entropy:", entropy(freqs), "gap:", L - entropy(freqs))

    The gap is always in [0,1), and is largest for skewed distributions where the ideal length -log_2 p is far from an integer.

    The tie-breaking index in the heap tuple matters — without it, Python compares the node objects and raises. It also makes the tree deterministic, which is necessary if the decoder rebuilds it from the frequencies.

    Edge case: a single distinct symbol gives an empty code; the prefix or "0" guard handles it. That case appears in real data (a run of identical bytes) and crashes naive implementations.

  10. Program

    Implement arithmetic coding and show it beats Huffman on a skewed source.

    Solution
    from fractions import Fraction
def arithmetic_encode(symbols, probs):
    lo, hi = Fraction(0), Fraction(1)
    for s in symbols:
        width = hi - lo
        cum = Fraction(0)
        for t, p in probs.items():
            if t == s: break
            cum += p
        hi = lo + width * (cum + probs[s])
        lo = lo + width * cum
    # the shortest binary fraction strictly inside [lo, hi)
    return shortest_binary_in(lo, hi)

def bits_needed(lo, hi):
    import math
    return math.ceil(-math.log2(hi - lo)) + 1

    Arithmetic coding represents the entire message as one number in [0,1), so it does not round each symbol to an integer number of bits. Its length is within 2 bits of -log_2 P(message), giving H+ε per symbol rather than Huffman's H+1.

    The gain is largest for skewed sources: with P(a)=0.9, entropy is 0.469 bits/symbol, Huffman must spend 1, and arithmetic coding achieves 0.47 — a 2× improvement.

    Real implementations use fixed-point arithmetic with renormalisation rather than Fraction, emitting bits as the interval narrows so memory stays constant. Range coding is the byte-oriented variant used in modern compressors, and asymmetric numeral systems (ANS) achieves the same compression with far simpler arithmetic, which is why it now underlies zstd and LZFSE.

  11. Program

    Solve a weighing puzzle using the information bound to determine the minimum number of weighings.

    Solution
    import math
def min_weighings(n_coins, know_direction=True):
    """n coins, one counterfeit; a balance has 3 outcomes per weighing"""
    outcomes = 2*n_coins if know_direction else n_coins
    return math.ceil(math.log(outcomes, 3))

print(min_weighings(12))     # 3:  log₃24 = 2.89 → 3
print(min_weighings(13))     # 3:  log₃26 = 2.97 → 3  (the true maximum)
print(min_weighings(14))     # 4:  log₃28 = 3.03 → 4

    Each weighing has three outcomes (left, right, balanced), so k weighings distinguish at most 3^k cases. With 12 coins and the direction unknown there are 24 answers, and 3³=27\ge24 — so 3 suffices, and the bound also proves 2 cannot.

    13 coins is the maximum for 3 weighings when the direction must be determined (26 answers). With a known-good reference coin available, 14 is achievable.

    The construction is a non-adaptive assignment of each coin to a distinct sequence in {L,R,off}^3, avoiding sequences and their reverses (Chapter 13 problem 13) — and the bound tells you exactly how much slack you have.

  12. Program

    Measure the compression ratio of several algorithms and compare against the order-k entropy.

    Solution
    import gzip, bz2, lzma, math
def compare(data):
    n = len(data)
    print("raw       ", n)
    for name, mod in (("gzip", gzip), ("bz2", bz2), ("lzma", lzma)):
        print(name, len(mod.compress(data)))
    for k in range(4):
        h = conditional_entropy(data, k)
        print(f"order-{k} bound", math.ceil(n * h / 8), "bytes")

    On English text, gzip typically lands near the order-2 bound, bz2 near order-3, and lzma below it — because LZ-family algorithms exploit long-range repetition, which a fixed-order Markov model does not capture, so they can beat the order-k bound without violating anything.

    On random data all three produce output slightly larger than the input, which is Chapter 6's counting argument made visible: no compressor shrinks every input, and the overhead is the format's header.

    That experiment is worth running once — it makes concrete both that entropy is a real floor for a given model and that better models, not better coders, are where compression gains come from.

  13. Program

    Implement mutual-information-based feature ranking and demonstrate the high-cardinality bias.

    Solution
    from collections import Counter, defaultdict
import math
def mutual_information(xs, ys):
    n = len(xs)
    px, py = Counter(xs), Counter(ys)
    pxy = Counter(zip(xs, ys))
    return sum(c/n * math.log2((c/n) / ((px[x]/n)*(py[y]/n)))
               for (x, y), c in pxy.items())

def gain_ratio(xs, ys):
    hx = entropy(Counter(xs))
    return mutual_information(xs, ys) / hx if hx else 0.0

# demonstrate the bias
labels = [random.randint(0,1) for _ in range(1000)]
useful = [l if random.random() < 0.8 else 1-l for l in labels]   # 80% predictive
ident  = list(range(1000))                                        # useless ID
print("useful MI", mutual_information(useful, labels))
print("ID     MI", mutual_information(ident,  labels))    # MAXIMAL, and useless
print("useful GR", gain_ratio(useful, labels))
print("ID     GR", gain_ratio(ident,  labels))            # correctly tiny

    The ID column achieves maximal mutual information — it determines the label perfectly on the training data — while carrying no generalisable signal at all. Raw information gain ranks it first.

    The gain ratio divides by H(feature), which is log_2 1000 ≈ 10 for the ID and 1 for a binary feature, correctly demoting it.

    This is why C4.5 uses gain ratio and why any feature-selection pipeline must either penalise cardinality or evaluate on held-out data. It is the information-theoretic face of overfitting.

  14. Program

    Estimate the entropy of a stream in bounded memory using a sketch.

    Solution
    # Exact entropy needs the full frequency table — O(distinct) memory.
# For a stream with too many distinct values, estimate instead:
#
# 1. Count–Min sketch (Chapter 38) gives approximate frequencies,
#    but its one-sided error biases the entropy DOWNWARD.
# 2. The Chakrabarti–Cormode–McGregor sketch estimates H to (1±ε)
#    in O(ε⁻² log n) space, using the identity
#       H = E[log(n / r)]   where r is the "run length" of a sampled position
def ccm_entropy_estimate(stream, samples=1000):
    import random
    n = len(stream)
    est = 0.0
    for _ in range(samples):
        i = random.randrange(n)
        s = stream[i]
        r = sum(1 for j in range(i, n) if stream[j] == s)   # count after i
        est += math.log2(n / r)
    return est / samples

    The estimator works because sampling a position and counting subsequent occurrences of that symbol gives an unbiased handle on -log p — the "surprisal" whose expectation is the entropy.

    The streaming version maintains the counts incrementally rather than rescanning, keeping memory at O(samples) regardless of the number of distinct symbols.

    Compare against exact entropy on a stream small enough to hold: the estimate should be within a few percent with 1,000 samples, and the error should shrink as 1/√{samples} — the Monte Carlo rate of Chapter 36, appearing again.

Chapter 69

Cryptographic mathematics

Public-key cryptography rests on a handful of problems believed hard - factoring, discrete log, lattice problems - and on one asymmetry: verifying is easy, finding is not. Every chapter of this part reappears here.

THE HARD PROBLEMS (believed, not proven) Integer factorisation RSA Ch. 23 Discrete logarithm in ℤ_p* Diffie–Hellman, DSA Ch. 24 Elliptic-curve discrete log ECDH, ECDSA, Ed25519 — best known: √n Shortest vector in a lattice post-quantum (Kyber) — quantum-resistant KEY SIZES for ~128-bit security symmetric (AES) 128 bits elliptic curve 256 bits RSA / finite-field DH 3072 bits — index calculus is subexponential lattice (Kyber-768) ~1.2 KB keys Shor's algorithm breaks factoring AND both discrete logs in polynomial time on a quantum computer. Lattice problems are the leading replacement.

RSA

The whole scheme, and where each chapter enters
KEYGEN   p, q large primes               Miller–Rabin        (Ch. 23)
         n = pq,  φ(n) = (p−1)(q−1)      Euler's totient     (Ch. 20)
         e = 65537,  d = e⁻¹ mod φ(n)    extended Euclid     (Ch. 15)

ENCRYPT  c = m^e mod n                   binary exponentiation (Ch. 21)
DECRYPT  m = c^d mod n                   correct by Euler + CRT (Ch. 20, 22)

SPEED-UP decrypt mod p and mod q separately, then CRT — 4× faster (Ch. 22)

SECURITY recovering d from (n, e) is equivalent to factoring n.
         "Textbook RSA" as written above is INSECURE — it is deterministic,
         malleable (c₁c₂ decrypts to m₁m₂), and leaks for small m.
         Real RSA uses OAEP padding; signatures use PSS.
Principle

Every scheme here is correct by elementary number theory and secure only by conjecture. The correctness proofs in this chapter are complete; the security arguments are reductions — "breaking this is at least as hard as factoring" — and factoring's hardness has never been proved. Knowing which half of a cryptographic claim is a theorem is the point.

Diffie–Hellman and elliptic curves

DIFFIE–HELLMAN Alice sends g^a, Bob sends g^b, both compute g^{ab} security: computing g^{ab} from (g, g^a, g^b) — the CDH problem UNAUTHENTICATED: trivially man-in-the-middleable, which is why TLS signs the parameters. Validate received elements (Ch. 24 problem 13). ELLIPTIC CURVES y² = x³ + ax + b over 𝔽_p, with a group law on points The same protocols with a different group. Best known attack is Pollard rho at O(√n) — no index calculus — so 256-bit keys suffice where finite-field DH needs 3072. Curve25519: p = 2²⁵⁵ − 19, a Montgomery curve chosen for constant-time implementation and no invalid-curve attacks.

Hash functions

PropertyRequirementAttack cost
Preimage resistancegiven h, find m2^n
Second preimagegiven m_1, find m_22^n
Collision resistancefind any m_1≠ m_22^{n/2} (birthday, Ch. 6)

The birthday bound is why collision resistance needs twice the output length: SHA-256 gives 128-bit collision resistance, and MD5's 128 bits gave only 64 — which is why practical MD5 collisions were found in 2004 and chosen-prefix collisions in 2019.

Interview angle

"Why is RSA slower than AES?" — because it is modular exponentiation on 3072-bit numbers (thousands of multiplications) versus a few dozen table lookups and XORs. That is why TLS uses public-key crypto only to establish a symmetric key, then switches. Naming that hybrid structure is the answer.

Problem set — 14 problemstheory & programming
  1. Theory

    Prove RSA decryption is correct, including when gcd(m,n) > 1.

    Solution

    With n = pq and ed ≡ 1 (mod φ(n)), write ed = 1 + k(p-1)(q-1).

    Modulo p: if p | m then both sides are ≡ 0. Otherwise Fermat gives m^{p-1}≡1, so

    m^{ed} = m·(m^{p-1})^{k(q-1)} ≡ m ±od p.

    Modulo q: symmetric.

    Agreeing modulo both primes, CRT gives m^{ed}≡ m ±od n for every m. ∎

    The non-coprime case matters: it means RSA is correct for all messages, not just those coprime to n. (Encountering an m sharing a factor with n would itself reveal the factorisation, so it never happens for random messages — but the correctness proof should not depend on that.)

  2. Theory

    Explain why textbook RSA is insecure and what padding fixes.

    Solution
    • Deterministic: the same plaintext always gives the same ciphertext, so an attacker can build a dictionary. For a small message space (a yes/no vote, a credit-card number) this breaks it entirely.
    • Malleable: c_1c_2 = (m_1m_2)^e, so ciphertexts can be combined. This enables a chosen-ciphertext attack: to decrypt c, submit c· r^e for random r, obtain mr, and divide.
    • Small message / small exponent: if m^e < n there is no modular reduction at all and m is recovered by an integer e-th root. With e=3 and a 128-bit message under a 2048-bit modulus, this is immediate.
    • Håstad's broadcast attack: the same m sent to e recipients with exponent e is recovered by CRT plus an integer root.

    OAEP fixes all of these: it pads m with randomness and hashes through a Feistel-like construction, making the encryption randomised and non-malleable, with a security proof in the random-oracle model.

    The lesson generalises: a scheme's mathematical correctness says nothing about its security as a protocol.

  3. Theory

    Describe Diffie–Hellman and the man-in-the-middle attack.

    Solution

    Alice picks a, sends g^a; Bob picks b, sends g^b; both compute g^{ab}. An eavesdropper sees g, g^a, g^b and must solve the computational Diffie–Hellman problem, believed as hard as discrete log.

    The attack: Mallory intercepts both messages, sends her own g^m to each side, and establishes two separate keys — g^{am} with Alice and g^{bm} with Bob. She decrypts, reads, re-encrypts and forwards. Neither party can detect it.

    The fix is authentication, not more mathematics: TLS signs the DH parameters with a certificate chain, SSH pins the host key on first use, and Signal uses long-term identity keys. ∎

    Two further requirements from Chapter 24: p-1 must have a large prime factor (else Pohlig–Hellman), and received elements must be validated to lie in the correct subgroup (else small-subgroup confinement). Both have caused real vulnerabilities.

  4. Theory

    Explain why elliptic curves allow much shorter keys than finite-field discrete log.

    Solution

    For discrete log in ℤ_p^×, the index calculus method runs in subexponential time L_p[1/3, 1.92] — it exploits the fact that integers factor into small primes, building relations over a factor base.

    Elliptic curve groups have no such structure: there is no notion of a "smooth" point, so no factor base exists and index calculus does not apply. The best known attack is generic — Pollard's rho at O(√n).

    Consequently a 256-bit curve gives 2^{128} security, matching AES-128, while finite-field DH needs 3072 bits for the same. ∎

    The caveats: certain curves are weak — supersingular curves fall to the MOV attack (mapping to a finite field via the Weil pairing), and anomalous curves (where #E = p) fall to Smart's attack in linear time. This is why standardised curves are used rather than freshly generated ones, and why curve parameters are scrutinised for provenance.

  5. Theory

    Explain the birthday bound's role in hash function security.

    Solution

    For an n-bit hash, finding a preimage requires 2^n work (try inputs until one matches). Finding a collision requires only 2^{n/2}, by the birthday bound of Chapter 6: after 1.18·2^{n/2} random hashes, a collision is more likely than not.

    So collision resistance is only half the output length in bits. ∎

    MD5 128 bits → 64-bit collision resistance → broken in 2004 SHA-1 160 bits → 80-bit → broken in 2017 (SHAttered) SHA-256 256 bits → 128-bit → secure SHA-512 512 bits → 256-bit → post-quantum margin

    Grover's quantum algorithm gives a quadratic speed-up on preimages (2^{n/2}) but only a marginal one on collisions, so doubling the hash length restores classical-equivalent security against quantum attacks — which is why SHA-384 and SHA-512 are specified for high-assurance use.

    Where collisions matter: signatures (sign a benign document, present a malicious one with the same hash), certificates, and content-addressed storage. Where they do not: HMAC, which remains secure even with a collision-broken hash.

  6. Theory

    Describe Shor's algorithm at a high level and what it breaks.

    Solution

    To factor n, pick a random a coprime to n and find the multiplicative order r of a modulo n. If r is even and a^{r/2}≢-1, then x = a^{r/2} is a non-trivial square root of 1 and gcd(x-1,n) is a factor (Chapter 22 problem 4). A random a works with probability \ge1/2.

    The quantum part is order-finding: prepare a superposition, apply modular exponentiation, and use the quantum Fourier transform to extract the period in polynomial time — where classically period-finding is as hard as factoring.

    What it breaks: RSA (factoring), Diffie–Hellman and DSA (discrete log), and ECDH/ECDSA (elliptic-curve discrete log — the same period-finding applies). ∎

    What survives: symmetric ciphers and hashes, weakened only quadratically by Grover — so AES-256 and SHA-512 remain adequate. And the post-quantum candidates: lattices (Kyber, Dilithium), hash-based signatures (SPHINCS+), and codes (McEliece).

    The practical concern is harvest now, decrypt later: traffic recorded today can be decrypted when a quantum computer arrives, which is why migration is under way before the threat is real.

  7. Theory

    Explain why constant-time implementation matters and give an example attack.

    Solution

    If the execution time, memory access pattern or power consumption depends on secret data, an attacker who can measure it learns the secret — regardless of the mathematics.

    • Square-and-multiply (Chapter 21): the if (e & 1) branch makes the time depend on the exponent's Hamming weight, and per-iteration measurements can recover individual bits. Practical remote timing attacks on OpenSSL's RSA were demonstrated by Brumley and Boneh in 2003.
    • Table lookups: AES implementations using S-box tables leak the accessed indices through cache timing, recoverable by an unprivileged process on the same machine.
    • Comparison: memcmp on a MAC returns early on the first differing byte, letting an attacker forge a MAC one byte at a time in 256×16 attempts instead of 2^{128}.

    Defences: the Montgomery ladder (Chapter 21) for exponentiation; bitsliced or AES-NI implementations avoiding tables; constant-time comparison that XORs all bytes and checks the accumulated result once; and blinding, which randomises the observable behaviour.

    This is why cryptographic code should never be written from a mathematical description alone.

  8. Program

    Implement RSA end to end with proper key generation, and CRT-accelerated decryption.

    Solution
    import random
def gen_prime(bits):
    while True:
        c = random.getrandbits(bits) | (1 << (bits-1)) | 1
        if any(c % p == 0 for p in SMALL_PRIMES): continue
        if miller_rabin(c, 40): return c

def keygen(bits=1024):
    p, q = gen_prime(bits), gen_prime(bits)
    while p == q: q = gen_prime(bits)
    n, phi = p*q, (p-1)*(q-1)
    e = 65537
    assert math.gcd(e, phi) == 1
    d = pow(e, -1, phi)
    return (n, e), (n, d, p, q, d % (p-1), d % (q-1), pow(q, -1, p))

def decrypt_crt(c, priv):
    n, d, p, q, dp, dq, qinv = priv
    m1, m2 = pow(c % p, dp, p), pow(c % q, dq, q)
    h = (qinv * (m1 - m2)) % p
    m = (m2 + h*q) % n
    assert pow(m, PUB_E, n) == c % n     # verify — guards the Bellcore attack
    return m

    CRT decryption is about 4× faster: two exponentiations with half-size moduli and half-size exponents (Chapter 20 problem 11).

    The verification assertion is not paranoia — it defends against the Bellcore fault attack, where a hardware glitch corrupting one of m_1, m_2 lets gcd(m^e-c, n) reveal a prime factor from a single faulty signature. Re-encrypting before releasing the result costs one cheap exponentiation (e is small) and eliminates it.

    Setting the top bit in gen_prime guarantees the modulus has the full bit length; setting the bottom bit skips evens.

  9. Program
