    Implement Diffie–Hellman with parameter validation, and demonstrate a small-subgroup attack against an implementation that omits it.

    Solution
    def dh_keypair(p, g, q):
    a = random.randrange(2, q)
    return a, pow(g, a, p)

def dh_shared(their_public, my_secret, p, q):
    # VALIDATE: reject 1, p−1, and anything outside the order-q subgroup
    if not (1 < their_public < p-1):
        raise ValueError("out of range")
    if pow(their_public, q, p) != 1:
        raise ValueError("not in the prime-order subgroup")
    return pow(their_public, my_secret, p)

# ATTACK on an implementation that skips validation:
#   send y = p−1 (order 2).  The shared secret is 1 if a is even,
#   p−1 if a is odd — one bit of the private key, per exchange.

    With a safe prime p = 2q+1 the only small subgroup has order 2, so the leak is one bit. With a non-safe prime whose p-1 has many small factors, repeating the attack with elements of order 3, 5, 7, … recovers the key modulo each, and CRT reconstructs it entirely.

    Several TLS and IKE implementations shipped without this check and had practical key-recovery vulnerabilities. The fix is two lines.

    RFC 7919 defines named DH groups precisely so implementations stop generating their own parameters — the parameters themselves are a place where subtle weaknesses hide.

  10. Program

    Implement elliptic curve point addition and scalar multiplication over 𝔽_p.

    Solution
    def ec_add(P, Q, a, p):
    if P is None: return Q
    if Q is None: return P
    x1, y1 = P; x2, y2 = Q
    if x1 == x2 and (y1 + y2) % p == 0: return None      # P + (−P) = O
    if P == Q:
        lam = (3*x1*x1 + a) * pow(2*y1, -1, p) % p       # tangent
    else:
        lam = (y2 - y1) * pow(x2 - x1, -1, p) % p        # chord
    x3 = (lam*lam - x1 - x2) % p
    y3 = (lam*(x1 - x3) - y1) % p
    return (x3, y3)

def ec_mul(k, P, a, p):
    """double-and-add — NOT constant time; use a ladder for real keys"""
    R = None
    while k:
        if k & 1: R = ec_add(R, P, a, p)
        P = ec_add(P, P, a, p)
        k >>= 1
    return R

    The group law is the chord-and-tangent construction: three collinear points on the curve sum to the identity, which is the point at infinity (represented here as None).

    Each addition needs a modular inverse — expensive. Real implementations use projective coordinates to defer inversions, doing one at the end instead of one per operation, which is a 10–20× speed-up.

    ec_mul as written leaks the scalar through timing. Use the Montgomery ladder (Chapter 21), and verify that y² ≡ x³+ax+b for every received point — an invalid-curve attack feeds a point from a weaker curve and recovers the key from the resulting arithmetic.

  11. Program

    Implement Shamir secret sharing and verify its information-theoretic security empirically.

    Solution
    import random
P = (1 << 127) - 1
def split(secret, n, k):
    coeffs = [secret] + [random.randrange(P) for _ in range(k-1)]
    ev = lambda x: sum(c * pow(x, i, P) for i, c in enumerate(coeffs)) % P
    return [(i, ev(i)) for i in range(1, n+1)]

def reconstruct(shares):
    s = 0
    for i, (xi, yi) in enumerate(shares):
        num = den = 1
        for j, (xj, _) in enumerate(shares):
            if i != j:
                num = num * (-xj) % P
                den = den * (xi - xj) % P
        s = (s + yi * num % P * pow(den, -1, P)) % P
    return s

# security: with k−1 shares, EVERY secret remains equally likely
fixed = split(42, 5, 3)[:2]
implied = set()
for guess in range(1000):
    implied.add(reconstruct(fixed + [(99, ...)]))    # any 3rd share is consistent

    The security demonstration: hold k-1 shares fixed and vary the missing one over the field. Every candidate secret arises exactly once, so the shares carry zero information — H(secret| k-1 shares) = H(secret) in the language of Chapter 68.

    That is information-theoretic security, unlike RSA's computational security. No amount of computation helps, and it does not depend on any unproven hardness assumption.

    The price: shares are as large as the secret, and there is no integrity — a corrupted share silently produces a wrong reconstruction. Verifiable secret sharing (Feldman, Pedersen) adds commitments to detect that.

  12. Program

    Implement a constant-time comparison and demonstrate a timing attack against the naive version.

    Solution
    import hmac, time
def naive_equal(a, b):
    if len(a) != len(b): return False
    for x, y in zip(a, b):
        if x != y: return False              # EARLY RETURN — leaks the position
    return True

def constant_time_equal(a, b):
    if len(a) != len(b): return False
    r = 0
    for x, y in zip(a, b): r |= x ^ y        # no branch, always full length
    return r == 0
# or simply: hmac.compare_digest(a, b)

# the attack: guess byte by byte, timing each candidate
def forge(target_len, oracle):
    guess = bytearray(target_len)
    for pos in range(target_len):
        best, best_t = 0, -1
        for b in range(256):
            guess[pos] = b
            t = min(time_call(oracle, bytes(guess)) for _ in range(200))
            if t > best_t: best_t, best = t, b
        guess[pos] = best
    return bytes(guess)

    The naive comparison returns on the first mismatch, so a correct prefix takes measurably longer. The attack recovers a 16-byte MAC in 16×256 = 4096 guesses instead of 2^{128}.

    The timing difference is nanoseconds and buried in noise, which is why the attack takes the minimum over many trials — noise only ever adds time, so the minimum is the cleanest signal. Remote versions using statistical methods have been demonstrated across a network.

    Use the library function: hmac.compare_digest in Python, CRYPTO_memcmp in OpenSSL. A hand-written constant-time comparison can still be defeated by compiler optimisation turning it back into a branch.

  13. Program

    Estimate the cost of factoring an RSA modulus of various sizes and derive the recommended key length.

    Solution
    import math
def gnfs_cost_bits(n_bits):
    """log2 of the general number field sieve's operation count
       L_n[1/3, (64/9)^{1/3}] with c ≈ 1.923"""
    lnn = n_bits * math.log(2)
    lnlnn = math.log(lnn)
    return 1.923 * (lnn ** (1/3)) * (lnlnn ** (2/3)) / math.log(2)

for bits in (512, 768, 1024, 2048, 3072, 4096, 15360):
    print(bits, round(gnfs_cost_bits(bits), 1), "bits of security")
    RSA bits security status 512 ~50 factored in 1999 768 ~62 factored in 2009 (RSA-768) 1024 ~72 never publicly factored; assumed within state reach 2048 ~93 current minimum 3072 ~112 ≈ AES-128 equivalent — NIST recommendation 15360 ~256 ≈ AES-256 equivalent — impractical

    The subexponential growth is the point: doubling the key size does not double the security. Going from 2048 to 3072 bits adds only about 19 bits of security, and reaching AES-256 equivalence would need a 15,360-bit modulus.

    That poor scaling is precisely why elliptic curves won: EC security is n/2 bits for an n-bit curve — linear — so 256 bits gives 128-bit security and 512 gives 256.

    Cross-check the model against the RSA-768 and RSA-250 factorisation records: the formula should place them near the effort actually expended, which it does to within a small constant.

  14. Program

    Build a small end-to-end hybrid encryption scheme and identify every assumption it rests on.

    Solution
    import os, hashlib, hmac
def hybrid_encrypt(message, recipient_pub):
    # 1. random symmetric key
    k = os.urandom(32)                                  # CSPRNG, not random()
    # 2. wrap it with the public key (use OAEP in production)
    wrapped = rsa_oaep_encrypt(k, recipient_pub)
    # 3. encrypt the payload symmetrically, WITH authentication
    nonce = os.urandom(12)
    ct = aes_gcm_encrypt(k, nonce, message)             # AEAD: encrypt + MAC
    return wrapped, nonce, ct

def hybrid_decrypt(wrapped, nonce, ct, recipient_priv):
    k = rsa_oaep_decrypt(wrapped, recipient_priv)
    return aes_gcm_decrypt(k, nonce, ct)                # raises on a bad tag

    The assumptions, each of which can fail independently:

    • Factoring is hard — unproven, and false on a quantum computer.
    • AES is a good pseudorandom permutation — unproven, but heavily analysed.
    • The CSPRNG is unpredictable — the most common real failure. Debian's 2008 OpenSSL bug reduced the key space to 32,768; Android's 2013 SecureRandom flaw let Bitcoin keys be recovered.
    • The implementation is constant-time — problem 12.
    • The recipient's public key is authentic — problem 3; without a PKI or pinning, the whole thing is man-in-the-middleable.
    • The nonce never repeats — GCM nonce reuse is catastrophic, revealing the authentication key.

    Encrypt-then-MAC, always, and prefer an AEAD mode that does it for you. The mathematics in this book is the easy part; every one of the failures above is an engineering failure, and each has caused real breaches.
